Joan of England surviving and marrying Pedro) or more decisive battle of Najera (with Henry being killed or captured in battle). The former is definitely plausible, but would alter 1350s and 1360s quite a bit, while the later doesn’t strike me as all that consequential (after all in 1367 Henry has a son as well as two brothers who could potentially lead the Trastamara party to victory even without Henry). IMHO the main reason for Pedro losing the Castilian Civil War were not particular mistakes on his part or successful moves on Henry’s, but rather the military dominance of du Guesclin’s routier army over Castilian one. So, if we want Pedro to retain his throne, we need to either occupy or counterbalance routiers until the Caroline Phase of the Hundred Years’ War starts. The latter was successfully done IOTL with the help of Edward the Black Prince in 1367, but the relations between Pedro and Edward quickly deteriorated mainly because Edward didn’t receive his pay as per treaty of Libourne and thus Pedro was left to his own devices in 1368-1369 and was defeated and killed. Presumably Pedro didn’t pay Edward simply because he was unable to raise such an enormous sum. The PoD I present is Pedro marrying Philippa of Clarence as part of negotiations with English. Philippa is the eldest granddaughter of Edward III and has just reached marriageable age in 1367. IOTL, she married Edmund Mortimer but of course king of Castile is a way more prestigious match (there are conflicting records about when exactly Philippa was betrothed to Edmund IOTL, but for the purpose of this PoD let us pick the latest option 1368). Pedro on the other hand is in his thirties, has not legitimate issue and both his wife and his beloved mistress are dead since 1361. The purpose of the marriage is twofold: firstly, to bring Castile closer to England and secondly to be a neat way to subsidize Edward’s expedition. I am not sure how large Philippa’s dowry was IOTL, but presumably if she has a royal marriage, it definitely should be quite large. So Edward’s army can at least partly be subsidized with his niece’s dowry. I am not sure if such an arrangement is plausible, but if it does happen consequences are massive. Presumably if the relationship between the Black Prince and Pedro is unstrained (or at least is significantly better than IOTL), the second invasion of Henry and de Guesclin would seem futile and probably doesn’t happen. In 1369 the Caroline Phase begins (even if IOTL Charles V summoned Edward because he already realized that Castille would fall to Henry, which is debatable, ITTL Charles presumably understands that Edward would help Pedro no matter what and thus he might as well go on with his plan). Thus, Henry would have very little military support and will stand no chance against Pedro and his allies. Possible consequences of the PoD: 1. Castille itself has a radically different social structure. a. IOTL Henry and his heirs had to give out large parts of royal domain for their supporters from lesser nobility that formed new aristocratic elites (since pedristas were active until mid-1380s Trastamaras needed their continous support for an extended period of time and thus royal domain suffered greatly). Quoting from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: The new dynasty came to power having given lavish grants and titles to supporting nobles, and territorial concessions to their royal allies in France and the Crown of Aragon. Henry II’s initial hold on the crown was a tentative one. New men came to the fore demanding a share of the victory, and the king also granted them substantial privileges and lands. Historians have long argued that the first decades of Trastámara rule witnessed the disappearance of the old nobility, a nobility dating to the late eleventh and twelfth centuries, and its replacement by a new nobility. In reality, the transformation was signaled by the rise to prominence of lesser branches of the great old noble houses, with a few new lesser nobles rising to very high status. This promotion in rank was tied to the granting of large estates and to extensive royal privileges. Such erosion of the royal domain and authority had, in turn, disastrous consequences for Castile over the next hundred years. Not unlike France or England in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the rise of the nobility led to waves of violence and instability. Securely grounded in their new economic power and high standing, the Castilian nobility challenged royal authority and even coveted, as was the case in the reigns of John II and Henry IV, the control of the Crown. Pedro unlike Henry is a legitimate king and thus doesn’t need such drastic measures to obtain necessary support. b. In the first half of XIV century one of the main pillars of royal power was municipal nobility (or more precisely non-noble municipal knights). At first kings bought their support against magnates by granting municipal knights’ extensive privileges, but since the latter felt constant pressure by disenfranchised bourgeoisie, they continuously welcomed royal entrenchment in cities and thus by 1340s urban centers were under firm royal control. Once again, quote from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: In less than 50 years the non-noble knights monopolized municipal offices in most Castilian cities, bought most of the land around the cities, and gained control, as they did in Burgos and Avila, of the most important ecclesiastical benefices. In return the king hoped for, and often received, their military support against the magnates and access to the cities’ fiscal resources. Moreover, as the non-noble knights gained control of their respective cities, they came into conflict with those below them. Pressured from below by the disfranchised petite bourgeoisie, the non-noble knights welcomed royal interference in the affairs of the cities and, by the 1340s, the takeover of municipal administration by royal officials (the regimiento) became a political reality. For a brief period, royal control of the urban centers became one of the most significant gains of the Castilian monarchy, but then the disorders of the late fourteenth century weakened royal control anew. IOTL many cities supported Pedro against Henry and thus were severely punished by victorious Trastamaras which greatly weakened both cities themselves and royal control over them. Thus, if Pedro retains his throne Castile is a lot more centralized with a strong royal power based on resources from a reasonably large royal domain as well as prosperous cities under firm royal control which is a stark contrast to magnate-dominated early Trastamara Spain. 2. Pedro IOTL had a firm alliance with Portugal. His uncle Pedro of Portugal helped him in his wars against both Peter of Aragon and Henry of Trastamara. When Pedro of Castile was slain, it was Portugal that was the main base for anti-Trastamara action in Iberia. Ferdinand of Portugal, Pedro of Castile’s cousin waged several wars against Trastamaras (first claiming the crown of Castile in his own right, later supporting John of Gaunt’s claim). Pedro of course is a very strong clamant to Portuguese throne in his own right, but he can further cement his claim by marrying Beatrice of Portugal to his son (who presumably should be born in early to mid 1370s roughly similarly to OTL Roger Mortimer birth date and thus ideally match Beatrice). Moreover, before Trastamara coup Portugal and Castile had the same allies and aligned economic interests (both benefited greatly from maritime trade between Northern Europe and Mediterranean, both had Genoa as a most important trade partner and England as a main ally outside of Iberia). IOTL when Portuguese interregnum happened the nobility was split with a significant portion of it supporting Trastamara claim. It were municipal elites of 4 main Portuguese cities (Lisbon, Porto, Coimba and Evora) that bankrolled anti-Trastamara faction. The main reason for these was economic (i. e. retention of profitable maritime trade with Genoa, England etc.) as well as desire to cancel Ferdinand’s pro-noble reforms (which were conducted in order to fund extremely expensive campaigns against Castille). If IOTL Pedro continues to rule Castille, Portuguese municipal elites have no reason to dislike the union with neighboring kingdom (because Ferdinan’s reforms would be unnecessary and Castile and Portugal economic and political interest would continue to be closely aligned) and thus we can encounter Castilian-Portugese union in 1380s. 3. Pedro had an advantage in the War of Two Peters against Peter of Aragon. Presumably if Henry of Trastamara is no longer a threat, he can continue pressing Aragon for economic, political (most important one being the termination of Trastamara support) and perhaps even territorial concessions (getting back Alicante, Elche and Orihuela as part of kingdom of Murcia) 4. If Pedro marries Philippa, presumably John Gaunt and Edmund Langley would have alternative brides. IOTL the marriages happened to establish a claim over kingdom of Castile. ITTL Pedro would have legitimate heirs related to English royal family without such a match and thus daughters of Peter with at best debatable legitimacy are not ideal brides for English prices. Does anybody have suggestions who John and Edmund would marry in such a scenario? 5. Perhaps the most consequential consequence of the PoD is alternative Caroline Phase of HYW. The battle of La Rochelle that crippled English fleet IOTL was won by Castilian navy. If Castile continues to be an English ally, Castilian navy either doesn’t participate or participates on English side. Thus, English are able to get significant reinforcements to Poitou and Saintonge as well as £12,000 that were supposed to be used to pay for service of local troops (IOTL this booty fell to the hands of Castilians). This potentially a least allows English to retain control over Poitou, Saintonge and Angoumois and perhaps even reverse some French gains made in previous years. Moreover with English fleet still dominating the waters around France, the main reason for the disastrous Great Chevauchee of 1373 is gone. ITTL, it makes a lot more sense to bring reinforcements by see, as was done in previous years. Thus, the Caroline Phase of HYW can be radically altered in 1372-1373, perhaps to the extent of it being a draw rather than decisive French victory. All these consequences seem rather juicy, but I am not sure if the marriage of Pedro and Philippa is all that plausible. What do you guys think? (of course if you have comments on consequences of PoD rather than the PoD itself, I would be happy to hear those too).
items.model_answer:
If Peter of Castile married an English princess in the 1360s, the most important consequence would be the earlier and firmer alignment of Castile with Plantagenet England against France and its allies. In real history, Peter only became closely tied to England during his civil war with his half-brother Henry of Trastámara, and after Peter’s death his daughters married John of Gaunt and Edmund of Langley, giving the English royal house a later claim to Castile. A marriage in the 1360s would have brought that connection forward, possibly changing both the Castilian civil war and the wider Hundred Years’ War.

The marriage would probably have strengthened Peter diplomatically. He was already under pressure from Castilian nobles, from Aragon, and from French-backed forces supporting Henry of Trastámara. An English princess as queen would have made Peter a formal ally of Edward III and the Black Prince before the crisis reached its peak. That could mean English troops, money, and diplomatic backing arriving earlier, not merely in 1367 at the Battle of Nájera. If the alliance were credible, some Castilian nobles might hesitate before defecting to Henry, knowing that rebellion against Peter could bring English intervention.

The biggest possible change is that Henry of Trastámara might fail to take the throne. In real history, Henry, aided by French mercenaries under Bertrand du Guesclin, overthrew Peter in 1366; Peter was briefly restored by the Black Prince in 1367 but lost again and was killed in 1369. If Peter had been married to an English princess, England might have had a stronger reason to keep him in power after Nájera rather than treating the campaign as a costly temporary expedition. An English queen, especially if she produced a son, would make Peter’s regime more useful to England and would give the Plantagenets a direct dynastic stake in Castile.

If Peter survived and founded an Anglo-Castilian line, the balance of power in western Europe would shift sharply. Castile possessed a valuable Atlantic fleet. In real history, after Henry II established the Trastámara dynasty, Castile became an important French ally, and Castilian naval support helped France against England, especially in the 1370s. A pro-English Castile would deny France that support. It might prevent or alter disasters such as the English defeat at La Rochelle in 1372, and it would make English communications with Gascony safer. France would face England not only from the north and southwest, but also with a hostile or semi-hostile Castile to the south.

That said, the marriage would not automatically save Peter. His main problem was not a lack of royal blood but his political conduct. He alienated much of the Castilian nobility, had a reputation for brutality, and was entangled in scandals over his marriages and mistresses. An English marriage could even worsen his position if Castilian elites saw him as dependent on foreigners or if English demands for repayment and privileges became unpopular. The Black Prince’s real intervention in Castile failed partly because Peter could not or would not pay the promised costs. A marriage alliance would not remove that structural problem.

France and Aragon would also respond aggressively. A Plantagenet-Castilian alliance would be alarming to Charles V of France and to Peter IV of Aragon. They would almost certainly double down on support for Henry of Trastámara. The Castilian civil war might therefore become even more clearly a theater of the Hundred Years’ War: England backing Peter, France and Aragon backing Henry. The war could last longer and become more destructive, even if Peter ultimately still lost.

The succession issue is crucial. If the English princess bore Peter a legitimate son, Henry’s claim would be much weaker, and England would have a powerful reason to defend that child’s rights. If there were only daughters, the later situation might resemble the real Lancastrian claim to Castile, but earlier and stronger. A daughter of Peter and an English princess could become a major dynastic prize, potentially tying Castile to the English royal family for generations.

So the most plausible outcome is not a peaceful Anglo-Castilian union, but a sharper and earlier polarization of Iberian politics. Peter would gain a stronger chance of survival, and England would gain the possibility of turning Castile into a major ally rather than seeing it become a French partner. If Peter remained politically reckless, however, the marriage might only make the civil war larger, more international, and more expensive, without preventing his eventual overthrow. The greatest long-term consequence, if the marriage produced heirs and Peter stayed in power, would be the absence of a French-aligned Trastámara Castile and a much stronger English position in the later Hundred Years’ War.

items.question: What If Europe colonized the Americas four centuries earlier? 1092 Instead of 1492
human_answers: Lots of feedback and responses! Thank you all! I'll get to responding to other replies later on. The Crusades! That's a good point for the year 1092 and the 11th century. Also lots of good points here. Very good points. Crusader-style polities and principalities in the New World, given the attitudes of the 11th century. 1. Why wouldn't a less-weakened Muslim power establish their own colonies? As long as they're in Iberia or Morocco, they got a good chance of colonization with that geography, I think? 2. Also why not? What if the Apache or some other First Nations group taking over the North American interior, like a counterpart to the Mongols. Hopefully less bad and deadly and painful though, though that's probably too much to ask for when it comes to warfare in general. "What if the Americas were colonized by Europe beginning in 1292?" Could be worth it's own thread! Here in this one we're talking about what if 1092 instead of 1292, or OTL 1492.

That's a fun scenario to consider. One way to get Medieval America... Not sure about the naval tech of the time though. Or the ressources given the voyage between Europe and the Americas are going to be months long. These are the two crucial things that need to be fixed to get the possibility. The North Route via Greenland and Vinland probably is the best shot to make this work. Think the issue is the fact the Atlantic Ocean is pretty devoid of islands that can make effective island-hoping stops. There are the islands of Macaronesia (Azores, Canarias, Madeira, Cape Verde) close to Europe but otherwise it's a long trip until you reach the Carribeans or one of the American coasts. This isn't the same situation as the Pacific where you have tons of small islets... unless you go into ASB territory and raise the Azore plateau but that basically is making Atlantis a real thing... Naturally this situation limits the abilities of Muslim powers to colonize. Europeans at least have the Viking routes, even if that requires a successful Vinland. Though one has to remember the legend of Abu Bakr II of Mali, the most likely fictionnal predecessor of Mansa Musa. It's a stretch and we're more dealing with an African power than a European or Arabo-Muslim one, but the distance between West Africa and Brazil is a lot shorter... But then again, it's basing ourselves on a myth.

As for how would see a medieval colonization of the Americas, I would expect it happened across the Northern Atlantic and would likely focus first on the region around St Lawrence Bay, which offer several good settlements, than we would see it spread up the St, Lawrence River and later down the East Coast. Early settlements would simply be normal Norse settlements, and outside Norse settlers the main early source of “settlers” would be slaves. The need for labor would drive this slave trade and the victims of this slave trade would likely mainly come from the British islands, the Baltics, Central Europe and the post Frankish kingdoms in order of importance and it would likely disappear by the 13th century. The early settlements would likely mostly be peasants republics, as the Norse seems to mostly have established those on the frontiers. Over time we will likely see consolidation of power under large land owners both secular and ecclesia and the rise of city states. Also as the Norse runs into more powerful native societies, we may also see more centralized frontier states lead by Norse war leaders, these may also turn on the less centralized Norse states and begin to establish true kingdoms. As the population we also see the arrival of Low German merchants, who establish merchant quarters in the cities, we will likely see German artisans also moving. We could also see something like the Ashkenazi migration to Poland, but it’s more likely that Low Germans simply will fill that niche as they did in the Baltic and Nordic countries. This may result in the rise Low German city states. At the same time the Catholic Church will likely introduce more warm weather crops as the Norse moves south. As the economy of Norse America grows and expand, others will likely look into establish alternative trade route to it. Here we may see the Portuguese doing their own Columbus expedition in the early 15 century. At that point I would expect a European presence already in the Caribbean, even if it’s not fully developed. So the Portuguese establish trade routes to the Caribbean and introduce Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cash crops. We likely also see the rise off the African slave trade, but with greater European and Mestizo presence in the region already, it likely doesn’t reach OTL levels and the more traditional European structure likely means a more serfdom like structure for the African slaves. I suspect the Norse will run into the Mesoamericans in the 14th century and we will see it falling to Norse invaders or crusaders, with it being relative far away from Norse American strongholds (which will likely be the Mississippi and St. Lawrence basins and the East Coast), I expect the model of conquest will be more like the Baltic crusades. Conquest mostly by knightly monastic orders and Mexico under a knightly Grandmaster. We could easily see a repeat in the Andeans, but we could also just instead see Christian missionaries converting them.

I am not familiar with the shipbuilding industry, but I believe this is possible. There was no fundamental difference like scale or materials between shipbuilding in the 15th and 11th century. They likely needed only to devise a few new designs, or simply undertake bold try using the vessels they already have. As for the difference? An 11th-century conquest of the Americas would have been far more likely to result merely in the emergence of independent states, rather than colonies subservient to Old World powers. At best, the Italian city-states might have established a few small commercial colonies (perhaps in the Caribbean region?), but inland colonies dominating an entire continent would have been highly unlikely. This aligns more closely with the norms of that era, and the comparatively weaker commercial and artisanal capabilities of Europe would not have generated the centripetal force required to establish such a relationship; Europe could not produce so many goods that American colonists were unable to manufacture for themselves. Two rather interesting questions: 1. Could a less weakened Iberian/North African Muslim power have established its own colonies in the Americas? 2. Could a nomadic polity have been established in the North American interior?

The major issue is that open ocean travel isn't really possible before the 15th century so you'd be island hopping like the Norse did. That's certainly possible but your probably looking at a more Polynesian or Greek heroic age style model (or for that matter the Norse in Iceland and Greenland) where people are leaving to found a separate colony rather than one controlled from the Metro-pole as its to far away. Also most of the early arrivals will be in the North (Canada, then moving into New England and points south as the Little Ice age bites) and while trade webs will probably see the European diseases spread there is a good chance the native powers will have time to recover before actual Europeans reach them. That could allow the Mexican civilizations and the Inca a good chance to survive especially if they've obtained European tech in trade before the newcomers have the forces to go after them (the Aztec are probably doomed whatever as the events of OTL strongly suggest they were hated by all and someone was taking them out eventually). Also its likely they understand pretty quickly this is a new land and not a route to China (or at least not an easy one, especially once they finally sight the great desert of the Plains prairie and realize just how big America really is) so there will probably be a much stronger focus on going south to round Africa to reach the Spice islands. With actual transoceanic travel developed much earlier (and the need to improve links with the New World driving sailing tech along at a fair clip) that's likely to see Portugal starting its investigations long before Spain is finished with the Reconquista and probably with England and France nipping at her heels this time. An early rediscovery (or more dissemination of the original Norse discovery) probably doesn't completely prevent the Crusades (there is still the issue of Jerusalem) but with a bigger target for expansion and as an outlet for violence the majority of settlers will probably go there rather than the rather precarious Outremer and even if the First Crusade succeeds it may not establish an enduring polity (they had enough trouble getting immigrants as it was. Usually Europeans only went East when the states were in deep trouble). Although with a Europe that has an outlet for its expansionist desires in the Far West and doesn't feel so under siege for the first time in centuries might be able to patch things up with Islam a bit more easily. Hard to say about Religion although by 1092 the Great Schism has already happened so the Catholics will be very much the first ones there and its hard to say if there will even be a Reformation after four centuries of altered history. However if the Crusades are averted, or at least blunted there is a good chance Byzantium survives in its original form and without the damage from the Latin occupation it might be able to hold out and reform enough that they can avoid falling to the Ottoman's. Also Venice and the Italian city states may not rise as quickly if the focus on trade switches to the Atlantic (especially if the wealth of America is discovered).
items.original_question: What if Europe colonized the Americas four centuries earlier? 1092 instead of 1492 What if widespread European colonization of the Americas started 400 years earlier in 1092, the end of the 11th century? The idea I got in my head so far involves rapid advances in naval/seafaring technology to allow for trans-oceanic voyages, and the sponsor of the first voyage and colony I'm thinking would be the Duchy of Normandy, but this can change if that's not plausible enough. What I want out of the timeline spawned by the question of thread title, is a medieval retro-future colonial-frontier sort of scenario, also going by another idea-spawning question. What if the 11th century had the technology of the 15th century? What sort of tech advances, and other sorts of points of divergence, would be needed to make the beginning of European colonization of the Americans begin its proliferation in 1092 instead of 1492? And what other ideas and questions and things should I also take into consideration? My apologies for not being able to go in-depth at explaining scenarios. I'm unfortunately a very simple person with a limited education and understanding of history and other topics needed for writing alternate history. I hope to get a discussion going that will help broaden my horizons of learning more history to write better alternate history.
items.model_answer:
If Europe had colonized the Americas in 1092 rather than 1492, the result would probably have been less like the Spanish conquest and more like a long, uneven medieval frontier across the Atlantic.

The most important difference is that Europe in 1092 was not the Europe of Columbus, Cortés, and Pizarro. It had no powerful Atlantic nation-states like unified Spain, no mature Portuguese oceanic empire, no large-scale capitalist plantation system, no transoceanic bureaucracies, and no firearms or cannon comparable to those of the sixteenth century. Western Europe was still feudal, fragmented, crusading, and relatively poor. So an early colonization of the Americas would likely begin with small coastal settlements—Norse, Norman, English, French, or Iberian—rather than immediate continent-wide conquest.

Disease would still be the decisive factor. Smallpox, measles, influenza, and other Old World diseases would likely devastate Indigenous populations just as they did after 1492. But the timing would change everything. In 1092, the Aztec and Inca empires did not yet exist. The Mexica had not built their empire in central Mexico, and the Inca state had not expanded across the Andes. Earlier contact might prevent those empires from forming in the way they did. Instead, disease and trade would disrupt earlier societies: Mississippian cultures in North America, the Maya successor states, Toltec-influenced Mexico, Andean kingdoms, Caribbean peoples, and many others.

European military conquest would be harder than it was in the 1500s. Medieval Europeans had steel weapons, horses, armor, and ships, but not the same gunpowder advantage. If horses, pigs, cattle, wheat, and other Old World organisms spread through the Americas centuries earlier, Indigenous societies would have much more time to adapt. Horse cultures might emerge by the 1200s or 1300s instead of after 1600. Native polities that survived the first epidemics could become militarily stronger, more mobile, and better able to resist later European expansion.

So the Americas by 1492 would likely already be a deeply mixed world: Christian missions and medieval colonies along some coasts, Indigenous states transformed by disease and livestock, hybrid trade societies, and perhaps powerful Native kingdoms using horses, iron, and European diplomatic alliances. Instead of a sudden “Age of Discovery,” there would be a centuries-old Atlantic world.

Europe would also change dramatically. American crops such as maize, potatoes, beans, tomatoes, and cacao might reach Europe, Africa, and Asia centuries earlier. Potatoes and maize could increase population growth earlier than in real history, possibly strengthening medieval kingdoms and reducing some famines. Access to American silver, furs, timber, and land could make Atlantic Europe richer earlier, shifting power away from the Mediterranean sooner. The rise of Portugal, Spain, France, and England as Atlantic powers might happen earlier, though in different forms.

The slave trade would probably develop differently. In 1092, the massive plantation economy of the later Caribbean and Brazil did not yet exist. Sugar plantations were known in the Mediterranean, and slavery existed in Europe, Africa, and the Islamic world, but the huge racialized Atlantic slave system of the 1500s–1800s had not yet formed. If American plantations developed slowly over the medieval centuries, African slavery might still expand, but perhaps less suddenly and under different religious and political justifications.

The biggest global effect would be that the “modern world” starts earlier, but not necessarily faster. Earlier colonization would not instantly produce the Renaissance, capitalism, or modern science. Medieval Europe lacked the institutions and technology to exploit the Americas as efficiently as sixteenth-century Europe did. But over four centuries, the continuous exchange of crops, animals, diseases, metals, people, and ideas would reshape both hemispheres long before the historical 1492.

In short: colonization in 1092 would probably mean earlier epidemics, earlier biological exchange, weaker initial European conquest, stronger surviving Indigenous adaptations, and a much older Atlantic world by the time 1492 arrived. The Americas would still suffer immense disruption, but the conquest would likely be slower, more medieval, more hybrid, and less dominated by the specific Spanish-and-Portuguese imperial model that shaped real history.

items.question: What If Henry dies in the joust and Anne gives birth to a son
human_answers: Judgement Day had finally come for Anne Boleyn. Allies and enemies, alike held their breath when the news broke that King Henry's widow was giving birth. It had been a miracle that she had managed to not miscarry on that fateful January day when her husband had fallen from his horse and would never wake up. When she had learned of Henry's death, Anne had fallen to her knees crying hysterically. However once her tears have passed and she has been calmed down, she immediately summoned the lords to form a regency council, making it clear that she will be regent, a fact that does not sit well with her uncle. Princess Elizabeth would be brought to court, both as a comfort to her mother, and in case she needed to be crowned. Lady Mary was removed from Hatfield and instead put under close guard at Hudson. The Seymours were sent away in disgrace. It was said that Queen Anne took a special delight in dismissing Jane Seymour, mocking her for ever thinking she could replace her. All of Europe held their breath as they waited to see what would happen. Not even the Pope was willing to make a move just yet, wanting to see where the land would lay. Finally on May 19, Anne went into labor. After ten grueling hours, the queen dowager finally brought her second child into the world. "Tis a healthy boy, Majesty, you have done it! You have birthed a prince!" the midwife exclaimed. "Nay, not a prince. A King. I have birthed a King!" Anne cried, a radiant smile on her face. "King Henry the Ninth!"
items.original_question: What if Henry dies in the joust and Anne gives birth to a son Might make this a full TL. Not sure yet. Here is what I am wondering. Let's say that Henry dies and Anne carries her son to term. What happens? Would the people pick Mary when there is chance for a male heir? I know Norfolk and his ilk would probably not turn on Anne when there is a chance that he could be Lord Protector for fifteen years. What about Elizabeth in the meantime, would she be crowned before Anne gives birth just in case Anne gives her a sister?
items.model_answer:
If Henry VIII had died in the 1536 jousting accident and Anne Boleyn had then given birth to a healthy son, the most likely result is an infant Tudor king with Anne as the central political figure, rather than Anne’s fall and execution.

Under the 1534 Act of Succession, Henry’s marriage to Anne was lawful and their children were the legitimate heirs, while Mary, Henry’s daughter by Catherine of Aragon, was excluded. If Anne’s son were born after Henry’s death, he would almost certainly be recognized by Anne’s supporters as king from birth. He might have reigned as Henry IX, though his name would depend on what Anne chose. Until his birth, Elizabeth would technically be the designated heir, but a male child would supersede her.

The immediate problem would be the regency. Anne herself would have a strong claim to influence as queen mother, but England was not accustomed to female political rule, and powerful men such as Thomas Cromwell, Thomas Cranmer, the Duke of Norfolk, and other nobles would compete to control the infant king’s government. Anne might be named regent or might instead be forced to share power with a council. Her survival would depend on whether she could hold together the reformist faction and prevent conservative nobles from rallying around Mary.

Anne would almost certainly not be executed. The accusations against her in real history were tied to Henry’s desire to discard her and marry Jane Seymour. If Henry were dead and Anne had produced the long-desired son, the political logic reverses: she becomes the mother of the king and a protector of the Tudor succession. Her enemies might still attack her legitimacy or accuse her of misconduct, but removing her would risk destabilizing the infant monarch’s claim.

England’s Reformation would probably continue, and perhaps become more Protestant earlier. Henry VIII personally broke with Rome but remained doctrinally conservative. Anne Boleyn, Cranmer, and many of her allies were more sympathetic to evangelical reform. With Henry gone, the Church of England might move away from Catholic doctrine faster than it did under Henry, though perhaps not as radically or smoothly as under Edward VI. The dissolution of the monasteries, already beginning in 1536, would likely continue because it enriched the crown and nobility, but without Henry’s authority it might provoke stronger resistance.

Mary’s position would be dangerous but important. Catholic conservatives, supporters of Catherine of Aragon, and possibly Emperor Charles V could claim that Anne’s marriage was invalid and that Mary was the rightful heir. That could create a serious succession crisis, especially if the infant king were sickly or if Anne’s government appeared weak. However, unless there were a major rebellion or foreign intervention, most English elites would probably accept the baby king because he preserved the Tudor male line and offered continuity.

Elizabeth’s future would also change dramatically. She would no longer become queen unless her brother died without heirs, but she would remain a legitimate royal princess, probably raised in a Protestant court under her mother’s influence. Her life would likely be safer and more stable than in actual history.

The biggest long-term difference is that there would be no Jane Seymour marriage, no Edward VI, and likely no Marian restoration as it happened historically. England would probably be ruled for years by a regency government in the name of Anne’s son, with Anne Boleyn, Cranmer, and Cromwell shaping a more Protestant Tudor monarchy. The regime would be fragile, because an infant king and a controversial queen mother invite factional conflict, but if the boy survived childhood, Anne’s son would likely become the undisputed Tudor king and the English Reformation would take a different, probably more evangelical, path.

items.question: What If Britain and France made peace in 1811?
human_answers: I definitely agree that the conflict in Spain would continue, and that some form of renewed conflict in Europe down the line is inevitable, but I don’t think Napoleon wouldn’t try to conclude a peace with Britain, so long as it was on terms favourable to him. Now, whether that is possible is a rather different question. The Whigs at least had no interest in continuing to fund the peninsular war regardless, but in negotiations, they are likely to push for a restoration of Portugal and Hannover, and for France to at least withdraw from direct control of the rest of the Hanseatic cities and the Netherlands. It’s quite a lot for Napoleon to be willing to give up, though could possibly be paired with his longstanding designs on Sicily and a British withdrawal from Malta, as well as the return of occupied Dutch and French colonies. Regardless, I don’t think the British could get everything they want.

No mention has been made of the Continental System. I presume it is abolished as part of the peace treaty. And Britain's blockade is lifted. Anything less makes peace a non starter. Predictions from here: Overall peace is going to be short lived. Every one will be watching France waiting for a propitious moment to reduce the almost total hegemony France has. Nap will maintain a large military to enforce his hegemony. I don't know that this is sustainable. Spain will remain a bleeding ulcer. The Spanish people will continue to resist. Nap's best chance at lasting peace is to pull out and return a Bourbon to power. Remaining in a constant state of this kind of war drains resources, but brings no benefits. The best he can hope for (remaining in the conflict) is an uneasy truce where Joseph is somewhat accepted/propped up, while a low level of guerilla warfare continues. The entire Spanish colonial sphere is lost even faster than OTL. Cuba/puerto rico might remain attached, but I doubt it. I don't know whether Britain has destroyed Spain's infrastructure yet, but if not, Spain could actually emerge from the conflict in better shape without Britain's help than with it. Portugal might be able to hold out behind the line of T, as their soldiers have been trained up to a better level than before 1807, but as the British had supplied the top chain of command, they'll be left rudderless. I think their fate lies in how much stomach Nap has for continuing his Iberian adventure. It would be interesting to see what results if Nap simply walks away. OTL, the British acted as a regency while the Braganza court remained in Brazil. Joao did not want to return. Pedro was too young. Portugal is likely to be chaos. Should France manage to take control, Portugal itself may end up in better shape, but the entirety of the colonial sphere attaches to Brazil. I don't think the return of French colonies does much for France. Haiti is finished as a rich colony. Martinique and Guadeloupe, where Britain ironically enforced the status quo maintaining the slave system after capturing the islands, might still hold value. When the Nap Wars resume, Britain faces a hard choice - join in and try to reset the balance of power, or stay on the sidelines and have the European dynamic dictated to them. If they join in, they're quickly going to regret dropping out in the first place. They had France on the ropes in Portugal/Spain, and now they'll have to start all over again. Who knows what has become of Wellington.

The default of the Revolution certainly left its mark, but Napoleon was also ideologically opposed to debt, in part because of fiscal conservatism (there was a hyperinflation crisis during the Revolution), but also because it would have meant making himself dependent on the financial market, and he feared that the banker would try to exert political pressure on him. But I don't think he necessarily tried to raise a large amount of debt from the public market, he preferred to use a sinking fund controlled by one of his appointees for that. For the reparation, he had ways to force the issue, like sending his army in and making the host pay for its quartering. This was the way he was making his puppets, like the Kingdom of Italy, contribute, and alongside their allied contingent, it saved him as much money as the reparations brought him. For Prussia specifically, they were raising a large debt to pay the reparation, with Napoleon himself being one of their creditors, so they probably intended to pay. But you also have to take into account that Napoleon did not hesitate too much to raise taxes (he essentially brought back every indirect tax of the Ancien Régime) or defer payment, after the Restoration, the Bourbons had to pay the equivalent of one year of fiscal revenues in unpaid expenses.
items.original_question: What if Britain and France made peace in 1811? In 1810 King George III suffered a mental breakdown, and in early 1811, his son the Prince of Wales, later to reign as King George IV, was installed as regent by Parliament. The Prince Regent was widely expected to dismiss Spencer Percival’s government, and appoint Lord Grenville as Prime Minister, but was dissuaded from this course by his mother. Unlike the Tories, Grenville and the Whigs were sceptical of the conflict with France, particularly the expense of maintaining Wellington’s army in the Peninsula War, and had they taken power in 1811, whilst Wellesley’s army was holed up behind the lines of Torres Vedras, attempts at negotiating a peace with France are not an unrealistic prospect. Negotiations in 1807 touted an exchange of Sicily for Hannover, and Britain would retain the Cape Colony and Malta, whilst returning other Dutch and French colonial possessions, though these ultimately broke down over Sicily. Talks in 1808 even saw Napoleon offer to concede both Hannover and Portugal, though there is some question of how serious both sides were in this later negotiation. Both of these were also viewed by the Tory governments as a chance for a respite alike to Amiens, rather than to conclude the conflict. The Whigs, less intractable towards the idea of a French dominated Europe would be willing to pursue a long term peace. In addition to questions over Portugal, Hannover and the colonies though, France had by this point annexed the Netherlands and the Hanseatic cities, both of which are likely to be sticking points for British negotiators (although these annexations were in part to enforce the continental system). What terms could realistically be feasibly agreed by both sides at this time? With the end of the war with Britain in 1811, Napoleon’s invasion of Russia appears unlikely to my mind, though relations between the two emperors would undoubtedly continue to deteriorate. The peace would also presumably be unpopular domestically in Britain, where support for the war remained high. Austria, Prussia and Sweden all additionally had cause to want revenge against France and Napoleon, and so it seems unlikely that this peace would be entirely conclusive, and some form of renewed conflict seems eventually likely, even if it only comes with Bonaparte’s death. The aftermath of Amiens however suggests that this might well come sooner. There is however also the question of whether France could afford to maintain their precarious financial situation, and in particular continue to field their army without the subsides of allies, the reparations of former enemies and loot. It seems unlikely France can afford to demobilise in the face of their European rivals, so would this possibly prompt further campaigns? Perhaps against Russia regardless or the Ottomans?
items.model_answer:
If Britain and France had made peace in 1811, the most likely result would have been the survival of Napoleon’s empire for much longer, because the chain of events that destroyed him in 1812–1815 would probably have been broken.

In 1811 Napoleon was near the height of his power. He controlled or dominated most of western and central Europe, but he had two major problems: Britain was still financing resistance and maintaining naval pressure, and the Peninsular War in Spain and Portugal was draining French manpower. A peace with Britain would have removed the most persistent enemy from the war and would have greatly weakened the Spanish and Portuguese resistance, especially if Britain withdrew Wellington’s army and ended subsidies.

The biggest consequence would likely have been that Napoleon would not have invaded Russia in 1812, or at least would have had much less reason to do so. The Franco-Russian quarrel was partly about Poland and influence in eastern Europe, but it was also deeply tied to the Continental System, Napoleon’s economic blockade against Britain. If Britain and France made peace, the Continental System would become unnecessary. Russia would no longer be under the same pressure to exclude British trade, removing one of the main causes of the break between Napoleon and Alexander I. Without the disastrous Russian campaign, Napoleon would not lose the huge army whose destruction made the Sixth Coalition possible.

Britain, meanwhile, would remain the dominant naval and colonial power. A peace in 1811 would almost certainly have favored Britain at sea and overseas: Britain would keep much of its maritime supremacy and probably many of its colonial gains, while France would keep its dominance on the European continent. The result would be a Europe divided between a French-led continental order and a British-led global maritime order.

Spain would be the most uncertain issue. If Britain abandoned the Peninsular War, Napoleon might eventually impose control more effectively, perhaps keeping his brother Joseph on the Spanish throne or forcing a settlement favorable to France. But Spain would remain unstable. Guerrilla resistance, legitimacy problems, and the crisis in Spanish America would continue. French victory there would be easier without Britain, but not effortless.

There probably would have been no Congress of Vienna in the form we know it, no restoration of the Bourbons in 1814, and no Hundred Days in 1815. Napoleon’s legal and administrative reforms would have become more deeply entrenched across Europe. The Confederation of the Rhine, the Kingdom of Italy, the Duchy of Warsaw, and other Napoleonic satellite states might have lasted for years or decades, though probably under constant diplomatic strain.

The War of 1812 between Britain and the United States might also have been avoided or reduced. If Britain were no longer fighting France, it would have less reason to interfere with neutral shipping or impress sailors on the same scale. Anglo-American tensions would still exist, but one of the main causes of war would be weakened.

The peace would probably not have been permanent. Britain and France had fundamentally different interests: Britain wanted a balance of power in Europe and freedom of trade; Napoleon wanted a French-dominated Europe. Even if they made peace in 1811, mutual suspicion would remain. A later war could still break out over Spain, the Netherlands, trade, colonies, or eastern Europe.

So the most direct answer is: peace in 1811 would probably have prevented Napoleon’s rapid downfall. France would likely remain the dominant land power in Europe, Britain the dominant sea power, and the Napoleonic settlement would endure far longer. But the peace would be tense and unstable, because Britain was unlikely to tolerate permanent French control of Europe indefinitely, and Napoleon was unlikely to accept a Europe in which British influence remained unchecked.

items.question: What If the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant?
human_answers: You are thinking of the Mongol's as a unified force which by this time is not exactly correct. Hulegu and the Ilkhanate were based in Iran (mostly) so the OTL force would not be interested in expanding in Eastern Europe. Batu / Berke and the Golden Horde started their drift towards Islam in this period but their control over the European fringe via their vassals in Kiev and Muscovy wasn't absolute and relied on the tolerance of their Orthodox faith. Any attack on Europe may well become religious in nature (which by itself is an interesting counterfactual) and I suspect any support from the Russian principalities would be lukewarm perhaps even moving towards outright rebellion. It would also be short lived given that the Mongol Civil War is coming. Biggest outcome if the Russian principalities do revolt could be a more Islamised Russia which would be a huge change for world history.

Is there any reason to assume that the forests of western europe were somehow “denser” than those of the eastern? Specifically, those of the Central Russia? BTW, it is not like the Mongols uniformly came from the open steppe: IIRC, Subotai came from Uryankay area which, AFAIK, mostly forests and mountains and he was doing quite well in the Russian forests and pretty much everywhere else. Of course, the Southern direction was much richer than the western one but #1 was the eastern one - China. AFAIK, the South ended up being problematic due to a limited feeding base for the horses but all theories about Mongolian conquest of the west are seemingly ignoring allocation of the resources. The western campaign (including Russia) presumably started with a big force but its second stage, Hungary and Poland, was on a much lesser scale. The map on the OP has “Ulus Jochi” and “Ulus Batu” as separate entities but this was not the case: Batu was a titular head of the Ulus of Jochi. Was there an interest in Mongolia in expanding Ulus Jochi even further at the expense of other endeavors (and other family members)? IMO, this is unlikely because China remained the main theater (BTW, Subotai was sent there after the european campaigns). Were there unlimited human resources? Hardly: part of Hulagu’s force were troops “lended” by Batu. So, with what would Batu conduct his european conquest and why would the Great Khan be interested in its continuation? Formally, the task as formulated by Genghis was fulfilled: the Kipchaks punished and subdued and “the last sea” (Adriatics would do) reached. Was Batu too interested? It does not look like this was a case because he had to create a brand new state from the scratch with the very limited resources (something like 5,000 Mongols).
items.original_question: What if the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant? https://www.reddit.com/r/imaginarymaps/comments/pkb97x/what_if_the_mongols_invaded_europe_the_old_world A sudden interesting thought came to mind. What if, unlike in OTL, the Mongol Empire had not expanded into the Levant and had instead resumed its campaign into Europe? In this TL, during the reign of Möngke Khan, the Mongol Empire invaded Europe again instead of attacking the Abbasid Caliphate. Assume that, starting with the Kingdom of Hungary, they continue pushing westward into the Holy Roman Empire, France, and beyond Western Europe for as long as they keep winning. What I’m curious about is this: 1. What kind of POD would be needed for this to be possible? 2. To what extent would this actually be feasible? - Could the Mongol Empire conquer Western Europe as well, just as it did in Eastern Europe? - Or, unlike in Eastern Europe, would it struggle in Western Europe? 3. If this did happen, what changes would follow? - The Mongol Empire’s advance into Western Europe. - The survival of the Abbasid Caliphate.
items.model_answer:
If the Mongol Empire had redirected the forces used against the Levant and Middle East toward Western Europe, the most likely result would have been a devastating but uneven Mongol penetration into central and perhaps parts of western Europe, not a stable conquest of the whole continent.

In the short term, Europe would have been in serious danger. The Mongols had already shown in 1241–42 that they could destroy major European field armies, as they did against Poland and Hungary at Legnica and Mohi. A larger, sustained campaign backed by the empire’s best siege engineers could probably have overrun Hungary more completely, pushed deeper into the Holy Roman Empire, and threatened Austria, Bohemia, northern Italy, and perhaps France. European armies of the mid-thirteenth century were fragmented, aristocratic, and often inclined to accept open battle, which suited Mongol tactics. Many rulers would likely have been forced into tribute, flight, or temporary submission.

But a full Mongol conquest of Western Europe would have been difficult. The farther west they moved, the less favorable the geography became. Western Europe had dense forests, rivers, mountains, walled towns, and thousands of castles. These did not make conquest impossible, but they made it slow and expensive. Mongol armies depended heavily on mobility, pasture, and coordination across huge distances. The Hungarian plain was suitable for them; Germany, Italy, France, and the Low Countries were less so. They could win battles and devastate regions, but holding them permanently would have required garrisons, administrators, siege operations, and supply systems far from the Eurasian steppe.

Politically, the Mongols would probably have shattered some European kingdoms more than others. Hungary and Poland might have become tributary states or semi-dependent frontier zones. The Holy Roman Empire, already politically divided, might have fragmented further under pressure. The papacy would likely have called for a major anti-Mongol crusade, though coordination among European rulers would have been uncertain. France and England, being farther west and more administratively developed, might have had more time to prepare, fortify, and avoid decisive battle.

The biggest global effect would have been in the Middle East. If the Mongols did not invade the Levant and Mesopotamia, Baghdad might not have been sacked in 1258, the Abbasid caliphate might have survived longer, and the symbolic shock to the Islamic world would have been much reduced. The Mamluks of Egypt might not have gained the same prestige they historically won by defeating the Mongols at Ayn Jalut in 1260. The Crusader states might have lasted somewhat longer, because the balance among Mongols, Mamluks, and local Muslim powers would have changed.

For Europe, the consequences would likely have been traumatic but also transformative. Heavy Mongol pressure could have accelerated the development of stronger monarchies, better taxation, larger professional armies, and more systematic fortification. Regions like Hungary, Germany, and northern Italy might have suffered population loss and economic disruption. If northern Italy were badly hit, the later commercial and cultural rise associated with the Renaissance could have been delayed or redirected.

So the most plausible answer is: the Mongols could probably have ravaged and partly subordinated central Europe, and possibly launched deep raids into Western Europe, but they were unlikely to permanently conquer and administer all of Western Europe. The Middle East, meanwhile, would likely have emerged less devastated, while Europe would have faced an earlier and more intense military-political crisis.

items.question: What If Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop?
human_answers: I can easily see Quebec not wanting to be part of either France, or USA. So they'll opt for independence. France never really wanted it back, so they won't get into their own American Revolution. Even if they did, it is the cost that will impact the French Revolution. The cost will add to French woes. This notion that France will rise up in revolution because Quebec wants independence is erroneous. France wanted regime/gov't change, which is not at all what Quebec wants (independence). France will add Quebec to the list of grievances. That does NOT make Quebec the birthplace of this alt FR. There were various causes of the ARW. One of them was putting Ohio under Canadian jurisdiction. Plus the French and Indian War was fought over the Ohio Valley, and led to a lot of the grievances leading to ARW. No one considers Ohio the birthplace of the AR. Semantics? maybe, but I don't think so.

It is difficult to ascertain how the French in Canada felt, as they lived in a quasi-medieval subsistence economy. Although not under full-blown feudalism, their society was paternalistic, hierarchical, and agrarian. The Church and the seigneurs (many of the seigneuries were owned by religious orders) were the pillars of authority. This is crucial in explaining the lack of widespread revolutionary fervour. However, in the late eighteenth century, there remained a cultural and sentimental connection to France, particularly to the Ancien Régime and the monarchy. After the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, masses were said for them, and the French press in Quebec noted this. They were mourning the grandson of their last French sovereign, not celebrating the secular republic that executed him. In December 1778, from Boston, French Admiral d’Estaing called on the Canadiens to rise and rejoin their motherland, but this was difficult as Canada was where most British forces were stationed. It is unclear whether they wished to return to France, but the Continental Congress felt uneasy about the French returning to North America. Because the Canadiens were largely illiterate (literacy was still below 40% in 1850), it is difficult to say whether they were politically sophisticated, as the colony had been largely marginal and lacked a large merchant class under French rule. Education was not widespread and was largely controlled by seminaries or convents. It was even less politically sophisticated than the Spanish colonies in the Americas. My guess is that independence would have been the least likely of options, unless the Bishop of Quebec assumed the role of head of government.

Then the place will find a way to get out of American control ASAP. Mismatched expectations and all that because of a fundamental misreading by the Continental Army/Congress of the situation, particularly WRT the Quebec Act. The French never wanted to retain Canada après la Conquête because the sugar colonies in the Caribbean were far more valuable, plus lots of bad blood between the Canadiens and Versailles about which direction their part of New France should go. You'd basically be accelerating the French Revolution's TL but with a Canadien cause - and this time the British would come off as the good guys by allying with the habitants, whether or not it takes it back under its wing or accepts it as an independent country but under the British sphere of influence. And it finds a way to get out of the US ASAP, particularly if the initial military occupation goes as OTL and they basically alienated everyone. More probable than getting annexed by the US. Considering Quebec in this case would be a direct cause for the French Revolution ITTL, that's easy to remark on. While still predominantly Francophone (albeit with Canadian French given the same recognition as, say, Brazilian Portuguese), society and culture would take a more, say, Argentine or Uruguayan-like direction but w/ its own quirks (including probably far more indigenous influence) and probably different relationships among groups that would be relatively more egalitarian and opposed to reinstating the colonial relationship. Considering the British would still be next door viz. Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, as well as the HBC doing its thing, British influence would remain strong and that would include the cultural sphere, too.

It depends on how the Americans treat the Canadiens, and how they handle the Iroquois. If the Americans can't keep the Iroquois mostly neutral, and if they prevent them from trading with the Canadiens, then Quebec will want want to leave in a hurry. If the Americans could be deft in the administration of Quebec, better in battle, luckier with allied victories, and more skillful in peace negotiation I think there is a good chance that the Canadiens would want to be in a confederacy, or a customs union with a mutual defense pact. The centralizing reforms of the Constitution would likely have been opposed by the Canadiens as antifederalism, which brings me to the next point, though it is possible they could remain in the union if it transitions from Articles of Confederation to Constitution. While the Canadiens would most likely have forbade slavery, that doesn't mean they would have been abolitionists in the vein of the northeastern Calvinists and Quakers. While they could have been like the 1840s and 1850s Free Soilers, their antifederalism and relative lack of industrialization might have moved them into common cause with Southern states. The Canadiens also could have been aligned with the "Westerners" in looking for federally funded internal developments to help with their access to Atlantic ports, and their access to settling Upper Canada and Indiana/Illinois Territory. Being so close to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland the Canadiens could also be interested in a strong navy. So perhaps an American Quebec could be allied with someone like Calhoun. As for the issue of Loyalist Migration, their emigration would likely have been reduced if they didn't have British Upper Canada as a destination. Many of the Loyalists would have resigned themselves to life in the new government. There still would have been Loyalist emigration from both America and Lower Canada, and there would still be a movement of Loyalists to Upper Canada and other territories despite them being no longer British Empire owned. So those populations would have thrown a new political impulse into the country later especially after the Constitution is ratified.

I'd assume a French route with independence after the French revolution. Maybe some nobility or rich flee to Quebec during the revolution. I'd think US keeps what it would get otl plus Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward island. Ontario might go to the U.S. While Newfoundland and Labrador goes to Quebec. The American loyalists could be moved into western Canada to try to colonize Western Canada. England might be more harsh in dealing with the Oregon territory. You could see a war over it with Quebec siding with a side. Should U.S. Win they might get British Columbia in the treaty. Quebec might get islands in Nunavut. Russia in this timeline would probably favor selling Alaska to England. With more northern territory. I can see the South looking for more Mexican territory. There's a possibility the slave and free state addition could continue on longer. This causes a delay of the civil war potentially.
items.original_question: What if Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop? So having just watched a new video from Blue, it gave me an idea of dusting off an old topic I used to talk about In 1775, the Continental Army under Generals, Richard Montgomery, Daniel Morgan, James Livingston, and Benedict Arnold (Yes, that Benedict Arnold) marched north into Canada in an attempt to capture Quebec from the British and persuade the French Canadians in joining the revolution. It went well for part of the expedition at first, with Montgomery nearly capturing British Govenor Guy Carleton in Montreal. Meanwhile Arnold's part journeyed through the wilderness to get to Quebec City, which was very difficult. However, by the time the Americans gotten to Quebec, a snowstorm occurred and the battle turned into an utter disaster. Montgomery got killed, Arnold was wounded, smallpox plagued the Americans, the British suffered few causalities, and the Americans managed to alienate the Canadians. Meanwhile, Carleton received reinforcements and made a counter offensive that drove the Americans back to Fort Ticonderoga. For context, what if the Americans captured Quebec? Say Montgomery captured Govenor Guy Carleton and the Americans managed to catch Quebec City by surprise. In my previous thread about the fate of Quebec (Roughly around Lower Canada; Upper Canada is a whole other can of worms), there were four possibilities I gave, but we're going to talk about three: A) French route- The Americans offer Quebec back to France for support in their war, meaning France regains Quebec by the end of the war B) American route- The Americans annex Quebec, making Quebec part of the USA. C) Independent route- The Americans make Quebec into a sister republic, making Quebec independent by the end of the war. (There's no British route since that OTL) Now, I want to focus on one particular aspect of the fate of Quebec: Culture. If Quebec wasn't under the British/TTL Canada, what would culture be like for the French Canadians. Depending on the route we take, how would culture, society, art, cuisine, fashion, etc, develop for the French Canadians? In the French route, how would Quebec be affected by the French Revolution? In the American route, how would Quebec develop under the USA? In the Independent route, how would Quebec develop stuck between the British and Americans while having access to the St Lawrence?
items.model_answer:
If Americans captured Quebec in 1775 and actually held it through the Revolution, Quebec would probably not become culturally “American” in the New England sense. It would more likely develop into a large French-speaking, Catholic, mixed-law society inside the United States, somewhat comparable to Louisiana but larger, more compact, and more demographically resilient.

The key fact is that the Canadiens were the overwhelming majority in the province. The American army could seize Quebec City, but it could not easily govern the St. Lawrence valley against a hostile rural population, a Catholic clergy, and French-speaking local elites. So if the Americans wanted to keep Quebec, they would have had to offer protections much like, or even broader than, those in the British Quebec Act of 1774: freedom for Catholic worship, protection of parish life, recognition of French civil law for property and family matters, and some role for local notables. Revolutionary anti-Catholic rhetoric existed in the Thirteen Colonies, but practical necessity would push the Americans toward accommodation.

Politically, Quebec might have become a fourteenth state or a semi-autonomous territory later admitted as a state. Its constitution would probably combine American republican institutions with French-Canadian local realities. The seigneurial system would likely be weakened or abolished earlier than it was historically, because American republican ideology disliked hereditary privileges and feudal dues. Habitants might become more clearly independent small proprietors. The Catholic Church would remain central to education, marriage, charity, and community identity, but formal church privileges such as mandatory tithes would probably be challenged sooner under American disestablishment principles.

Language would be the central issue. French would remain dominant in rural Quebec and in parish life for a long time because the population was compact, numerous, and had high birth rates. But English would expand earlier and more aggressively in commerce, courts, higher education, and federal politics. Montreal especially would likely become a bilingual but commercially English-leaning American city tied to New York, Albany, the Great Lakes, and the interior U.S. Quebec City would remain more French and Catholic, though less important as an imperial capital.

So Quebec would probably not be assimilated quickly. It was too populous and culturally cohesive for that. But it would face stronger long-term Anglicizing pressure than it did under British North America and later Canada, because the United States had no imperial reason to preserve a separate French-Catholic society as a counterweight to Anglo-American republicanism. Over the nineteenth century, conflicts over schools, courts, language in public business, and Catholic rights would likely become recurring political battles. French-speaking Quebecers might organize as a “French American” or “Canadien” bloc within U.S. politics rather than as the nucleus of a separate French Canada.

Culturally, the society would probably remain Catholic, parish-based, conservative in rural areas, and strongly attached to French language and family networks. But it would also be more republican, more legally American, and more commercially integrated with the northeastern United States. Its elites would include French-speaking lawyers and politicians working inside U.S. institutions, alongside an expanding English-speaking merchant class. The result would be a hybrid society: French in everyday life, Catholic in communal identity, American in constitutional structure, and increasingly bilingual in cities.

The largest difference from real history is that there would be no Quebec as the core of a later Canadian Confederation and no Quebec nationalism in quite the same form. Instead of defining itself against English Canada and Ottawa, Quebec would define itself as a French-Catholic minority society within the United States. Its struggles would look less like Canadian federalism and more like a larger, stronger version of Louisiana’s language-and-law exceptionalism, combined with the school and church conflicts common to Catholic minorities in nineteenth-century America.

If the American capture were only temporary, however, the effect would be very different: it would likely make the Catholic clergy and many Canadiens more suspicious of the Revolution and more attached to British protection. But if the Americans captured and retained Quebec, Quebec’s culture would probably survive, though in a more bilingual, republican, and U.S.-integrated form than the Quebec that actually developed within Canada.
