items.model_answer:
If Germany had obtained a reliable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade, the war would almost certainly have lasted longer and been far more costly for the Allies. But it would not automatically mean German victory.

The biggest change would have been oil. Germany’s war effort was chronically constrained by fuel: tanks could not be moved freely, aircraft training was reduced, the Luftwaffe lost operational flexibility, U-boats and surface forces were limited, and late-war armored counterattacks often failed partly because fuel was unavailable. A sustainable oil supply would have allowed Germany to train more pilots, keep more aircraft in the air, move panzer reserves more effectively, and sustain larger mechanized operations on the Eastern Front. The campaigns of 1942–44, especially in Russia and after Normandy, would have been much harder for the Allies.

Rubber would also matter because Germany depended heavily on tires, seals, hoses, and other industrial materials needed for trucks, aircraft, tanks, and mechanized logistics. Better rubber supplies would have improved mobility and maintenance. German armies often had excellent tactical units but weak logistical depth; reliable oil and rubber would have reduced one of their major operational weaknesses.

Food security would have strengthened the home front and freed Germany from some of the pressures that shaped its occupation policies. It would have reduced civilian hardship, helped sustain labor productivity, and made blockade warfare much less effective. However, Nazi racial ideology and exploitation of occupied Europe would likely still have produced brutal policies, especially in the East.

The Allied blockade would have lost much of its strategic value. Britain’s long-term strategy in both world wars relied partly on strangling Germany economically. If Germany could ignore that pressure, Britain would have been in a much worse position after 1940. German-occupied Europe might have become a more durable fortress, and an Allied return to the continent would have required even greater American and Soviet effort.

The Eastern Front is where the counterfactual matters most. With ample fuel and transport materials, Germany might have been able to conduct Barbarossa and later campaigns with better mobility and stronger reserves. It might have had a better chance of taking Moscow in 1941 or avoiding the disastrous overextension of 1942. It might also have avoided some of the paralysis that afflicted German forces at Stalingrad, Kursk, and during the Soviet offensives of 1944.

Even so, Germany would still face enormous problems. The Soviet Union had vast manpower, strategic depth, and growing industrial output. The United States had overwhelming economic capacity once fully mobilized. Germany was also fighting a coalition with superior naval power, greater access to global resources, and eventually overwhelming air power. More oil and rubber would not solve Germany’s manpower shortages, intelligence failures, ideological rigidity, weak grand strategy, or the basic problem of fighting Britain, the USSR, and the United States simultaneously.

So the likely result is not a simple German victory, but a much longer and more dangerous war. Germany might have forced a stalemate or a negotiated peace if the resource security existed early enough and if it used it strategically—especially if it avoided or limited war with the Soviet Union. But if Germany still invaded the USSR and still brought the United States fully into the war, the Allies would probably retain the long-term advantage, though victory might come later, at far higher cost, and possibly only after atomic weapons or even more destructive strategic bombing were used against Germany.

items.question: What If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around the 1900s?
human_answers: Well, according to Google "Canada's first CANDU prototype, the Nuclear Power Demonstration (NPD) reactor, required a significant amount of heavy water (D2O) for its moderator and coolant, generally around 1 tonne of heavy water per megawatt (MW) of capacity, translating to roughly 20-25 tonnes for its small 20 MWe output..." and "In the 1930's Norwegian company Norsk Hydro began industrial-scale extraction of heavy water (deuterium oxide) at its Vemork plant in Rjukan, using electrolysis as a byproduct of fertilizer production, " Finally from Wikipedia (yes, I know this may well be nonsense) "It was the world's first site to mass-produce heavy water (as a byproduct of nitrogen fixing), with a capacity of 1.2 tonnes per year. " So, by the late 1930's / early 1940's it might well be possible to build a 1 or 2MW CANDU stream generator using just one or two years production from the single Norsk Hydro plant. I assume Canadian hydro plants were built with higher capacity since they (the Canadians) managed to build commercial output (GW) plants requiring 200-300 tones of heavy water in a 'reasonable' timescale (ie. less than 200 years )

Believe it or not, my first engineering degree was in Nuclear Engineering (it was a dead field when I graduated 30 plus years ago, and still is, so I got another degree in Manufacturing Engineering). Yes, you can run reactors with natural enrichment, and the right neutron moderator - heavy water (as in the water molecules have Deuterium instead of your usual one proton no neutrons hydrogen) or graphite come to mind. Both would avoid the need to enrich the fuel (which is a major hassle to do). BUT, that's only part of the story - you need the instrumentation for monitoring the nuclear reactions (to make sure they're occurring, and not getting out of control) which is basically electronic in nature (sorry mechanical won't cut it). In the early 1900s, the field of electronics was embryonic at best. Then there's the material science aspect - you need materials seriously capable of dealing with the high reactor temperatures, and radiation effects (oh yeah, and the material can't interfere excessively with the neutron flux, which would disrupt the reaction) - sorry not happening, material science was in its infancy IMO. There is also the safety aspect - you need shielding for any radiation emitted from the reactor. The health aspects of radiation exposure were basically unknown, resulting in many people getting exposed to and dying of cancer (Marie Curie, early X-Ray technicians, the so called "Radium Girls" who painted the glowing dots on watch faces). In certain cases of extreme exposure (due to reactor surges, etc.), you can die from the radiation days after the exposure. In short, IMO, having a viable nuclear reactor in the early 1900s is a non-starter.

To your first part: Fair enough. It seems like this might require ASB, like just magically gifting people the entire lexicon of nuclear understanding and teaching them how to make purer graphite. I'm not sure I entirely agree with the second part. Were the engineers that built the Chicago Pile doing sophisticated core analysis? Did they know the neutron flux? I feel like you could "fly blind" and just go by heat/steam output, especially since "won't immediately melt down and ruin my investment" is probably considered sufficient by 1900s standards of safety (especially if the health effects of radiation are not yet understood). Granted, it seems very, very likely that the long term effects of this mentality would make for a much more radioactively contaminated world... Ah, but I didn't say for generating electricity, per se. A nuclear boiler just for steam would be useful. And I doubt they'd come up with a design that requires steam generators or controlling boron concentration in the coolant: I wouldn't expect anything like a PWR with its separation between a primary and secondary loop. More like a BWR or RBMK, where the radioactive steam is directly used. If the objective is electricity, it may require a bit longer than early 1900s. But by the time you have coal plants coming online, you have everything you need for the conventional thermal plant.

To elaborate on some things: as far as I can tell, there are possibly 3 historical reactor designs that used unenriched/natural uranium: heavy-water moderated CANDU reactors, graphite-moderated gas-cooled reactors (Magnox and UNGG), and possibly the graphite-moderated Soviet RBMK reactors (although RBMK reactors typically used low-enriched uranium). Heavy water's out of the question; it was only discovered in the 1930s, and even WW2-era methods for extracting heavy water were massively energy-intensive. NPD, the first CANDU reactor producing some 20 MW of electricity, required 28,660kg of heavy water. Using pure electrolysis to extract the heavy water - the initial method used to extract heavy water at Vemork - required about 58,000 kilowatt hours per pound of heavy water, or 3.6 billion kilowatt-hours to produce all the necessary heavy water. As a quick comparison, the US' entire monthly electricity generation in April 1922 was about 3.6 billion kilowatt hours. That means the NPD reactor, if it obtained heavy water using pre-WW2 methods, could run for 20 years straight and not break even on the power needed to create the heavy water necessary to run the plant (not to mention some heavy water will be lost in operation) before the development of postwar heavy water production methods. UNGG and RBMK definitely used zirconium cladding for their fuel elements (necessary because zirconium has a smaller neutron absorption cross-section and is resistant to corrosion); the issue is that metal zirconium wasn't commercially synthesized until 1925, and it wasn't commercially synthesized cheaply until after WW2. The specific zirconium alloys used in the fuel claddings weren't developed until the postwar either. RBMK reactors operate with water at pressures of about 1,000 psi; that wasn't achieved by land-based power generation systems until 1925. Uranium metal used in the gas-cooled reactors is difficult to work with considering it corrodes a lot of metals when molten, thus requiring graphite molds of decently high purity (maybe not as pure as nuclear graphite, but boron has to be minimized). Also the furnaces used to cast the uranium were vacuum induction furnaces, a technology not invented until the 1920s. Turning the uranium metal into fuel rods that can be inserted also required a ton of research and development to the point where it was once considered the most critical job at Hanford for the Manhattan Project.
items.original_question: What if A nuclear reactor, four decades early? I posit that with the technology of the early 1900s, a nuclear reactor could've been theoretically possible had the theory been understood. Uranium enrichment is entirely out of the question, but not all reactor designs require it. The industrialists of the 1900s had access to graphite, yellowcake, and boron, which would allow the creation and control of a graphite-moderated natural uranium reactor, so long as the graphite was pure enough (I am admittedly unsure if that level of purity would be possible, but I am presuming so given what little I know of the process). Is there any plausible scenario where the discovery of nuclear fission is pushed back far enough for our enterprising titans of industry to begin harnessing nuclear steam, short of dropping off a modern nuclear physics textbook in their engineers' laps? If so, what effects would this have on the world?
items.model_answer:
If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around 1900, the first major effect would not be an immediate “atomic age” like the 1950s, but a strange early version of it: nuclear power as a new heat source entering a world still dominated by coal, steam engines, empires, and early electrical grids.

A reactor in 1900 would most likely have been used to make steam for electricity or industrial heat. It would not have instantly replaced coal, because coal was cheap, rail networks were built around it, and electrical demand was still relatively limited. Early reactors would probably have been large, inefficient, poorly shielded, and dangerous by modern standards. But they would have been revolutionary in principle: a small amount of uranium could produce enormous heat, and countries that understood this would quickly see uranium as a strategic resource.

The scientific consequences would be enormous. Nuclear physics, radiochemistry, radiation medicine, and materials science would advance decades earlier. So would the grim side: radiation sickness, contamination, and occupational cancers would likely appear before anyone had a mature theory of radiation safety. Early nuclear programs might produce severe accidents, especially if engineers treated reactors like unusual boilers rather than fundamentally different machines. Regulation and health physics would be born through trial and error.

Geopolitically, uranium would become important much earlier. European empires and the United States would survey colonies and territories for uranium deposits just as they did for coal, oil, rubber, and metals. Places such as the Belgian Congo, Canada, Central Asia, and parts of Australia could become even more strategically significant. Nuclear technology would probably be guarded as a military-industrial secret almost from the start.

The largest historical question is warfare. If reactors existed by 1900, nuclear weapons would become possible earlier, but not automatically. A reactor can produce plutonium, but making a bomb requires understanding chain reactions, neutron behavior, critical mass, high explosives, precision engineering, and radiochemical separation. Those fields were immature in 1900. Still, with a working reactor as a starting point, governments would learn quickly. By the First World War, the major powers might at least suspect that explosive nuclear devices were possible. A wartime crash program could perhaps produce a crude weapon in the 1920s or 1930s rather than 1945.

That means World War I might not be fought with atomic bombs, but it could create the first nuclear arms race. If one side believed the other was close to a uranium or plutonium weapon, nuclear research would become a priority alongside poison gas, submarines, aircraft, and artillery. If nuclear weapons appeared in the interwar period, the politics of the 1930s and World War II would be radically changed. Nazi Germany, the Soviet Union, Britain, France, Japan, and the United States would all treat nuclear capability as a central matter of survival. The first use of nuclear weapons might happen earlier than Hiroshima and Nagasaki, possibly in a European war rather than the Pacific.

Civilian energy would also change, but more gradually. Nuclear power could reduce coal dependence in industrial countries, especially for electricity generation. Cities might have somewhat less coal smoke, and long-term carbon emissions could be lower. But oil would still dominate transport unless nuclear electricity accelerated electrified railways, trams, and industry. Cars, ships, and aircraft would still need liquid fuels for a long time. So climate change might be less severe, but it would not vanish.

There would also be institutional consequences. Because nuclear power combines civilian energy, military potential, and environmental danger, states would likely become more centralized and technocratic earlier. Large research laboratories, secrecy regimes, radiation standards, and international arms-control debates might emerge in the 1910s or 1920s instead of the 1940s and 1950s. An “International Atomic Energy” style organization could appear after World War I if the danger became clear, though great-power rivalry might make effective control difficult.

In short, an operating reactor around 1900 would probably not give Edwardian society clean unlimited power overnight. It would first create a powerful but hazardous industrial technology, then a strategic resource race, then an earlier nuclear weapons problem. The twentieth century would likely become nuclear sooner: less coal smoke, faster physics, earlier radiation disasters, earlier state secrecy, and very possibly an atomic arms race before or during the Second World War rather than at its end.

items.question: Skywalker Ranch Foundation: What If Lucasfilm Was Never Sold to Disney
human_answers: Lucas didn’t expend much effort in assembling the rest of the Creative Council. It was mostly a collection of people who had defined Lucasfilm properties for a generation. The first member was Kiri Hart, Lucasfilm’s resident surveyor of canon. Doug Chiang was the second to agree. He had created the stunning visual spectacles that were Naboo and Coruscant in The Phantom Menace. He had made the prequels more mythic in appearance than the originals and that was someone Filoni felt this new Foundation needed. Kathleen Kennedy was the last member. She had overseen the creation of many classics, mostly outside of Lucasfilm. Even if that wasn’t the case, Filoni could not pretend there wasn’t a corporate aspect to the Foundation. The corporation was what would keep the Foundation propped up. Filoni felt both eager to get underway and terrified about what would happen in this meeting. Lucas had essentially anointed him his successor. There was a lot to live up to, but Filoni trusted Lucas’ judgement and that was the only consolation he could come up with. Filoni walked into the boardroom and he clapped his hands. “Hey, everyone. Thank you for coming”, he said. The creators nodded in Filoni’s direction as he sat down. Doug pushed his notepad to the centre of the desk as Kiri closed her binder full of canon notes. “I know what you’re thinking. This is new territory for me too. But, let’s see how this pans out”, Filoni replied. The creators didn’t respond. “Our mandate is clear. We have the responsibility to protect what Lucasfilm stands for. We need to tell new stories while protecting what the old ones stand for”, As some of the creators shifted position in their seats, Dave continued. “This is about the generations of people who see Lucasfilm as the pillar of mythic entertainment”, he said. “What do we do first?” Kennedy asked. “The Foundation goes public in October. Before then, I want a clear statement of what the Foundation will stand for. We don’t want our fans to have any doubt about our integrity”, Kiri nodded, but asked. “What is our integrity? What do we stand for?” Dave looked around the table. “We stand for storytelling and for what it can bring to the world”, he said. “That is a noble goal, Dave. But we can’t forget that part of this Foundation is a business. We need to operate within current and upcoming industries. We need to form connections”, Kennedy replied. Doug then replied. “I don’t think Dave is forgetting that, but we need to tell the industry that we decide what stories are told. Too many stories are being decided in high rise boardrooms”, Filoni nodded. “Exactly. There is a balance we need to respect”, he said. “Creative sovereignty will be our first pillar then. We will work with the industry, but we won’t let them rewrite our stories to fit social media trends”, Kiri replied. Dave nodded in her direction. “We also need to figure out a commercially viable way to support new creators. Are we going to let everyone with a camera and dream camp outside of Skywalker Ranch and hope for their shot?” Kennedy asked. “Once we work out that process, how do we protect their work?” she continued. “Okay, so we’ve decided on our values. Creative sovereignty, visual and emotional integrity and creator support”, Dave said as he counted the values on his fingers. “Who wants to work on the statement?” he called out. Kiri and Doug stood up. “We’ll get it started”, Dave nodded as he looked at Kennedy. “I’ll get the production framework going”, she said. Filoni laid back in his seat. This first meeting was remarkably painless, but he suspected this was where the ease of the job ended. Comments We are a long way off from dealing with the sequels, but they will be addressed eventually. I will be preserving the Mandalorian, since that was Filoni's pet project for a while. And yes, Lucasfilm will be retaining their relationship with Disney. If there is something like Galaxy's Edge, it won't be entirely based around the sequels.
items.original_question: Skywalker Ranch Foundation: What if Lucasfilm Was Never Sold to Disney (I originally intended for this to be a timeline which would've covered the production of a Clone Wars-style animated series set in a different version of the sequel trilogy, but when I determined that Disney was too business oriented to create something like what I was making, I went back to the drawing board and I came up with this instead. This will be my first production timeline so I may or may not update this on the regular, but I wanted to do something to mark the 10th anniversary of The Force Awakens) Anyway, sound off on what you think. # June 2012 “Well done, everybody!” Dave Filoni shouted when he saw the final animation of The Wrong Jedi, the last episode of The Clone Wars Season 5. There was loud applause from across the room. Filoni looked back towards George Lucas. He could’ve sworn he saw a tear in the old man’s eye. The Clone Wars was out for another season. The final step was to send the seasons to Cartoon Network to show the fans. Filoni thought this was probably the best season yet. He wasn’t surprised since he knew he had the best team in the business working alongside him. But, the celebration couldn’t last forever. He had to work with his team on the next season. Lucas had been a felt absence through the production of Season 5, but he had his input on scripts he thought were special. Filoni smiled as he wondered how long he could keep luring Lucas back to Skywalker Ranch. Before the team could leave, Lucas called out. “Before you leave, I have an announcement to make”, he said. The team turned to face Lucas, but Lucas raised his hand. “Not here. Let’s go somewhere less shadowy”, he said. Lucas led his team out of the Ranch proper and towards the artificially created lake that sat in the middle of the Skywalker Ranch complex. Filoni was never tired of the verdant paradise that Skywalker Ranch was. “Alright, George. What’s up?” Filoni asked with a brief smile. Lucas looked to his fellow creators and took a deep breath. “I don’t know what to say, so I am just going to come right out and say it. I will be stepping down from Lucasfilm at the end of the year”, The creators looked at each other. Lucas’s felt absence suddenly made sense. There was no shock or gasp of surprise. Instead, there was a quiet acknowledgement. “Are you sure you want that?” Filoni asked. “Yes. I’ve been thinking about it for about a year. I’ve told my stories and I want to spend the rest of my life with my family”, “Who’s going to take over?” Kliner asked. “Kathleen Kennedy is going to be handling the corporate side of things, but that’s not why I called you here”, Lucas continued. The shock of the news that one of Spielberg’s top collaborators was going to run Lucasfilm briefly subsided as they waited for Lucas. “I’ve been considering what to do with this alliance that I’ve spent the better part of my life putting together. When I first built this place, I had just dodged a bullet when A New Hope smashed the box office. I’ve put my life and my psyche on the line to not only make art for people to enjoy, but to make an environment where filmmakers can tell their stories”, Lucas said as he stretched out his arms to take in the entirety of the Ranch. “You’ve certainly accomplished that”, Athena Portillo said to everyone’s agreement. “I’ve considered selling all of this to Disney. They have reach that I can only dream of, but I’ve had my doubts”, he said as he turned around from the lake. “When I first became a filmmaker, I hated the studio system. They were all hacks who made films based on what was popular at the time. I’m not saying Disney is a company full of hacks, but I don’t want their corporate attitudes diluting what I, Gary, Ralph, Ben and Maria created thirty years ago. I want this place to remain pure”, Lucas continued. “I’m sorry, George, but what are you trying to say?” Kliner asked. Lucas exhaled. “I’ve talked with Kathy and Brennan. They were reluctant at first, but they’ve agreed to keep Lucasfilm as an independent entity. Not only that, but they’ve agreed to begin laying the groundwork for the Skywalker Ranch Foundation”, “And what is that?” Filoni asked. “It is what is going to keep Lucasfilm in the public consciousness for the next decade or so. It is going to protect the integrity of everything we’ve made here. Not just Star Wars, but Indiana Jones, Willow and everything else that has this place’s name on it. Nobody will be able to touch the properties inside this building until they can prove they can do the work necessary to preserve it”, Before the creators could ask further questions, Lucas continued. “But the Foundation will also produce new content that fits what this place stands for. We’re still putting the infrastructure together, but it will produce new content outside of the studio system, just like back when the original trilogy was being produced”, “Who’s going to lead this Foundation?” Filoni asked. “Like I said, Kathy is going to lead the corporate side of it, but she won’t be the voice of the Foundation. The Foundation will be led by creators”, Lucas replied. He then looked towards Dave and walked towards him. “When you first joined Lucasfilm in 2008, I was surprised by how connected you were to what this company stood for. You weren’t just a director, you were a storyteller through and through. That’s the kind of person I need keeping the Ranch intact. I want you to be the first leader of the Creative Council”, Dave felt his cheeks turning red. He suddenly felt like he had been pulled back in time to when he first joined Lucasfilm. He thought that had been a joke at first. This didn’t feel like a joke. This was something Dave couldn’t put into words. “You want me to be in charge of your legacy? George, I’m flattered, but that’s a whole different thing from making a TV show”, Dave pointed out. “Just keep the story straight. That will be your job. You will have other creators working alongside you on the Council and these people will stay on to help you in the trenches”, Lucas reassured him as he pointed to the creators, some of whom Filoni had known since he first joined the company. The creators watched as Dave looked out across the water. He could’ve sworn Binary Sunset was playing in the back of his head. This was his threshold. He thought he had crossed that line in 2008, but he had been wrong. Lucas wasn’t just trusting him with his story, he was trusting him with what Lucasfilm was going to stand for after he was gone. Dave separated himself from the real world for a moment. He saw X Wings and TIE Fighters flying over the Ranch, he could hear the ethereal hum of lightsabers and finally, he heard Yoda’s famous phrase. “Do or do not. There is no try”, Filoni turned around. “I’ll do it”, he said which led to applause from his fellow creators and Lucas shaking his hand. “Lucasfilm couldn’t be in better hands”, Lucas simply said.
items.model_answer:
If Lucasfilm had never been sold to Disney in 2012, Star Wars would probably have remained a smaller, more tightly controlled franchise shaped by George Lucas, Kathleen Kennedy, and Lucasfilm’s own priorities rather than by Disney’s global franchise machine.

The biggest change would be creative pace. Disney quickly produced the sequel trilogy, standalone films, Disney+ series, theme-park lands, and a constant flow of merchandise. An independent Lucasfilm likely would have moved more slowly. George Lucas had sequel-trilogy ideas of his own, and if he had stayed in control, Episodes VII–IX might have followed his treatments more closely, possibly exploring the Whills, the Force at a microscopic or mythic level, and the generational aftermath of the Empire in a very different way from Disney’s films. Whether audiences would have liked that version more is impossible to know, but it almost certainly would not have looked like The Force Awakens, The Last Jedi, and The Rise of Skywalker as released.

Television would also have developed differently. The Mandalorian, Andor, Ahsoka, Obi-Wan Kenobi, and other Disney+ projects depended heavily on Disney’s streaming strategy and budget. Without Disney+, Lucasfilm might still have pursued live-action television, especially the long-discussed Star Wars: Underworld, but production would likely have been slower, more expensive, and dependent on outside distributors such as Fox, Netflix, Amazon, or HBO. Animated series such as The Clone Wars and Rebels-style projects might have continued, but the scale of the Star Wars television universe would probably have been much smaller.

Financially, Lucasfilm would have remained valuable but more exposed. Disney absorbed the risk of making multibillion-dollar films, building Galaxy’s Edge, funding streaming shows, and integrating Star Wars into consumer products, parks, publishing, and games. Independent Lucasfilm could still license products and partner with studios, but it would not have had the same global corporate infrastructure. Star Wars would likely have stayed more “event-based” and less constant.

For George Lucas personally, the most important difference concerns philanthropy. In reality, Lucas sold Lucasfilm to Disney for about $4 billion and pledged much of the proceeds to education-focused philanthropy. If he had not sold, he would still have been extremely wealthy, but he would not have had the same immediate liquidity from the Disney deal. A hypothetical “Skywalker Ranch Foundation” could have become a major cultural and educational institution centered on film, storytelling, technology, archives, and media literacy, but it would probably have grown more gradually unless Lucas sold other assets or transferred Lucasfilm profits into it.

Skywalker Ranch itself might have become even more central in this alternate timeline: a private creative campus, archive, retreat, and possibly a foundation headquarters dedicated to cinema education, sound design, digital filmmaking, and preservation. Lucas has long been interested in education, independent creativity, and the intersection of art and technology, so a foundation tied to the Ranch would likely have supported schools, young filmmakers, film history, technical training, and perhaps public access to Lucasfilm’s archives.

Disney, meanwhile, would have been a different company. It would not have had Star Wars as a pillar of Disney+, consumer products, and theme parks. There would be no Galaxy’s Edge in its current form, no Disney-era sequel trilogy, and no Star Wars as a central part of Disney’s streaming identity. Disney might have leaned even harder on Marvel, Pixar, live-action remakes, and original streaming brands.

So the likely result is this: Star Wars would have been less prolific, less corporatized, and probably more idiosyncratic, but also less globally integrated and financially secure. Lucasfilm might have preserved more of George Lucas’s personal vision, while sacrificing the speed, scale, and market reach that Disney brought. A Skywalker Ranch-based foundation could have become a major educational and cultural legacy project, but without the Disney sale, its resources and public impact would likely have been slower to materialize.

items.model_answer:
If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions, the most plausible result would have been an earlier but limited commercial circumlunar capability, not a full Apollo-style lunar program.

A modified Crew Dragon launched by Falcon Heavy could probably have supported a lunar flyby mission: a free-return trajectory around the Moon with no lunar orbit insertion or landing. That was essentially the concept SpaceX announced in 2017 for private passengers before later shifting attention to Starship. With enough investment, SpaceX might have flown such a mission in the early 2020s, perhaps before Artemis II, giving it a major symbolic victory: the first privately operated crewed mission beyond low Earth orbit.

But Dragon and Falcon Heavy were not naturally suited for sustained lunar exploration. Crew Dragon was designed for low Earth orbit. It would have needed upgrades for deep-space communications, longer-duration life support, radiation protection, navigation beyond Earth orbit, thermal control, and high-speed lunar-return reentry certification. Falcon Heavy, while powerful, could not easily send a fully capable lunar spacecraft, service module, and lander in one launch. Lunar orbit missions would likely have required extra propulsion modules or multiple launches. Lunar landings would have required a separate lander architecture, making the system complicated and expensive.

The biggest political effect would have been pressure on NASA’s SLS/Orion program. If SpaceX had demonstrated that Falcon Heavy and Dragon could send people around the Moon at far lower cost, critics of SLS would have had a stronger argument. NASA might have been pushed to use more commercial hardware for Artemis, especially for cargo, Gateway support, or alternative crew transport. Still, SLS and Orion probably would not have disappeared quickly because they were protected by congressional, industrial, and institutional commitments.

For SpaceX, the tradeoff would have been significant. Continuing to optimize Falcon Heavy and Dragon for lunar missions would likely have diverted money, engineers, and urgency away from Starship. SpaceX might have achieved a nearer-term lunar flyby success, but at the cost of delaying the fully reusable heavy-lift system it ultimately saw as more transformative. Falcon Heavy/Dragon could have been a bridge to the Moon; Starship was intended to be the permanent transport system.

So the likely counterfactual is: SpaceX might have flown private astronauts around the Moon earlier and strengthened the case for commercial deep-space missions, but it probably would not have built a sustainable lunar landing program with Falcon Heavy and Dragon alone. The architecture would have been impressive, cheaper than traditional government systems, and politically disruptive, but technically constrained compared with the later Starship vision.

items.original_question: What if the Brits had carried out a second attack at Taranto? Could the Italian army have been pushed out of Albania, Libya and some of their islands (both in the Dodecanese and at home) in 1940-41 with greater efforts by the Brits to send more surplus men, ships, advanced tanks and aircraft? Remember the Regia Marina was larger than the Kriegsmarine
items.model_answer:
If the British had carried out a second attack on Taranto soon after the famous raid of 11–12 November 1940, the most likely result would have been a greater temporary crippling of the Italian battle fleet, but not a decisive change in the war by itself.

The first raid was already highly successful: British Swordfish torpedo bombers from HMS Illustrious damaged three Italian battleships, including Littorio, Caio Duilio, and Conte di Cavour. Cavour never returned to service, while the others were out for months. A follow-up strike might have tried to finish off damaged ships, hit the remaining battleships, or attack repair facilities, fuel stores, and harbor infrastructure. If it had succeeded, the Regia Marina’s battleship force could have been reduced even more severely, perhaps for most of 1941.

That would have strengthened British naval freedom in the central Mediterranean. Convoys to Malta, operations supporting Greece, and British movements off North Africa might have faced less threat from Italian heavy ships. It could also have deepened the psychological shock Taranto produced: the Italian fleet might have become even more cautious, and the British might have enjoyed a longer period of effective naval superiority.

But there are important limits. A second attack would have been much harder than the first. The Italians would have been fully alerted, harbor defenses would have been ready, smoke screens and anti-aircraft fire would have been heavier, and the surviving ships might have been moved or better protected. The Royal Navy also had only a small number of carrier aircraft available, and HMS Illustrious was itself a precious asset. A failed or costly second raid could have weakened British carrier strength at a critical time.

Even if the second attack had been very successful, it probably would not have knocked Italy out of the naval war. Italy still had cruisers, destroyers, submarines, aircraft, and bases across the central Mediterranean. Axis supply to North Africa depended not only on battleships but also on air cover, merchant shipping, port capacity, and later German intervention. From early 1941 the arrival of the Luftwaffe in the Mediterranean sharply increased the danger to British ships regardless of the condition of the Italian battleship fleet.

So the probable counterfactual is: a second Taranto attack might have made the British position in the Mediterranean stronger for several months and perhaps made Italian naval strategy even more defensive. It could have eased British operations around Malta, Greece, and North Africa in the short term. But it is unlikely on its own to have transformed the wider course of the Mediterranean war, because air power, logistics, and German intervention soon became just as important as the Italian battle fleet.

items.original_question: Impact of French soldiers in the Atlantic Wall? But what could have been the impact of let's say 100,000 French soldiers helping Germany on D-Day? I assume they would have to be conscripted from the industrial workforce in Germany? In that case, would that impact production? And what could be the performance of those soldiers fighting clearly for Germany as late as 1944?
items.model_answer:
If Vichy France had somehow supplied 100,000 French troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944, it would probably have made the Allied invasion harder and bloodier, but it is unlikely to have stopped it.

The first issue is plausibility. By 1944 Vichy France was no longer a truly independent military actor. Germany had occupied all of France after Operation Torch in 1942, the Vichy armistice army had largely been disbanded, and German authorities did not fully trust French forces. To field 100,000 French troops for the Atlantic Wall, Germany would have had to rearm, organize, and trust a large collaborationist French force at exactly the moment when French resistance activity was rising and Allied liberation seemed likely. That would have been risky.

If those troops existed, their impact would depend heavily on where they were deployed. Spread thinly along the entire Atlantic coast from Norway to the Spanish border, 100,000 men would not have changed much. The Atlantic Wall was enormous, and many German coastal units were already static, under-equipped, and unable to maneuver quickly. Additional French troops in that role might have manned bunkers, guarded rear areas, and freed some German units for other duties, but they would not by themselves have solved Germany’s main problems: Allied air supremacy, naval gunfire, logistical disruption, and confused German command arrangements.

If, however, a large portion of those 100,000 French troops had been concentrated in Normandy, the effect could have been more serious. They might have reinforced beach defenses, guarded key roads and bridges, and added depth behind the German coastal positions. At places like Omaha Beach, where the landing was already close-run, additional determined defenders could have increased Allied casualties and perhaps delayed the securing of the beachhead. They could also have made the early Allied buildup more difficult in the first several days after D-Day.

Even then, they probably would not have defeated the invasion. The Allies had overwhelming naval and air superiority, massive reserves, and the ability to land and supply far more troops once a foothold was established. The German side’s critical weakness was not simply lack of manpower; it was the inability to move reserves freely under Allied air attack, shortages of fuel and transport, and strategic confusion over where the main invasion would occur. Unless the French troops were well-trained, well-equipped, fully loyal, and placed at the decisive point before 6 June, they would not have changed the overall outcome.

Their reliability would also have been questionable. Many Frenchmen in 1944 expected Germany to lose. Some Vichy or collaborationist units might have fought hard, especially ideological anti-communists or Milice-type formations, but many regular French troops would have had little enthusiasm for killing British, American, Canadian, or Free French liberators. Desertion, passive resistance, intelligence leaks to the Resistance, or surrender in large numbers would have been likely risks. The Germans understood this, which is one reason they preferred to rely on German formations and non-French auxiliaries rather than rebuild a large French army inside occupied France.

Politically, the consequences would have been severe. A 100,000-man Vichy contribution to the Atlantic Wall would have made Vichy’s collaboration appear even more direct and military, not merely administrative. After liberation, the purge of collaborators would probably have been harsher, French internal divisions deeper, and Charles de Gaulle’s claim that Vichy did not represent the true France even more important. It might also have strengthened the legitimacy of the Resistance and Free French forces, who could present themselves not only as fighting Germany but also as fighting a collaborationist French army.

So the most likely result is this: the Normandy campaign becomes somewhat harder, Allied casualties rise, and the German defense may last longer—perhaps by days or weeks if the troops are concentrated and reliable. But the strategic balance still favors the Allies. The extra French troops would not compensate for Allied control of the sea and air, Germany’s logistical collapse, and the broader deterioration of the German war effort in 1944. Vichy’s participation would probably have changed the political memory of liberation more than the final military outcome.

items.model_answer:
If World War I had broken out in 1905 instead of 1914, it would probably have been a shorter, less global, and more favorable war for Germany and Austria-Hungary than the actual war became.

The key difference is that Europe’s alliance system was not yet as fully hardened. France and Russia were allied, but Russia in 1905 was in terrible condition: it had just been defeated by Japan, was facing revolution at home, and had much of its military prestige and capacity damaged. Britain had reached the Entente Cordiale with France in 1904, but the full Anglo-French-Russian alignment was not yet complete; the Anglo-Russian Entente would not come until 1907. So in 1905 Britain might have been more hesitant to enter a continental war unless Germany violated Belgian neutrality or directly threatened the Channel coast.

That would have given Germany a major strategic advantage. German leaders in the early 1900s sometimes feared that Russia would become much stronger over time, so a 1905 war would have looked like a “preventive war” fought before Russia recovered. If Germany attacked France while Russia was weak, France would have been in a much more dangerous position than in 1914. A German victory in the west would have been more plausible, especially if Britain stayed neutral or entered late.

The war would also have looked different militarily. Many of the weapons associated with World War I existed already—machine guns, heavy artillery, rail mobilization, barbed wire—but aircraft, tanks, poison gas, submarines, and motorized logistics were far less developed. There could still have been trench warfare, especially in northern France and Belgium, but the conflict might not have become the same vast industrial slaughter that occurred from 1914 to 1918. It might have resembled a brutal late-19th-century continental war more than the fully industrialized total war of 1914.

The Balkans would also have been different. Serbia was already a source of tension, but the Balkan Wars had not yet happened, Bosnia had not yet been formally annexed by Austria-Hungary, and the Ottoman Empire still controlled more territory in Europe. So the nationalist chain reaction that helped produce the 1914 crisis would have been less mature. A 1905 world war would more likely have begun from the First Moroccan Crisis, German-French rivalry, or a deliberate German attempt to exploit Russian weakness.

Russia would likely have suffered badly. A major European war in 1905 could have intensified the Russian Revolution of 1905 and perhaps forced the tsar to grant even greater reforms, or even face collapse much earlier than 1917. But because socialist and revolutionary forces were less organized than they later became, the outcome might have been a constitutional monarchy or military-authoritarian regime rather than a Bolshevik revolution.

Austria-Hungary might have survived longer if Germany won quickly. Without the prolonged exhaustion of 1914–1918, the Habsburg Empire might not have collapsed when it did. Likewise, the Ottoman Empire might have remained intact longer if it avoided deep involvement or if the war stayed mostly European.

The United States would probably have played a much smaller role. In 1905 it was already an emerging power, but it was less financially and militarily central than it became during the actual First World War. A 1905 war would likely have been decided mainly by European powers, not by American intervention.

So the most likely result is this: a 1905 World War I would have been less global, less technologically modern, and possibly shorter. Germany would have had a better chance of defeating France and Russia before Britain and the United States could decisively shape the outcome. Instead of the post-1918 world of Versailles, fascism, Bolshevism, and a shattered central Europe, the result might have been a German-dominated continental order established a decade earlier, with Russia weakened and Britain forced to decide whether to accommodate or contain German power.

items.original_question: What if A clash between Rockefeller/Cisneros vs Quayle/Alexander in the US 1996 elections I'm trying to create a 1996 US election scenario where the Democrats have the Jay Rockefeller/Henry Cisneros ticket, while the Republicans have the Dan Quayle/Lamar Alexander ticket. I have a test map showing which states are likely to be won by each party, but there are some states where I'm not sure who would win. That's why I'm asking for help figuring out how many states the Democrats and Republicans would win. I appreciate any suggestions P.S. I forgot to add Indiana as a Republican.
items.model_answer:
If the 1996 election had been an open-seat race between a Democratic ticket of Jay Rockefeller/Henry Cisneros and a Republican ticket of Dan Quayle/Lamar Alexander, the Democrats would probably have been favored, but by less than Bill Clinton’s real 1996 margin.

Jay Rockefeller would have run as a moderate-to-liberal, establishment Democrat: pro-health care, pro-education, fiscally respectable, and with appeal in Appalachia and parts of the industrial Midwest. Henry Cisneros would have added diversity, urban-policy credibility, and potentially stronger Latino appeal, especially in states like New Mexico, California, Arizona, and Texas. The ticket would likely have presented itself as competent, pragmatic, and broadly in continuity with the economic recovery of the Clinton years.

Dan Quayle, however, would have been a weak Republican nominee. By 1996 he still carried the image problem from his vice presidency: young, gaffe-prone, and not widely seen as presidential. Lamar Alexander would have strengthened the ticket somewhat by adding executive experience, moderation, and Southern appeal, but he probably would not have fully neutralized doubts about Quayle at the top of the ticket.

The political environment also favored Democrats. The economy was strong, crime was falling, and the Republican Congress had been hurt by the 1995–96 government shutdowns. Even without Clinton personally on the ballot, the Democratic nominee would benefit from peace, prosperity, and public resistance to Newt Gingrich-style Republican conservatism.

The likely result: Rockefeller/Cisneros defeats Quayle/Alexander, probably by a modest but clear margin.

A plausible electoral map would have Democrats holding the Northeast, the Pacific Coast, Illinois, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, West Virginia, and likely New Mexico. Republicans would remain strong in the Deep South, Great Plains, Mountain West, Indiana, and probably Tennessee because of Alexander. Texas would be closer than usual because of Cisneros, but still likely Republican in 1996.

Popular vote might look something like:

Rockefeller/Cisneros: about 48–50%  
Quayle/Alexander: about 42–45%  
Ross Perot or another Reform candidate: about 5–8%

Electoral vote estimate: Rockefeller/Cisneros around 300–340 electoral votes, Quayle/Alexander around 200–240.

So the short answer is: Rockefeller/Cisneros likely wins, not in a Clinton-style landslide, but comfortably enough because Quayle would have been a vulnerable nominee in a Democratic-leaning 1996 environment.

items.question: What If Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest
human_answers: I would think that you would see a Nelsonian style of celebration and loss. Assuming that the weather was clear enough to allow for Odell, who was alone, to witness their summit and subsequent descent and deadly fall, the MAJOR issue is that Odell does not have a camera on him. The one thing that would irrefutably prove that Mallory and Irvine summited the mountain and then died on their decent would be a photograph, even a distant one, of them on or practically at the summit. Now, Irvine or Mallory did have a camera on them, the near legendary Kodak that is still missing to this day and may hold the truth of whether or not they made it. Assuming that Odell witnessed the summit and the subsequent fall, AND he could record where their bodies fell or near where they fell, then it becomes an issue of finding their bodies and the Kodak. Odell was a respected and trusted witness so i do not think that many would dispute his claim, but finding their remains and the camera would be a major point of corroborating his account. If their bodies and the camera were found, with photographic proof that they did make the summit found in it, it would be both widely celebrated and mourned. Mallory and Irvine would be national heroes in Britain and probably recognized across the world for their achievement. They were historically given a memorial service at St Paul's in London, which was widely attended by many people up to an including the then Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII. Unlike Franklin or Scott, who were either not found or left where they died, Mallory's body at the least was in a location that its recovery was certainly possible, an Irvine's body may have ended up in a similar location if their death was witnessed. If their bodies were recovered, probably with a sponsored expedition, i could easily see a joint funeral for both in St. Paul's, potentially even reaching a State Funeral with full Royal attendance. Then you have the lasting impact that this would have on the psyche of Britain and the world. After the 1924 Expedition there was a major underswell in mountaineering circles, especially British ones, and to a lesser extent in the greater British populace, that Everest was "unfinished business." While there was a drop off in attempts after the 1924 failure, there was a massive resurgence in the 1930s, a pause during the war for obvious reasons, and then a similar surge in the 1950s culminating in the 1953 success. If Mallory and Irvine reached the top in 1924, that would greatly decrease the interest in Everest. Ironically, Mallory's and Irvine's death, and the debate that raged and still rages over whether they made the summit or not, drove the popularity and allure of the mountain far beyond what it would be if they succeeded but died on the way down. There probably would be several more attempts in the aftermath, at least one of which would probably be sponsored by groups like the British Alpine Club or the Royal Geographic Society as a symbolic summit and successful decent in tribute to Mallory and Irvine. I wouldn't be surprised if they hauled a plaque all the way up there to set up a memorial for them. But Everest probably wouldn't have the same level of mystique is has today. By provably succeeding and dying in the aftermath, Mallory and Irvine would probably completely reshape how we see Everest. Edit: Having gone over this again, the nerd in me now wants the Kodak to be a legendary item in a video game OR an SCP entry. would be a fun nod to an event few people would ever know about.

Yes ! I didn't knew they had had found Irvine (well, his foot at last). https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/sandy-irvine-body-found-everest Unbelievable. And then there is this Holly cow they were so close - less than 400 meters to 8848 ! I understand better why so many people are confident they made it to the summit. Also the missing photography of Mallory wife. Unfortunately poor Irvine was found much lower and inside a melting glacier. Hopefully they will found more remains within the next few years. And that infamous camera. What we know for sure: the cylinder, the ice axe and Mallory's body tells us they were roped together at a minimum of 8475 metres, before they fell. Bummers, that's 2133 meters below. Talk about a fall, even if the glacier probably lowered the body on the moutain, along the years. The remaining question is: did the fall happened while climbing, less than 400 m from glory - or descending, having done it ? And there, is the missing photography of Mallory wife. AAAAARGH we are so close from knowing the truth.

So I can tell you that summit fever is very real. I have never climbed anything like Everest obviously but I have scaled (as in hiked) a few 14,000 footers in Colorado and even with that I can state with authority that due to the combination of being tired and euphoric on the way down along with the general feeling that the mission has been accomplished, the brain is not working quite right. That's just reality. Plus, you now have gravity pulling you along. Given that I agree that it is far more likely Mallory and Irvine fell on the descent, either after making the summit or deciding to turn back for whatever reason. While it is unlikely they would have turned back that close to the summit we can't dismiss it either. 400 meters from the summit may not sound like much but at that altitude is actually a very long distance and maybe the combination of bad weather, declining oxygen supplies, or overall uncertainty caused them to turn around. My personal opinion - they made it to the top (it part because I want it to be true) and fell badly on the way down but until we can get actual physical evidence that clearly shows they made the summit that's all it is, an opinion.

Interestingly a lot of practical research has gone into trying to answer the question of whether or not the clothing worn by Mallory and Irvine would have been sufficient to enable them to survive the extreme environment. This has included tests in weather chambers and even a 2006 Everest expedition with climbers wearing exact replicas of Mallory's clothing. The overall conclusion of these tests in generally that the clothing itself was actually quite comfortable and well insulated and that provided Mallory and Irvine kept moving and didn't stop for any length of time or encounter any serious deterioration in weather conditions they could have continued to "operate effectively". Weather chamber tests showed that with the clothing they had Mallory and Irvine could have survived temperatures of −30 °C. Although it was also found that if wind speed picked up the insulation of the clothing would only just be sufficient to −10 °C. While a lot of luck would have been required its not beyond the realms of possibility that Mallory and Irvine could have succeeded in the right conditions. A bigger factor would have probably been whether or not they were carrying sufficient oxygen and if their relatively primitive breathing apparatus could be relied on not to fail (One of the reasons why Mallory chose the relatively inexperienced Irvine to accompany him on his summit attempt was due to the latter's expertise with the breathing apparatus).

They never intended to climb the second step. In fact, no one knew the second step existed in 1924. And Mallory wrote that he considered the NE ridge route impossible. Odell's sighting put them at the base of the summit pyramid, above the third step, anyway. Mallory very clearly explained his intended route in his letters, which was to bypass the steps and either take the zig-zag or the couloir. Anker is ... a controversial source on anything 1924. He has a habit of disregarding any evidence that contradicts his theories on Mallory/Irvine. It's more likely than not that they summited and died on the way down, by virtue of the fact that they died . The vast majority of climbers who've died on Everest got summit fever and died on the descent because they pushed themselves way too hard to reach the peak. Michael Tracy is a grump, but he's done more to shed light on the truth of 1924 Mallory/Irvine than basically anyone else. This video is one of his that cover's their intended routes. We'll never know what actually happened of course – the '99 team utterly botched their investigation upon finding Mallory, and given Irvine's foot was found in the Rongbuk Glacier, his body probably fell clean off the mountain below Mallory in '24 so we're unlikely ever find it. But barring new evidence, the most plausible theory is that they made the summit and died on the descent that evening/night.
items.original_question: What if Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest In 1953 the New Zealand Mountaineer Edmund Hillary and Nepalese Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people to reach the summit of Mount Everest (8.849m). However there remains to this day an enduring question about whether or not Hillary and Norgay actually were the first people to reach the summit of Everest or simply the first to do so and survive the experience. In 1924 during the second British expedition to attempt to conquer Everest British climbers George Mallory and Sandy Irvine set off on the expeditions third attempt to reach the summit. An attempt from which neither man would return. On the morning of the 6th of June Mallory and Irvine had set off for the summit from their final camp (8,138 m on the North Ridge). Their progress was tracked and filmed by expedition leader Noel Oddell who had positioned himself on a ridge further down the mountain to observe and record the expected first summit of the mountain. Mallory and Irvine were last spotted through a gap in the clouds approximately 240 metres from the summit still proceeding onwards. After this the pair simply disappeared. Despite many searches in the days and years following their disappearance the pair would not be seen again for another 75 years when Mallory's remarkably well preserved body would be discovered at an altitude of 8,156m. In the 1933 expedition an ice axe that could only have belonged to Mallory or Irvine was discovered at an altitude of 8,380m proving that the pair had reached at least this altitude. The location and state of Mallory's body (Irvine's partial remains in the form of a detached foot would later emerge from a glacier at a much lower altitude) indicated that he had suffered a fall which had resulted in his death either as a direct result or by later exposure likely during a decent of the mountain. The body revealed circumstantial evidence that suggests Mallory might have successfully reached the summit. Mallory carried a photo of his wife with the intention of leaving it on the summit. No such photo was found on the body. Given the excellent preservation of the body and personal possessions, the absence of the photo suggests he may have reached the summit and deposited it there. Mallory's snow goggles were in his pocket, indicating he may have died at night; that he and Irvine had made a push for the summit and were descending very late in the day. Given their known departure time and movements, had they not made the summit, it is unlikely they would have still been out by nightfall. Perhaps the one artefact that may put the mystery to bed is the Kodak pocket camera that Irvine was known to be carrying and which he presumably would have used to take a photo of the first successful ascent had such a thing occurred and may still contain useable photographs of the attempt. Assuming that Mallory had been successful in reaching the summit and managed to avoid whatever calamity befell on their decent and are able to survive the whole ordeal what would the the effects have been of Mount Everest having been summited for the first time by George Mallory in 1924? How would this have affected the history of Everest and expeditions to climb the mountain after 1924? How would Mallory and Irvine's achievement have been received and remembered?
items.model_answer:
If George Mallory and Andrew Irvine had reached Everest’s summit in 1924 and survived, the biggest immediate change would be symbolic: Britain would have claimed the first ascent of the world’s highest mountain nearly three decades before Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay did in 1953.

Mallory would likely have become one of the most famous explorers of the twentieth century, comparable to Shackleton or Lindbergh. The ascent would have been celebrated as a triumph of British endurance, imperial prestige, and old-style amateur exploration. Irvine, much younger and less famous, would probably have been remembered as the brilliant technical partner whose oxygen equipment helped make the climb possible.

The 1953 Everest expedition would not have had the same historic meaning. Hillary and Tenzing might still have climbed Everest, but they would have been making an important repeat ascent, not the first ascent. Tenzing’s global fame and symbolic importance for Nepal, India, and Sherpa mountaineers might have been reduced or delayed. Hillary’s later humanitarian work in Nepal may still have happened if he climbed there, but his status as “first on Everest” would not have existed.

Mountaineering history would also have changed. A successful 1924 ascent would have proven much earlier that Everest could be climbed with the relatively primitive clothing, ropes, and oxygen systems of the time. It would have encouraged more high-altitude expeditions in the 1920s and 1930s, especially British ones. However, Everest itself would still have remained difficult to revisit because access depended on Tibetan and later Nepalese politics, and the Second World War would still have interrupted Himalayan exploration.

The famous mystery of Mallory and Irvine—whether they reached the summit before dying—would never have become one of mountaineering’s great legends. Mallory’s line, “Because it’s there,” would likely still be famous, but attached to a confirmed success rather than a tragic disappearance.

The broader world would not have changed dramatically. A 1924 Everest success would not have altered the fall of the British Empire, the coming of World War II, or the later commercialization of Everest. Modern Everest tourism was driven much later by air travel, wealth, fixed ropes, guiding companies, and improved equipment. Those forces would still have emerged.

So the main counterfactual outcome is this: Everest would have become a British interwar triumph rather than a postwar Anglo-New Zealand-Sherpa triumph. Mallory and Irvine would be remembered not as tragic almost-heroes, but as the undisputed first men to stand on the roof of the world.

items.original_question: What if Pop Culture gets 1st Amendment and Union Protections for Production and Distribution Early From 1930 to 1968, the Motion Picture Production Code ("Hays Code") governed the production and distribution of motion picture content in the United States of America - a self-imposed by movie studios and exhibitors set of guidelines about what could and could not be shown/mentioned/referred to in film (be it a feature whether live-action or animated, a short whether live-action or animated, a serial chapter, or a documentary newsreel). Similar sets of guidelines governed graphic novels, comic books and newspaper comic strips (the Comics Code from 1954 to 2011), the National Association of Broadcasters' Code of Practices for Television Broadcasters (the so-called Television Code from 1952 to 1983) with a similar set of guidelines for radio, and the near-censorship of video games by the North American nations' governments before the Entertainment Software Association came up with the voluntary, self-regulating Entertainment Software Rating Board to inform consumers about content. There were various religious and secular moralistic censorship groups across the United States at the time dedicating themselves to preserving morality and good taste in American culture of the time through literature, music, sports, comic strips, motion pictures and radio. Various Tinseltown scandals led up to the 1915 U.S. Supreme Court case Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio which unanimously held that free speech protections of the U.S. Constitution's 1st Amendment did not extend to motion pictures. But for our purposes, let's examine what if instead the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that radio, literature, comic strips, music and motion pictures were in fact protected by the 1st Amendment. If the Supreme Court were to decide that no local, state, or federal political body had the right to regulate or censor the production and distribution of any work of radio, film, literature, music within reason and neither did any religious or business organization within reason, then what? If the National/Catholic Legion of Decency, the National Board of Review and the Motion Picture Association (then the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America) were ordered by the Supreme Court to within reason allow for almost any type of motion pictures to be created so long as no people (especially children) and or animals were harmed by the making of a film, where should they go from here? items.model_answer:
If film, comics, and broadcasting had received strong First Amendment protection and effective union protection much earlier in the twentieth century, American popular culture would probably have become more politically open, more formally experimental, and more professionally organized decades sooner. But it would not simply have become “free.” Market pressure, racism, sexism, advertiser control, studio ownership, and public moral campaigns would still have shaped what audiences saw and heard.

For film, the biggest change would have been the weakening or possible nonexistence of the Hollywood Production Code system as it actually operated from the mid-1930s to the 1960s. In real history, movies were long treated as a business subject to censorship rather than as protected expression; the Supreme Court did not clearly recognize film as First Amendment speech until 1952. If that recognition had come in the 1910s or 1920s, state and local censorship boards would have had less power, and studios would have had less incentive to accept strict self-censorship under the Hays Code. American cinema might have retained more of the frankness associated with “pre-Code” films: more open treatment of sexuality, crime, labor conflict, corruption, interracial life, gender nonconformity, and political radicalism. Social-problem films, anti-lynching films, pro-labor films, and films critical of capitalism or militarism might have been more visible earlier.

Earlier union protections would also have changed Hollywood from the inside. Actors, writers, directors, animators, technicians, and below-the-line workers would likely have gained better wages, safer hours, clearer screen credit, grievance procedures, and bargaining power sooner. The studio system might still have existed, but its most coercive features—long-term contracts, blacklisting threats, exploitative schedules, and control over artists’ public lives—would have been harder to maintain. Residuals and reuse payments might have emerged earlier, especially once television began recycling films. On the other hand, stronger unions could have raised production costs and reduced the studios’ ability to churn out large numbers of low-budget films, so the industry might have become somewhat smaller, more negotiated, and more strike-prone.

The blacklist era would likely have been less devastating if both expressive and labor protections had been stronger. First Amendment doctrine alone would not have stopped private studios from refusing to hire suspected communists, but stronger unions with enforceable protections against political retaliation could have made mass blacklisting harder. The careers of many writers, actors, directors, and composers might not have been destroyed, and American film and television might have had a more continuous left-liberal, socialist, and anti-fascist tradition after World War II.

Comics would probably have developed as a more adult and diverse medium much earlier. In real history, the 1950s moral panic over juvenile delinquency led to the Comics Code Authority, which severely restricted crime, horror, sexuality, political ambiguity, and social criticism. If comics had been treated clearly as protected speech, and if comics writers and artists had had stronger labor organizations, publishers would have had more room to resist censorship campaigns and distributors. Horror, crime, romance, satire, and political comics might have survived as mainstream genres instead of being pushed underground or sanitized. The American “graphic novel” tradition could have emerged earlier, not waiting as long for underground comix, alternative comics, and later literary comics to legitimize the form.

Labor protections in comics would have had especially large consequences. Many creators in the early comic-book industry lost ownership, credit, and profits from characters that became extremely valuable. Stronger unions or guilds might have produced better contracts, creator royalties, health benefits, and rights reversion. The superhero genre might still have become dominant, but its economic structure would have been different: characters like Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Captain America, and later Marvel heroes might have generated more income and control for their creators. This could have encouraged more experimentation, because artists and writers would have had a better chance of benefiting from original work.

Broadcasting is more complicated because radio and television use the public spectrum, and the government would still have had a licensing role. Even with earlier First Amendment protection, courts might have allowed more regulation of broadcasting than of print because of spectrum scarcity and the perceived public-interest obligations of licensees. Still, stronger constitutional protection would have limited government pressure over political content, indecency, and controversial speech. Radio in the 1920s and 1930s, and television after World War II, might have included more radical politics, more labor voices, more minority programming, and more open criticism of government and corporate power.

Unions in broadcasting would also have mattered. Performers, writers, journalists, technicians, and musicians could have secured better wages, working conditions, authorship credit, and reuse payments earlier. Newsrooms might have been more insulated from owner and sponsor pressure if journalists had stronger collective rights. Entertainment workers would have had more leverage as radio programs moved into television and as recorded broadcasts, syndication, and reruns became profitable.

The broader cultural effect would likely have been an earlier breakdown of the sharp division between “respectable” high culture and “suspect” mass culture. Film, comics, radio, and television would have gained legitimacy sooner as forms of art, journalism, and political expression. American audiences might have encountered mature themes, anti-racist arguments, sexual frankness, labor politics, and formal experimentation earlier and more regularly.

But the change would not have eliminated censorship-like forces. Advertisers could still refuse sponsorship. Theater chains and distributors could still avoid controversial work. Religious groups, parent groups, and patriotic organizations could still organize boycotts. Southern segregationists could still pressure studios and broadcasters over racial content. Corporate owners could still prefer safe, profitable entertainment. Unions themselves might also have reflected the exclusions of their time, including racial and gender discrimination.

So the most likely result is not a fully liberated media landscape, but a less timid and less centralized one. American mass media would probably have become more adult, more politically varied, and more creator-conscious by the 1930s or 1940s rather than by the 1960s and after. The Production Code, the Comics Code, and the blacklist would either have been weaker or harder to enforce. Creators would have had more bargaining power, audiences would have seen a wider range of stories earlier, and the United States would have developed a more robust culture of popular artistic freedom well before the late twentieth century.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. Sure, the 3x difference in energy usage is going to be difficult to bear, but between that and losing a total war/starving, people will just build more power plants and mine more fossil fuels or mineral nitrates/phosphates.
