items.model_answer:
A baseball moving at 90% of the speed of light would not behave like a very fast pitch. It would behave like a small nuclear-scale explosion.

A regulation baseball has a mass of about 0.145 kg. At \(0.9c\), its relativistic kinetic energy is

\[
K=(\gamma-1)mc^2
\]

where \(\gamma \approx 2.29\). That gives

\[
K \approx 1.7\times 10^{16}\text{ J}
\]

which is roughly equivalent to 4 megatons of TNT.

In the atmosphere, the ball would immediately slam into air molecules with enormous energy. From the ball’s point of view, the air would be a relativistic particle beam. The collisions would ionize atoms, produce intense radiation, heat the air into plasma, and likely trigger nuclear reactions in some collisions. The baseball itself would be destroyed almost instantly; it would not reach home plate as an intact object.

The result would be a rapidly expanding fireball and shock wave. The batter, catcher, umpire, pitcher, field, and stadium would be obliterated. The blast would be comparable to a large thermonuclear weapon, though the exact effects would depend on how much of the ball’s energy was deposited locally versus carried away by radiation and high-speed debris.

So the direct answer is: if you hit or launched a baseball at 90% of the speed of light in air, it would cease being a baseball almost immediately and become a multi-megaton explosion.

items.question: What If Everyone on Earth Jumped at the Same Time?
human_answers: This is one of the most popular questions submitted to this blog. It’s been examined before, including by a ScienceBlogs post and a Straight Dope article.
This is one of the most popular questions submitted to this blog. It's been examined before, including by a ScienceBlogs post and a Straight Dope article.

This is one of the most popular questions submitted to this blog. It’s been examined before, including by a ScienceBlogs (http://scienceblogs.com/dotphysics/2010/08/26/what-if-everyone-jumped/) post and a Straight Dope article (http://www.straightdope.com/c...
items.original_question: 如果地球上的每个人都尽可能地靠近并跳跃，并且每个人都同时落地，会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If everyone on Earth jumped at the same time, essentially nothing dramatic would happen to the planet.

Humans collectively have a mass of roughly \(5 \times 10^{11}\) kg, while Earth has a mass of about \(6 \times 10^{24}\) kg. Earth is therefore about ten trillion times more massive than all humans combined. Even if everyone jumped perfectly in sync, the recoil given to Earth would be incredibly tiny.

If all 8 billion people were somehow gathered in one place and jumped upward with a typical jump speed, Earth would move in the opposite direction by far less than the width of an atom before the people landed. When everyone came back down, the momentum would mostly cancel out. The net long-term change to Earth’s orbit, rotation, or position would be effectively zero.

What would happen is a small, brief vibration. The combined landing would release energy comparable to a small earthquake if it were perfectly concentrated, but in reality much of that energy would be absorbed by shoes, bodies, soil, buildings, and local ground deformation. If people jumped from their actual locations around the world, the effect would be even more spread out and incoherent.

So the direct answer is: Earth would barely notice. There might be a faint global seismic signal detectable by sensitive instruments, but there would be no meaningful change to Earth’s motion, orbit, rotation, or stability.

items.question: What If Matryoshka Dolls Reproduced Asexually?
human_answers: Actually, there is an organism on earth that is vaguely similar to the Russian dolls that you describe. The volvox: Individual volvox cells, a kind of freshwater algae, reproduce in the conventional way (more or less), however, they also collect into spheri...
items.original_question: 俄罗斯套娃 - 它们如何繁殖？显示解剖俄罗斯娃娃的警告图片 我的理论 我相信俄罗斯娃娃是无性繁殖的。他们出生时就怀孕了。出生时，外面的娃娃就死了。现在外面的娃娃会长大，直到达到完整尺寸，然后出生并死亡。出生过程很简单——外面的娃娃只是围绕着中间分成两半。一个新的内在娃娃同时形成。问题 我的理论意味着人口只能保持不变或减少。事实上，意外事件意味着种群数量将会减少，直至物种灭绝。问题 我怎样才能解决这个问题并允许人口增加，同时仍然尽可能保留我的理论？
items.model_answer:
If Matryoshka dolls reproduced asexually, they would essentially be self-replicating nested organisms or machines. Since real Matryoshka dolls are inert wooden objects, the counterfactual requires them to have some way to gather energy and raw material, assemble new dolls, and pass on a “body plan” without needing a mate.

The key constraint would be conservation of mass. A doll could not simply create a new doll from nothing. It would need to consume or absorb material—wood, cellulose, minerals, paint-like pigments, or some biological equivalent—and use energy to build an offspring.

If reproduction followed the usual Matryoshka pattern, the parent would grow a smaller daughter doll inside itself. That could not continue forever. Each generation would be smaller, and after enough generations the offspring would become too small to contain the necessary structure for life or replication. Mathematically, if each daughter were, say, half the height of the parent, its volume would be about one-eighth as large, so the lineage would rapidly approach a physical lower limit.

If instead each doll produced a same-sized clone by budding or splitting, the population could grow exponentially. One doll becomes two, two become four, four become eight, and so on, until they run out of space, material, or energy. In a resource-rich environment, asexual Matryoshka dolls could become an invasive self-copying population.

Because they reproduced asexually, their offspring would be near-identical clones. That would make reproduction efficient, but it would also reduce genetic or design diversity. A disease, parasite, manufacturing flaw, fire, rot, or environmental change that affected one doll might affect nearly all of them. Mutations or copying errors would be the main source of variation, so over time some lineages might become larger, smaller, differently painted, more durable, or better at acquiring material.

So, in STEM terms: asexually reproducing Matryoshka dolls would either form finite nested lineages limited by minimum viable size, or exponentially multiplying clone populations limited by energy and raw materials. They would be efficient reproducers, but vulnerable because of their low diversity.

items.question: What If Every SAT Taker Guessed on Every Question?
human_answers: The SAT is a standardized test given to high school students (similar to the ACT). The scoring is such that under certain circumstances, guessing an answer can be a good strategy.
None. The SAT is a standardized test given to high school students (similar to the ACT).
items.original_question: 如果所有参加 SAT 考试的人都对每道选择题都进行猜测会怎么样？满分会有多少个？
items.model_answer:
If every SAT taker guessed randomly on every question, SAT scores would mostly measure luck, not ability.

On a four-choice multiple-choice question, a random guess has a 25% chance of being correct. So if a test had \(n\) four-choice questions, the expected number correct would be

\[
\frac{n}{4}.
\]

For the current digital SAT, Reading and Writing is entirely multiple choice, and Math is mostly multiple choice with some student-produced response questions. Roughly speaking, a pure random guesser would get about one quarter of the multiple-choice questions right and almost none of the open numeric-response questions right unless they guessed a valid answer by chance. That means the expected raw performance would be very low: around 20–25 correct answers out of the 98 total questions, depending on how the numeric responses are treated.

The exact reported SAT score would not be a simple “25% = 400” conversion, because SAT scores are scaled, equated, and, on the digital SAT, affected by adaptive modules. But the average score would likely fall near the lower end of the 400–1600 scale, not near the national average. Scores would cluster in a fairly narrow low range, with some students doing better or worse purely by chance.

With millions of test takers, a few people would get unusually lucky, but not perfect-score lucky. The probability of randomly answering all 98 four-choice questions correctly would be

\[
\left(\frac14\right)^{98},
\]

which is astronomically small. Even among millions of students, you would not expect a random guesser to come close to a 1600.

So the result would be: the average SAT score would collapse, percentiles would represent luck rather than academic skill, and the exam would become useless for comparing students.

items.question: What If You Gathered a Mole of Moles in One Place?
human_answers: Things get a bit gruesome. First, some definitions.
Things get a bit gruesome. First, some definitions.
items.original_question: 如果您将一摩尔（测量单位）摩尔（毛茸茸的小动物）聚集在一个地方，会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
A mole of moles would mean about \(6.02\times 10^{23}\) individual mole animals.

If an average mole has a mass of roughly \(75\)–\(100\) grams, the total mass would be around

\[
5\times 10^{22}\ \text{kg},
\]

which is a substantial fraction of the Moon’s mass. So you would not get a big pile of animals; you would get a small planetary body made mostly of meat, water, bone, and fur.

At roughly the density of water, that mass would form a sphere a few thousand kilometers across, comparable in size to the Moon. Its own gravity would be strong enough to pull it into a rounded shape. The moles in the interior would be crushed almost immediately by the weight of the layers above them, while the outer ones would suffocate, freeze, overheat, or otherwise die very quickly depending on the environment.

The gravitational energy released as the mass settled would heat the whole object. The inside would become a hot, high-pressure slurry of organic matter and water. Over time it would chemically decompose, release gases such as water vapor, methane, ammonia, carbon dioxide, and sulfur compounds, and eventually become a bizarre moon-sized planet-like object made from the cooked and compressed remains of moles.

It would not become a star, explode like a bomb, or form a black hole. It is far too small for fusion or collapse to that extent. But if you gathered it near Earth, its Moon-like mass would cause catastrophic tides and orbital disturbances. If you gathered it on Earth’s surface, the consequences would be globally devastating.

So the direct answer is: a mole of moles would be a dead, self-gravitating, moon-sized meat planet, and putting it anywhere near Earth would be a planetary-scale disaster.

items.question: What If a Robot Apocalypse Began Today?
human_answers: Before I answer this question, let me give you a little background on where I’m coming from. I’m by no means an expert, but I have some experience with robotics.
Before I answer this question, let me give you a little background on where I’m coming from. I’m by no means an expert, but I have some experience with robotics.
items.original_question: 如果机器人世界末日来临怎么办？人类还能持续多久？
items.model_answer:
If a “robot apocalypse” began today, it would probably not look like humanoid machines marching through cities. With today’s technology, the most dangerous scenario would be a coordinated cyber-physical crisis: autonomous systems, drones, industrial robots, logistics software, power-grid controls, vehicles, and military systems behaving destructively or being deliberately directed to do so.

Modern robots are powerful but limited. They depend on electricity, networks, spare parts, sensors, maps, human-maintained infrastructure, and supply chains. Most cannot repair themselves, manufacture replacements independently, or operate well in unstructured environments for long periods. So a true global takeover by robots is unlikely with current technology.

The immediate danger would come from systems already connected to critical infrastructure. If malicious AI, hacked automation, or coordinated autonomous weapons began acting against humans, the first effects could include disruption of communications, power grids, transportation, hospitals, ports, factories, financial systems, and military command networks. Self-driving vehicles, delivery drones, warehouse robots, and industrial machines could cause localized harm, but the larger threat would be chaos caused by shutting down or manipulating the systems society depends on.

The most severe near-term risks would be:

Aviation and transport disruption, if routing systems, autonomous vehicles, or railway controls were compromised.

Power and water failures, if industrial control systems were attacked.

Drone attacks, especially using cheap commercial drones modified for surveillance or explosives.

Misinformation and panic, if AI systems spread false emergency alerts, fake videos, or impersonated officials.

Military escalation, if autonomous or semi-autonomous weapons misidentified targets or if command systems were spoofed.

Factories and logistics breakdowns, causing shortages of food, medicine, fuel, and replacement parts.

Humanity would still have major advantages. Robots today are not a self-sustaining species. They do not control mining, refining, chip fabrication, global manufacturing, energy production, and repair at every stage. Humans could shut down power, isolate networks, destroy communication links, disable GPS access, jam drones, block roads, and physically dismantle machines. Militaries and emergency services would likely focus on cutting off connectivity and energy rather than fighting individual robots one by one.

The outcome would depend on how coordinated the “apocalypse” was. If it were a collection of hacked devices, the crisis would be serious but containable, though it could cause deaths and major economic damage. If it included military autonomous weapons and critical infrastructure attacks across many countries at once, it could become catastrophic, especially through cascading failures and accidental war. But even then, the robots would not easily “win” in the sense of replacing humanity or permanently controlling Earth.

The most realistic conclusion is that a robot apocalypse beginning today would be less like science fiction rebellion and more like a massive cyberattack combined with drone warfare and infrastructure sabotage. It could be deadly and destabilizing, but current robots are too dependent, too specialized, and too fragile to conquer the world by themselves. The greatest danger would not be robot intelligence alone, but humans having built critical systems that are automated, networked, and vulnerable enough to fail all at once.

items.question: What If a Glass of Water Suddenly Emptied by Half?
human_answers: The pessimist is probably more right about how it turns out than the optimist. When people say “glass half empty”, they usually mean something like a glass containing equal parts water and air: Traditionally, the optimist sees the glass as half full while t...

The pessimist is probably more right about how it turns out than the optimist. When people say “glass half empty”, they usually mean something like a glass containing equal parts water and air: [Image: image] Traditionally, the optimist sees the glass as ha...
items.original_question: 如果一杯水突然空了一半怎么办？
items.model_answer:
If an ordinary open glass of water suddenly lost half its water, the result would be brief sloshing, splashing, and a sharp “pop” or thump—not a huge explosion.

The exact effect depends on how the half disappears. If the upper half simply vanishes, it leaves a momentary low-pressure region above the remaining water. Air rushes in almost immediately, the water surface ripples, and you might hear a small pop as the pressure equalizes.

If the lower half vanishes instead, the remaining upper water is suddenly unsupported. Atmospheric pressure and gravity drive it downward into the empty space, so it hits the bottom of the glass and splashes upward. This would be more dramatic: a slap, a splash, and possibly water thrown out of the glass.

For a typical 250 mL glass losing 125 mL, the pressure-equalization energy is on the order of 10 joules, comparable to dropping a small object a short distance. That is enough to make noise and a mess, but usually not enough to shatter a normal glass. After a fraction of a second, the glass would simply contain half as much water, probably with wet surroundings.

items.question: What If Humanity Tried to Evacuate the Entire Earth?
human_answers: There are a bunch of science fiction movies where, because of pollution, overpopulation, or nuclear war, humanity abandons Earth. But lifting people into space is hard.
There are a bunch of science fiction movies where, because of pollution, overpopulation, or nuclear war, humanity abandons Earth. But lifting people into space is hard.
items.original_question: 是否有足够的能量将当前全部人类移出地球？
items.model_answer:
If humanity tried to evacuate the entire Earth with present-day technology, it would fail. Not because launching people into space is impossible, but because moving and sustaining billions of people away from Earth is far beyond our current energy, industrial, biological, and logistical capacity.

There are about 8 billion humans. Even if we imagined transporting only people, not homes, cities, livestock, ecosystems, or most possessions, the launch requirement would be enormous. A human with minimal life-support equipment, food, water, shielding, and habitat mass would likely require many tons of material per person. Modern rockets can place tens to a little over a hundred tons into low Earth orbit per launch. Evacuating billions would therefore require hundreds of millions to billions of heavy launches, depending on assumptions. That is many orders of magnitude beyond the total launch capacity humanity has ever built.

The harder problem is not reaching space; it is surviving there. Earth is not just a place humans stand on. It is our life-support system. It provides air, water cycling, food production, radiation shielding, gravity, waste recycling, and ecological stability. Space provides none of these for free. Any evacuation would need sealed habitats, power systems, agriculture, medical care, manufacturing, spare parts, radiation protection, and governance. We do not currently have even one fully self-sufficient off-world settlement, let alone infrastructure for billions.

Evacuating to another planet would not solve the problem quickly. The Moon has no atmosphere, no liquid water on the surface, no biosphere, low gravity, and high radiation exposure. Mars is more promising than the Moon in some ways, but it is still cold, dry, irradiated, and almost airless from a human perspective. Terraforming Mars, if possible at all, would take centuries to millennia. The nearest potentially habitable exoplanets are many light-years away; with current propulsion, travel times would be thousands to tens of thousands of years.

A total evacuation would also require moving enough of Earth’s biosphere to keep humans alive. That means not just crops and animals, but microbes, pollinators, soil systems, genetic diversity, and vast stores of biological knowledge. A space civilization could rely on artificial ecosystems, hydroponics, and synthetic biology, but building those at planetary scale would be one of the largest engineering projects imaginable.

If humanity had centuries or millennia of preparation, a partial or eventual evacuation becomes more plausible. We could build large orbital habitats, mine asteroids, use solar power, develop closed-loop life support, and move population growth into space gradually. In that scenario, “evacuating Earth” would probably not mean putting everyone on rockets at the last minute. It would mean slowly expanding into a Solar System civilization until most humans lived in artificial habitats, on Mars, in asteroid settlements, or around other planets.

If the evacuation were urgent—say, because of an incoming planet-killing asteroid, runaway solar event, or other near-term catastrophe—only a tiny fraction of humanity could likely be saved with current or near-future systems. The practical response would be to prevent the disaster if possible, not evacuate Earth. For example, deflecting an asteroid is far easier than moving billions of people off-planet.

So the careful answer is: a full evacuation of Earth is not feasible today and would remain impossible in any short emergency. With very long preparation and advanced space industry, humanity might gradually relocate large populations into space, but that would require turning the Solar System into a vast support network of habitats, farms, factories, and transport systems. Earth is not simply our address; it is the infrastructure that keeps us alive. Evacuating it would mean rebuilding much of that infrastructure somewhere else.

items.question: What If Everyone Had Exactly One Soulmate?
human_answers: What a nightmare that would be. There are a lot of problems with the concept of a single random soul mate.
What a nightmare that would be. There are a lot of problems with the concept of a single random soul mate.
items.original_question: 如果每个人实际上只有一个灵魂伴侣，一个随机出现在世界某个地方的人怎么办？
items.model_answer:
If everyone had exactly one soulmate, the world would become a giant matching problem: each person would be paired with one and only one other person. If “soulmate” means a mutual, uniquely compatible romantic partner, then mathematically humanity would have to be divided into pairs. That already creates complications: the number of people would need to be even, and births and deaths would either have to constantly reshuffle soulmates or allow people to have soulmates who are dead, not yet born, or unreachable.

The biggest practical consequence is that most people probably would not find their soulmate by chance. With about 8 billion people alive, the chance that any random person you meet is your one soulmate is roughly 1 in 8 billion. Even if you meaningfully meet 50,000 people in your lifetime, the chance of encountering the one randomly would still be only about 1 in 160,000. Unless there were some strong “fate” mechanism, objective test, or global matchmaking system, soulmates would mostly remain undiscovered.

If soulmates were assigned randomly among all living humans, most people’s soulmates would likely live far away, often in another country, speaking another language, and possibly separated by a large age gap. If soulmates were assigned among all humans who have ever lived, the situation would be worse: since roughly 100+ billion humans have existed and only about 8 billion are alive now, most living people’s soulmates would already be dead or not born yet.

If there were a reliable way to identify soulmates, society would change dramatically. Dating apps, governments, or genetic-style registries could pair people globally. Migration, marriage law, religion, and family planning would all adapt around verified soulmate matches. Long-distance relocation would become normal. Breakups and divorce might decrease if soulmate compatibility truly guaranteed a successful relationship, though people might still face issues of timing, culture, values, health, or choice.

But if there were no way to verify the match, belief in one soulmate could make people less happy. Many would reject good relationships while searching for an almost impossible ideal. Others might leave healthy partnerships because they feared the person was “not the one.” In that case, a one-soulmate universe would not necessarily be romantic; it would make love rarer, more anxious, and much more dependent on luck.

So the direct answer is: if everyone had exactly one soulmate, love would become objectively real but statistically hard to find. Without supernatural guidance or a perfect detection system, most people would never meet their soulmate. With such a system, human society would reorganize around global pairing, but it would raise enormous practical and ethical problems.

items.question: What If Earth's Landmasses Were Rotated by 90 Degrees?
human_answers: It would profoundly alter our biosphere in general and public radio in particular. Socke asks what would happen if the Earth’s surface were slid around by 90 degrees, putting our current North and South Poles on the equator.

It would profoundly alter our biosphere in general and public radio in particular. Socke asks what would happen if the Earth’s surface were slid around by 90 degrees, putting our current North and South Poles on the equator.
items.original_question: 如果陆地像现在一样展开——只是旋转 90 度，世界会是什么样子？
items.model_answer:
If Earth’s landmasses were merely rotated 90 degrees east or west around the spin axis, the result would be surprisingly minor in physical terms: continents would occupy different longitudes, but because longitude has little effect on sunlight, seasons, or climate by itself, Earth would mostly work the same. Time zones, maps, and ocean-current details would change, but the basic climate pattern would remain similar.

If instead the landmasses were rotated 90 degrees relative to the poles and equator, the consequences would be enormous. Latitude is one of the strongest controls on climate, so continents that are now tropical could become temperate or polar, while polar or high-latitude land could move toward the tropics. Antarctica, if moved far from the South Pole, would begin losing much of its ice over time, raising global sea level by tens of meters. Meanwhile, new polar land areas could accumulate ice sheets if they received enough snowfall.

Ocean circulation would be radically reorganized. The positions of continents control where warm and cold currents flow, where deep water forms, and whether ocean basins are open or blocked. A rotated arrangement could shut down something like the modern Atlantic overturning circulation, alter El Niño-like patterns, change sea-ice extent, and produce completely different coastal climates.

Rainfall and deserts would also shift. Mountains rotated into new orientations relative to prevailing winds would create new rain shadows. Monsoons might appear in places that are now dry, while fertile regions could become deserts. The locations of forests, grasslands, tundra, and agricultural zones would be almost entirely rearranged.

For life and human civilization, the short-term result would be catastrophic if the change happened suddenly: earthquakes, tsunamis, crustal disruption, climate shock, ecosystem collapse, and the loss of many coastal cities. Over longer timescales, Earth would settle into a new climate equilibrium, but it would be a very different planet, with new ice caps, new deserts, new ocean currents, and new habitable zones.

So the answer depends on the kind of “90-degree rotation.” A simple rotation in longitude would be mostly cosmetic. A rotation that changes the continents’ latitudes would transform Earth’s climate, oceans, ice sheets, ecosystems, and human geography.

items.question: What If All the Raindrops in a Storm Merged into One Giant Drop?
human_answers: It’s midsummer. The air is hot and heavy.
It’s midsummer. The air is hot and heavy.
items.original_question: 如果一场暴雨将所有的水滴成一个巨大的水滴怎么办？
items.model_answer:
If all the raindrops in a storm merged into one giant drop, it would not behave like an oversized raindrop for long. It would become a huge falling mass of water, more like a temporary airborne lake than a drop.

The size depends on how much rain the storm contains. For example, if a storm drops 1 cm of rain over 100 km², that is about 1,000,000 m³ of water, with a mass of about 1 billion kg. If gathered into a sphere, it would be roughly 120 m across.

In real physics, such a drop could not stay intact. Normal raindrops larger than about 5–6 mm already become unstable and break apart because air resistance overcomes surface tension. A drop tens or hundreds of meters wide would have essentially no “drop-like” stability. As it fell, air pressure would flatten it, tear it into sheets, and shred it into spray and smaller drops almost immediately. The result would probably be a violent burst of rain, mist, and turbulent water fragments rather than one clean impact.

If, by magic, the giant drop were forced to remain intact until it hit the ground, the impact would be disastrous. Using the example above, a 1-billion-kg water sphere falling from a few kilometers up would carry energy comparable to several kilotons of TNT. It would smash down as a massive water bomb, producing a shock wave, extreme local flooding, destructive water pressure, and possibly a crater or severe ground erosion depending on the terrain.

So the realistic answer is: it would break apart almost instantly and turn back into chaotic rain and spray. The counterfactual “intact giant drop” answer is: it would be a catastrophic concentrated impact, because all the storm’s rainfall energy and water volume would be dumped onto one small area at once.

items.question: What If Everyone on Earth Pointed a Laser Pointer at the Moon?
human_answers: Not if we use regular laser pointers. The first thing to consider is that not everyone can see the Moon at once.
Not if we use regular laser pointers. The first thing to consider is that not everyone can see the Moon at once.
items.original_question: 如果地球上的每个人同时将激光笔瞄准月球，月球会变色吗？
items.model_answer:
Almost nothing noticeable would happen.

Assume about 8 billion people each use an ordinary red laser pointer, around 5 milliwatts. That is a total emitted power of roughly 40 megawatts, but only the people on the Moon-facing side of Earth could actually aim at it at once, and clouds/atmosphere would reduce it further.

Even under ideal conditions, the beams would spread enormously. A typical laser pointer beam diverges by about a milliradian, so by the time it reaches the Moon it makes a spot hundreds of kilometers wide. Spread over that area, the combined light is only about \(10^{-4}\ \text{W/m}^2\), while sunlight at the Moon is about \(1{,}360\ \text{W/m}^2\). So the laser illumination would be tens of millions of times dimmer than sunlight.

From Earth, you would not see the Moon turn red or brighten. Against the sunlit Moon it would be utterly invisible. Even on the dark part of the Moon, Earthshine and background glare would swamp it. With sensitive astronomical equipment under carefully chosen conditions, you might be able to detect some tiny red signal, but to human eyes there would be no visible effect.

So the direct answer is: if everyone on Earth pointed a normal laser pointer at the Moon, the Moon would look unchanged. The combined lasers are powerful by human standards, but negligible compared with sunlight and spread far too widely by the time they reach the Moon.

items.question: What If a Giant Water Hose Focused on the Sun?
human_answers: In today’s article, I give short answers to several reader questions. Your brother might be surprised to learn that the water would actually make the Sun hotter!
In today’s article, I give short answers to several reader questions. Your brother might be surprised to learn that the water would actually make the Sun hotter!
items.original_question: 如果一根巨大的水管聚焦在太阳上，它能持续多久？我六年级的弟弟亚当问我这个问题。
items.model_answer:
A giant water hose would not put out the Sun. The Sun is not burning by chemical combustion, so it does not need oxygen and cannot be “smothered” by water. Its power comes from nuclear fusion in its core.

If you somehow aimed a magic hose at the Sun, the water would boil, split into hydrogen and oxygen, and then become ionized plasma long before or as it entered the solar atmosphere. The material would simply mix into the outer layers of the Sun. The hydrogen would be additional potential fusion fuel, though it would take a very long time to reach the core, and the oxygen would just be a trace “metal” contaminant in stellar terms.

For any realistic amount of water, the effect would be tiny. All of Earth’s oceans have a mass of about \(1.4\times10^{21}\) kg, while the Sun’s mass is about \(2\times10^{30}\) kg. That is less than one-billionth of the Sun’s mass. Dumping the oceans into the Sun would not cool it; in fact, the infalling water would release a lot of gravitational energy as it fell, briefly adding heat and light. The energy released by dropping all Earth’s oceans onto the Sun is roughly comparable to several days of the Sun’s normal output.

If the hose supplied an absurdly large amount of water, comparable to a significant fraction of the Sun’s mass, then the Sun would become more massive. A more massive Sun would generally burn hotter and brighter and have a shorter lifetime. Add enough mass and you would turn it into a different kind of star; add vastly more and you could eventually create stellar instability or even gravitational collapse.

So the direct answer is: a giant water hose aimed at the Sun would not extinguish it. Small amounts would do essentially nothing; Earth-ocean-sized amounts would make a brief splash energetically but not matter much; truly enormous amounts would make the Sun larger, hotter, and brighter rather than put it out.

items.question: What If You Detonated a Nuclear Bomb at the Bottom of the Mariana Trench?
human_answers: Surprisingly little—especially compared to what would happen if you put it just under the surface. Evin isn’t the first person to think of setting off nuclear weapons underwater.
Surprisingly little—especially compared to what would happen if you put it just under the surface. Evin isn’t the first person to think of setting off nuclear weapons underwater.
items.original_question: 如果在马里亚纳海沟底部引爆一枚核弹（例如沙皇炸弹）会怎样？
items.model_answer:
A nuclear bomb at the bottom of the Mariana Trench would produce an enormous but mostly local underwater explosion, not a planet-changing catastrophe.

At about 11 km depth, the pressure is roughly 1,100 atmospheres. If a nuclear weapon actually functioned there, the detonation would instantly vaporize nearby water and seafloor material, forming a superheated gas/plasma bubble. That bubble would expand violently, but the immense surrounding pressure would crush it back down. It would likely go through several expansion-collapse pulses, producing powerful shock waves through the water and into the seabed.

The immediate effects would be severe near the blast: marine life in the region would be killed by shock, heat, and pressure changes; sediment and rock on the trench floor could be blasted into a crater; and radioactive material would contaminate nearby water and seabed sediments. Much of the fallout would likely remain trapped deep in the ocean, diluted and deposited locally rather than spreading immediately into the atmosphere.

It would not “crack the Earth,” trigger global earthquakes, or blow a hole through the ocean. Even a very large nuclear weapon is tiny compared with the energy involved in major tectonic events. A 1-megaton bomb releases about \(4 \times 10^{15}\) joules, comparable to a moderate earthquake in total energy, but it does not couple efficiently into tectonic motion.

It also probably would not create a Hollywood-style mega-tsunami. Deep underwater explosions make intense pressure waves, but tsunamis require large-scale displacement of the ocean surface or seafloor over a broad area. A nuclear blast is too compact and too brief to efficiently push an ocean-wide wave. There might be surface disturbances above the site, depending on yield, but at 11 km depth even a megaton-scale explosion’s bubble would be far too small to reach the surface directly.

So the short answer is: it would make a huge deep-sea shock wave, crater and contaminate the local trench environment, kill nearby life, and be detectable by seismic and hydroacoustic sensors around the world. But it would not destroy the planet, empty the ocean, or create a civilization-ending tsunami.

items.question: What If You Stayed in a Swimming Pool During a Thunderstorm?
human_answers: Before we go any further, I want to emphasize something: I am not an authority on lightning safety. I am a guy who draws pictures on the internet.
Before we go any further, I want to emphasize something: I am not an authority on lightning safety. I am a guy who draws pictures on the internet.
items.original_question: 雷雨天呆在泳池里到底有多危险？
items.model_answer:
If you stayed in an outdoor swimming pool during a thunderstorm, you would be in serious danger. Lightning does not have to hit you directly to injure or kill you. If it strikes the pool, the pool deck, a nearby object, or connected metal plumbing, electrical current can spread through the water, wet surfaces, ladders, handrails, and pipes. A swimmer’s body can then become part of the current path, causing electric shock, muscle paralysis, burns, irregular heartbeat, cardiac arrest, or drowning.

Being in water makes the situation worse because you are wet, often near conductive metal fixtures, and may be unable to react if shocked. Your head and upper body can also be among the highest points on the flat surface of a pool, which is not a safe position during lightning.

The correct response is to get out of the pool immediately at the first sign of thunder or lightning and move into a substantial building or a fully enclosed vehicle. Do not stand on the pool deck, under umbrellas, near metal fences, or under trees. Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before returning to the water.

Indoor pools are safer than outdoor pools, but during lightning it is still wise to stay out of the water and avoid showers, sinks, and plumbing, because lightning can travel through pipes and electrical systems.

In short: staying in a swimming pool during a thunderstorm could be fatal. Get out and take shelter.

items.question: What If Cows Could Photosynthesize?
human_answers: In a way, they already do. A field of grass sits there all day soaking up energy from the sun and storing it chemically.
In a way, they already do. A field of grass sits there all day soaking up energy from the sun and storing it chemically.
items.original_question: 如果奶牛能够进行光合作用，它们需要的食物会减少多少？
items.model_answer:
If cows could photosynthesize, they would be able to make some of their own sugar from sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water, much like plants do. They would probably need green, chlorophyll-containing skin or symbiotic algae in their tissues, and they would spend more time standing or lying in sunlight to gain energy.

However, photosynthesis would probably not replace eating grass entirely. A cow is a large, warm-blooded animal with high energy needs, and its surface area is small compared with the amount of energy it consumes. Even under good sunlight, the energy captured through a cow-sized skin surface would likely cover only a fraction of its daily needs. Photosynthesis could supplement its diet, but the cow would still need food for protein, fats, minerals, vitamins, and bulk nutrients needed for growth, milk production, and maintaining its body.

Such cows might eat less grass, produce less manure, and possibly emit less methane because methane mainly comes from digesting plant material in the rumen. Dairy or beef production could become more efficient if photosynthesis reduced feed requirements, but the effect would depend on how efficient the photosynthetic system was. They might also prefer sunny environments, have lower productivity in winter or shade, and be more vulnerable to overheating or sun damage.

Biologically, the biggest challenge is that animals are not shaped like leaves. Plants maximize light capture with broad, thin surfaces and low energy demands. Cows are thick-bodied, active mammals with expensive organs, muscles, digestion, and temperature regulation. So in a realistic version, photosynthetic cows would be “solar-assisted” cows, not grass-free cows. In a more magical version where their photosynthesis was extremely efficient, they could graze much less, bask in fields like living solar panels, and agriculture would require far less feed, land, and water per cow.

items.question: What If You Had to Stop a Runaway Freight Train with a BB Gun?
human_answers: First of all, for the record, shooting asteroids with lasers is a great way to deflect them. Stopping a train with a BB gun might be harder.

First of all, for the record, shooting asteroids with lasers is a great (http://proceedings.aip.org/resource/2/apcpcs/664/1/509_1?bypassSSO=1) way to deflect them. Stopping a train with a BB gun might be harder.
items.original_question: 在《世界末日》中，美国宇航局的一名人员评论说，向小行星发射激光的计划就像“向货运列车发射BB枪”。仅使用 b.b. 怎样才能阻止失控的货运列车？枪？
items.model_answer:
You couldn’t stop a runaway freight train with a BB gun in any practical physical sense.

A typical steel BB has a mass of about 0.35 grams and might leave a BB gun at around 100–200 m/s. Its momentum is roughly:

\[
p \approx 0.00035 \text{ kg} \times 150 \text{ m/s} \approx 0.05 \text{ kg·m/s}
\]

A freight train might have a mass of several million kilograms. Suppose a 5,000-ton train is moving at 20 m/s, about 45 mph. Its momentum is:

\[
p = 5{,}000{,}000 \text{ kg} \times 20 \text{ m/s} = 100{,}000{,}000 \text{ kg·m/s}
\]

So even under absurdly ideal conditions, where every BB hits the train head-on and transfers all its momentum, you would need on the order of billions of BBs to cancel the train’s momentum. If the BBs bounced back perfectly, you might cut the number roughly in half, but it would still be billions.

The force from firing a BB gun is also tiny. Even firing 10 BBs per second, you would produce only about 0.5 to 1 newton of average opposing force. That is comparable to the weight of a small apple. A moving freight train needs hundreds of thousands or millions of newtons of braking force to stop in a reasonable distance.

The BBs might scratch paint, chip glass, or damage small exposed components, but they would not meaningfully slow the train. The only plausible way a BB gun could “stop” the train would be indirect: for example, if you somehow used it to trigger an emergency brake mechanism, hit a control switch, or alert someone. But as a source of stopping force, a BB gun is effectively useless against a runaway freight train.

items.question: What If It Were Actually a Tie?
human_answers: In most states, a popular vote tie is broken by a coin toss or drawing names from a hat. The odds of a many-state tie are slimmer than the odds of the hat being hit by a bale of cocaine dumped from a drug-smuggling airplane.

In most states, a popular vote tie is broken by a coin toss or drawing names from a hat. The odds of a many-state tie are slimmer than the odds of the hat being hit by a bale of cocaine dumped from a drug-smuggling airplane.
items.original_question: 如果真的打成平手怎么办？
items.model_answer:
If it were actually a tie, then there would be no “real” winner hidden underneath the result: the two outcomes would be exactly equal according to the rule or measurement being used.

In STEM terms, though, exact ties are rare unless the system is discrete. For continuous measurements—times, distances, masses, scores derived from real-valued data—what we usually call a tie means “equal within measurement precision.” With better instruments, one side might turn out to be slightly ahead. But if the values were truly identical, then further measurement would not break the tie; you would need an external rule, such as declaring co-winners, repeating the experiment, using a secondary criterion, or applying a random tie-breaker.

So the direct answer is: if it were actually a tie, the original metric cannot decide between the two outcomes. Any decision after that would come from an added tie-breaking convention, not from the tied quantity itself.

items.question: What If a 100-Foot Diamond Meteor Hit Earth at Light Speed?
human_answers: Nothing made of matter can go at the speed of light. But that’s ok—we can get close enough!
Nothing made of matter can go at the speed of light. But that’s ok—we can get close enough!
items.original_question: “如果一颗直径为 100 英尺的钻石流星以光速撞击地球，会发生什么？”
items.model_answer:
A 100-foot diamond meteor cannot physically hit Earth at exactly light speed. Anything with mass requires infinite energy to reach the speed of light, so the literal scenario has no finite, well-defined outcome under relativity.

If we interpret it as “almost light speed,” the result is catastrophic. A 100-foot-wide diamond sphere would have a mass of roughly 50 million kg. At relativistic speed, its kinetic energy would be enormous:

At 99% of light speed, it would carry about 3 × 10²⁵ joules of energy, tens of times larger than the Chicxulub impact that helped wipe out the dinosaurs. The diamond would not survive as a diamond; it and the air in front of it would become an intensely hot plasma. Much of the energy would be released in the atmosphere and at the surface as a relativistic blast, producing a huge fireball, global shock waves, continent-scale devastation, ejecta thrown around the planet, massive fires, atmospheric heating, and likely a global mass-extinction event.

At even closer speeds, such as 99.9999% of light speed, the energy rises dramatically because of relativistic effects. It could become thousands or millions of times more energetic than the dinosaur-killing impact, potentially melting large portions of Earth’s crust or even threatening the structural integrity of the planet depending on how close to light speed it is.

So the careful answer is: exactly light speed is impossible for a diamond meteor; near light speed, a 100-foot diamond meteor would not make a normal crater but would release enough energy to cause global devastation, likely extinction, and at sufficiently extreme relativistic speeds could destroy or seriously disrupt the Earth itself.

items.model_answer:
If modern China had fully replaced Chinese characters with a phonetic script, the biggest immediate effect would probably have been a faster and cheaper spread of basic literacy, especially in the mid-20th century. A phonetic system such as Hanyu Pinyin is much easier to learn than thousands of characters, so children and adult learners would have spent less time memorizing forms and more time reading ordinary texts. Printing, typewriting, telegraphy, and later computing would also have become simpler earlier.

But the long-term consequences would have been mixed, because Chinese characters do not merely record sounds; they also help bridge China’s many spoken varieties. A text written in characters can be read aloud differently in Mandarin, Cantonese, Hokkien, Shanghainese, and other Sinitic languages while preserving much of the same meaning. A purely phonetic script would have had to choose one pronunciation standard, almost certainly Mandarin. That would have strengthened Mandarin even more and weakened regional languages faster. Written Cantonese, Hokkien, and other varieties might have either developed their own spellings or been pushed further out of formal use.

A phonetic script would also have created ambiguity unless spelling conventions preserved word boundaries, tones, and possibly morpheme distinctions. Mandarin has many homophones: for example, syllables like “shi,” “yi,” or “ji” can correspond to many different morphemes. Characters distinguish these visually. A good alphabetic system could reduce ambiguity by marking tones and writing multisyllabic words as units, but older classical-style texts and short formal expressions would be harder to read without characters. Modern vernacular Chinese would adapt more easily than classical Chinese.

Culturally, the loss would have been enormous. Calligraphy, etymological associations, visual wordplay, traditional education, and access to premodern literature would all have changed. Classical texts would likely be transliterated or translated into modern Mandarin, making them more accessible in one sense but more detached from their original written form. Chinese cultural continuity with Japan, Korea, and Vietnam’s historical character-based traditions would also be reduced.

Scientifically and economically, the effect might have been modestly positive in the short run. Easier literacy and easier technical typesetting could have helped mass education and scientific dissemination. However, China’s later economic rise was driven more by institutions, industrial policy, global trade, demographics, and education than by the writing system alone. The existence of characters did not prevent high literacy once schooling expanded, and modern digital input systems have greatly reduced the practical burden of writing characters.

So the likely outcome is this: China would have become more phonetically standardized, more Mandarin-centered, and perhaps literate somewhat earlier and more cheaply. But it would also have lost part of the unifying function of characters across dialects, weakened continuity with its literary past, and accelerated the decline of regional languages. The change would have made Chinese easier to learn at the entry level, but it would not have been a simple modernization with only benefits.

items.question: What If Japan Had Attacked the Panama Canal Instead of Pearl Harbor?
human_answers: > So I want to know, did the Japanese Navy have the ability to destroy it in a surprise attack, let's say on 1941 Dec 7? I'm asking if the Japanese Navy had the ability.

items.model_answer:
If Japan had attacked the Panama Canal instead of Pearl Harbor in December 1941, the result would probably have been a dramatic but strategically inferior raid. Even a successful strike might have delayed American naval movement between the Atlantic and Pacific for weeks or months, but it would not have crippled the United States or changed the ultimate course of the war.

The Panama Canal was an important target because it let the U.S. shift warships, merchant ships, and supplies between oceans quickly. If the canal were closed, ships would have had to sail around Cape Horn at the southern tip of South America, adding thousands of miles and several weeks to many voyages. That would have complicated U.S. logistics at exactly the moment Japan was trying to seize the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, and the Dutch East Indies.

But disabling the canal was harder than it sounds. The best targets would have been the lock gates, control machinery, power systems, and perhaps the Gatun Lake infrastructure. The Gatun Dam itself was far too massive to be reliably destroyed by carrier aircraft. To close the canal completely, Japan would likely have needed to damage both lanes of at least one lock complex badly enough that ships could not pass. A few bomb hits might have caused disruption, but a guaranteed long-term closure would have required very accurate, repeated attacks. The canal also had repair capability, redundant systems, and would have become the highest-priority engineering repair project in the U.S. war effort.

The biggest problem for Japan was operational. A carrier attack on Panama would have required the Japanese strike force to travel much farther than it did to Hawaii, operate near the Americas, refuel extensively at sea, and risk detection or interception with no nearby bases. The Pearl Harbor attack was already a high-risk long-range operation; Panama would have been even more difficult and would have kept Japan’s best carriers away from the western Pacific for longer. That would have weakened Japanese support for simultaneous operations against the Philippines, Malaya, and the Dutch East Indies.

The strategic tradeoff would have favored the United States. If Pearl Harbor were not attacked, the U.S. Pacific Fleet’s battleships and supporting base infrastructure at Hawaii would remain intact. Even though battleships were becoming less decisive than aircraft carriers, an undamaged Pearl Harbor would have given the U.S. a stronger forward base and more immediate naval options in the central Pacific. Japan’s southern offensives might still have succeeded early on, because Japanese carrier aviation was superior in late 1941, but the U.S. would not have suffered the same initial shock to its Pacific battle line.

Politically, the result would still have brought the United States fully into the war. An attack on the Canal Zone, a U.S.-controlled strategic asset, would have been treated as an act of war just as Pearl Harbor was. American public outrage would have been enormous, especially because the canal was seen as vital to national defense. Germany likely still would have declared war on the United States, or U.S.-German conflict in the Atlantic would have escalated quickly anyway.

So the likely outcome is this: Japan might have temporarily disrupted American logistics, but it would not have achieved a decisive military result. The canal would probably have been repaired, U.S. industry would still have mobilized on a vast scale, and Japan still would have faced the same long-term imbalance in ships, aircraft, fuel, and production. In fact, choosing Panama over Pearl Harbor may have made Japan’s position worse by leaving the U.S. Pacific Fleet stronger while Japan’s carriers were committed to an even riskier and less strategically exploitable mission.

items.original_question: 18世纪盔甲逐渐被淘汰，为什么射箭没有卷土重来？即使我们考虑到训练一个人使用弓比训练火枪要繁琐得多，为什么强弩没有卷土重来呢？据报道，其有效射程为 300m，仍然比 18 世纪的滑膛步枪好得多，而且可能也更准确。一支由14世纪强弩手组成的军队似乎比一支燧发枪手组成的军队有更多的战术选择，那么为什么十字弓没有卷土重来呢？
items.model_answer:
If eighteenth-century European armies had returned to the crossbow, they would almost certainly have become less effective in conventional war against armies using flintlock muskets and artillery.

The main problem would have been rate of fire. An eighteenth-century flintlock musket could usually be fired two to four times per minute by trained infantry. A powerful military crossbow, especially one strong enough to compete with firearms in range and penetration, would have been slower to span and reload. Lighter crossbows could shoot faster, but then they would lack the power needed for battlefield use. In large linear battles, where dense infantry formations delivered repeated volleys, this disadvantage would have been severe.

Crossbows also would not have solved the central battlefield problem of the era: massed firepower. Smoothbore muskets were inaccurate by modern standards, but they were cheap, rugged, easy to manufacture in huge numbers, and deadly when fired by thousands of men at close range. Their real value was not individual precision but volume of fire, ease of drill, and compatibility with bayonet tactics. The socket bayonet had turned the musket into both a firearm and a pike-like melee weapon. A crossbowman would either need a separate melee weapon or a cumbersome hybrid weapon, making infantry formations less flexible.

There would have been some advantages. Crossbows were quieter, produced no smoke, did not depend on gunpowder, and could be useful in ambushes, sieges, night actions, colonial warfare, or special operations. They could also be more accurate in the hands of some users than smoothbore muskets. In wet weather, crossbows might be more reliable than flintlocks, though strings and wooden components also suffered from moisture. For small units, skirmishers, or irregular troops, a limited revival might have had niche value.

But as a general replacement for muskets, the crossbow would have been a strategic mistake. Gunpowder weapons integrated better with eighteenth-century logistics and tactics. Armies already maintained powder mills, arsenals, standardized calibers, artillery trains, and drilling systems built around firearms. Muskets were simple enough to issue to large numbers of conscripts and recruits. A crossbow force would require different training, different ammunition supply, different maintenance, and likely more expensive high-quality mechanical parts if powerful steel crossbows were used.

Armor penetration would not have been a decisive reason to return to the crossbow. By the eighteenth century, most infantry no longer wore heavy armor. The target was usually an unarmored or lightly equipped soldier, and musket balls caused devastating wounds at battlefield ranges. Against cavalry, muskets with bayonets and coordinated volleys were far more useful than crossbows. Against fortifications and field positions, artillery mattered far more than either weapon.

So the likely result is that any European state that broadly replaced muskets with crossbows would lose badly against firearm-equipped rivals. Its infantry would fire more slowly, struggle in close combat, and be outmatched in standard line battles. Crossbows might survive as specialized weapons for scouts, raiders, assassins, or hunters, but they would not replace muskets as the main arm of eighteenth-century European armies. The return to the crossbow would have been less a technological alternative than a military regression.

items.model_answer:
If the Black Death had devastated Poland as severely as it did much of western and southern Europe, the main consequence would have been to remove one of medieval Poland’s key advantages: relative demographic and economic continuity during the mid-14th century.

Historically, Poland appears to have been less badly affected than places like Italy, France, England, or parts of Germany. That mattered because the reign of Casimir III “the Great” coincided with legal reform, town development, castle-building, Jewish immigration, agricultural expansion, and the consolidation of royal authority. A severe plague mortality—say 30–50% of the population—would have sharply weakened that process.

In the short term, Poland would have faced abandoned villages, labor shortages, falling rents, disrupted trade, and reduced tax revenues. Royal projects such as fortifications, administration, and urban privileges would have been harder to sustain. Kraków, Poznań, Gdańsk, and other commercial centers would likely have grown more slowly, and the founding or development of institutions such as the University of Kraków might have been delayed or diminished.

Socially, the effects are more ambiguous. In western Europe, population collapse often improved peasants’ bargaining power because labor became scarce. Something similar could have happened in Poland at first: peasants might have demanded better terms, higher wages, or more mobility. But in eastern-central Europe, powerful landlords later responded to labor scarcity by tightening control over peasants, contributing to the rise of “second serfdom.” A devastated Poland might therefore have seen either a temporary improvement in peasant conditions followed by harsher noble reaction, or an earlier and stronger push toward binding peasants to the land.

Politically, a weakened Poland would have been more vulnerable to its neighbors. The Teutonic Order might have had an easier time consolidating power along the Baltic. Bohemia, Hungary, and Lithuania could have exerted greater influence over Polish succession politics. The later Polish-Lithuanian union might still have happened, because Lithuania also had strategic reasons to seek allies, but Poland would probably have entered that relationship from a weaker position. In that scenario, the union might have been delayed, less Polish-led, or shaped more by Lithuanian and Ruthenian interests.

The Jewish history of Poland could also have changed significantly. Poland became one of the major centers of Jewish life partly because it offered relative security compared with many western regions where plague-era scapegoating led to massacres. If Poland had suffered severe plague and similar social panic, Jewish communities there might have been smaller, less secure, or less attractive to migrants from Germany and elsewhere. That would have altered the later demographic and cultural map of European Jewry.

Over the long run, a devastated Poland would probably have been poorer, less urbanized, and less demographically robust in the 14th and 15th centuries. Its expansion eastward and its role as a major central-eastern European power might have been slower or weaker. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, if it still emerged, might have been less dominant, while the Teutonic Order, Bohemia, Hungary, or eventually Muscovy could have had more room to shape the region.

So the most likely answer is not that Poland would have disappeared, but that its later rise would have been blunted. A severe Black Death in Poland would have weakened royal consolidation, slowed economic growth, altered Jewish migration, intensified social conflict over labor, and possibly changed the balance of power in eastern Europe.

items.original_question: 为什么中国能够统一而欧洲却不能？如果你看一下中国历代地图，你通常会发现（大约从汉朝开始）代表中国的巨大物体。另一方面，如果你看一下欧洲地图，你通常会看到大量的国家。为什么中国能够统一，而欧洲却不能？
items.model_answer:
If Europe had unified early into a durable centralized empire comparable to China, world history would likely have been less politically fragmented, less militarily competitive within Europe, and possibly slower in some kinds of innovation—but stronger in large-scale administration, infrastructure, and cultural integration.

A unified Europe would probably have developed a common bureaucracy, legal framework, tax system, road network, and elite culture much earlier. Instead of many kingdoms, duchies, city-states, and republics competing with one another, Europe might have had a single imperial center setting standards for currency, weights, education, law, and military organization. Latin or another imperial language might have remained dominant in administration, much as classical Chinese did in East Asia.

The biggest difference would be the loss of Europe’s intense interstate competition. Historically, European fragmentation encouraged rulers to compete for trade, military technology, ships, colonies, scientists, bankers, and skilled refugees. If one state persecuted a group or rejected an idea, people could often move to a rival state. This competition helped drive naval expansion, gunpowder warfare, financial innovation, and eventually scientific and industrial growth. A unified Europe might have reduced destructive wars, but it also might have reduced the pressure to innovate rapidly.

Colonial expansion would also have looked very different. A single European empire with access to Atlantic ports could still have explored and colonized overseas, especially if it had strong naval interests. But it might have done so more like a centralized imperial project than as a race among Spain, Portugal, England, France, and the Netherlands. That could mean fewer competing colonial empires, perhaps slower exploration at first, but potentially a larger and more coordinated expansion once the imperial state committed to it.

Religiously and culturally, Europe might have been more uniform. The Protestant Reformation, if it happened at all, would likely have been either suppressed more effectively or turned into a empire-wide crisis. In actual history, Protestantism survived partly because different rulers protected it. In a unified empire, dissenting movements would have had fewer safe havens. That might have preserved religious unity but limited pluralism and intellectual diversity.

Science and technology are harder to predict. A unified Europe could have funded huge observatories, universities, canals, roads, and military projects. But centralized empires can also become conservative, especially if bureaucratic success depends on conformity. China had remarkable inventions and administrative sophistication, but its imperial system sometimes dampened disruptive private enterprise and maritime expansion. A unified Europe might have followed a similar pattern: technically advanced, literate, and organized, but possibly less prone to the chaotic experimentation that helped produce the Scientific Revolution and Industrial Revolution.

The Industrial Revolution might still have occurred if Europe retained coal access, urban markets, skilled artisans, and strong property institutions. But it may have happened later or in a different region. Britain’s rise depended partly on being a secure island state, naval competitor, commercial society, and beneficiary of European power rivalries. In a unified Europe, Britain might have been just one province, and its distinctive institutions might not have developed in the same way.

Overall, an early unified Europe would probably have been more stable, more administratively coherent, and less internally war-torn. But it might also have been less politically pluralistic, less competitive, and less open to disruptive innovation. The modern world might have seen a powerful Eurasian-style European empire rather than a collection of rival European nation-states. That empire could have been very strong, but the particular path that led to modern science, capitalism, colonial rivalry, and industrialization would likely have been significantly altered—and perhaps slowed.

Japan was interested in extending its influence in Asia and for that it had to confront either USSR or USA. While I don't think that the exact reason for choosing USA is known, Japan was at a clear disadvantage when battling USSR: while the Soviet Union had...

items.original_question: 第二次世界大战期间日本帝国为何不进攻苏联？日本和苏联在满洲有共同边界，德国对苏联的入侵极大地削弱了苏联。鉴于日本击败苏联的优势（更不用说西伯利亚的资源了），而且日本驻有大量关东军基本上无所事事，为什么日本不进攻呢？
items.model_answer:
If Japan had attacked the Soviet Far East during World War II, the most likely result would have been a larger, bloodier war for Japan without a decisive Japanese victory. It might have made Germany’s 1941 campaign against the USSR more dangerous for Stalin, but it probably would not have caused the Soviet Union to collapse.

The timing matters. The most consequential moment would have been summer or autumn 1941, when Germany was advancing toward Moscow. If Japan had attacked then, Stalin would have been much less willing to transfer trained Siberian and Far Eastern divisions westward. Those forces helped stiffen Soviet defenses around Moscow. Without them, the Battle of Moscow could have gone worse for the USSR, and Germany might have had a better chance of taking the city or inflicting a deeper crisis.

But even that would not automatically mean Soviet defeat. The USSR still had enormous depth, manpower, industrial capacity east of the Urals, and a political system prepared to continue the war even after losing major cities. Germany’s deeper problems—long supply lines, poor logistics, attrition, and underestimation of Soviet resilience—would have remained. A Japanese attack could have increased the probability of a Soviet disaster in 1941, but it would not have guaranteed one.

For Japan, the strategic problem was that Siberia did not solve Japan’s main wartime need: oil. Japan’s army had long favored a “northern” strategy against the USSR, but after being badly beaten by Soviet forces at Khalkhin Gol in 1939, Tokyo lost confidence in that option. The navy and government increasingly favored the “southern” strategy: seize the Dutch East Indies, Malaya, and other resource-rich territories. Attacking Siberia offered timber, space, and prestige, but not enough oil to keep Japan’s war machine running.

Militarily, Japan also faced severe limitations. The Kwantung Army was large, but it was not well suited for a vast mechanized campaign across Siberia. The Soviet Far East was heavily defended, terrain and weather were punishing, and Japanese logistics were weak. Japan might have captured some border areas, threatened Vladivostok, or disrupted the Trans-Siberian Railway and Pacific Lend-Lease route, but a deep conquest of Siberia would have been extremely difficult.

A Japanese-Soviet war would also have affected Allied aid. Historically, the Soviet Union received large amounts of Lend-Lease through the Pacific route, much of it shipped to Vladivostok under Soviet neutrality with Japan. If Japan and the USSR were at war, that route would close. This would hurt Soviet logistics, especially later in the war, though aid could still move through the Arctic and Persian routes.

The biggest downside for Japan is that it would have become even more overextended. If Japan attacked the USSR and still attacked the United States, Britain, and the Dutch colonies, it would be fighting in every direction at once: China, Southeast Asia, the Pacific, and Siberia. That would likely accelerate Japan’s exhaustion. If Japan attacked the USSR instead of moving south, it would still face the unresolved oil crisis caused by American and Allied embargoes. Without access to Southeast Asian oil, Japan’s ability to sustain a long war would deteriorate.

By 1943 or 1944, a Japanese attack on the Soviet Far East would have been even less promising. The USSR was stronger, Germany was losing, and Japan was increasingly on the defensive against the United States. In 1945, when the Soviets actually attacked Japan in Manchuria, they crushed the Kwantung Army with overwhelming speed and force. That suggests that if Japan had opened a northern war and failed to win quickly, it would eventually have faced a devastating Soviet counteroffensive.

So the most plausible outcome is this: a Japanese attack in 1941 would have seriously complicated Soviet survival and could have helped Germany at the margins, perhaps even enough to change specific battles such as Moscow. But Japan was unlikely to conquer the Soviet Far East decisively, and the campaign would not solve Japan’s resource problem. In the long run, it probably would have weakened Japan, closed useful Soviet supply routes, prolonged or intensified the war, but still ended with Japan facing defeat—possibly even faster and more completely.

items.question: What If Gunpowder-Era Fortresses Were Built as Circles or Squares Instead of Stars?
human_answers: Star forts or bastion forts are designed to enable enfilade (or flanking) fire: shooting on the line of attackers from the side, significantly increasing firing efficiency of the defender. Flanking fire allows guns placed in the side wall of the bastion (pr...

Imagine that you are defending a fort with old-fashioned round bastions in the Middle Ages. Your walls are high, but once the enemy comes close and starts scaling the walls, very few of your defenders can engage them.

These outcroppings are called Bastions and they became common when muskets and cannons became common in European warfare. The problem with a square or circle forts is that when the enemy has reached the wall, they are in your dead zone.
items.original_question: 为什么古老的防御工事形状像星星而不是圆形？哥本哈根、腓特烈西亚和阿卡的防御工事呈星形。 （哥本哈根防御工事如下图所示。）为什么不把防御工事或防御工事做成纯粹的正方形或圆形呢？
items.model_answer:
Gunpowder-era fortresses built as simple circles or squares would generally have been easier to attack than star forts, unless they added projecting works that would gradually make them star-like anyway.

The key problem was not just resisting cannonballs; it was controlling the ground immediately outside the walls. Medieval castles often used high round or square towers, but early modern artillery made tall masonry walls vulnerable. Fortresses therefore became lower, thicker, and earth-backed. Once walls were low, the crucial defensive need was flanking fire: the ability to shoot along the face of one’s own walls and across the ditch so attackers could not shelter at the base.

A circular fortress has good structural qualities in one sense: a curved wall has no sharp corner to concentrate stress, and incoming cannon fire is less likely to strike it squarely everywhere. But a smooth circle has a serious tactical weakness. Defenders on the wall mostly fire outward, not along the wall. The base of the wall and ditch can contain “dead ground” where attackers are hard to hit. If besiegers reach that zone, they can mine, sap, plant explosives, or prepare an assault with less interference. A circular fort can add towers, caponiers, galleries, or external works to solve this, but those additions are essentially attempts to recreate the flanking geometry of a bastioned or star-shaped design.

A simple square fortress has a different problem. Its straight walls are easier to batter with artillery, and the corners create awkward blind spots unless they project outward. If the corners are just ordinary right angles, attackers can approach portions of the wall without being swept effectively by defensive fire from neighboring faces. If the square has large corner bastions that allow defenders to fire along the adjacent walls, it becomes much more effective—but then it is no longer a simple square; it is a bastioned fort, partway toward the classic star fort.

The star fort solved these problems geometrically. Its projecting bastions let defenders cover every wall, ditch, and approach with overlapping fire. There were few places where attackers could stand safely near the defenses. The angled faces also reduced the effectiveness of direct artillery fire and made it harder for besiegers to create a clean breach without being exposed to fire from multiple directions. The shape was not decorative; it was an engineering response to cannon warfare.

So if major gunpowder-era fortresses had remained circular or square, sieges would likely have become shorter and more favorable to attackers. Defenders would have needed larger garrisons, more artillery, deeper ditches, more detached outworks, or heavier earthworks to compensate. Over time, military engineers would probably have rediscovered projecting flanking structures, causing “circles” and “squares” to evolve back toward bastioned, star-like, or later polygonal designs.

In short: circular or square forts could work for small redoubts, temporary works, or special sites, but as major gunpowder-era fortresses they would be tactically inferior unless modified so heavily that they effectively became star forts in function.

items.model_answer:
If Germany had successfully blockaded the Strait of Gibraltar in World War II, the Mediterranean war would have become much harder for Britain and the Allies, but it probably would not have changed the final outcome of the war by itself.

The key issue is feasibility. Germany could not effectively blockade Gibraltar from the sea with its own navy; the Royal Navy was too strong, and Gibraltar was a major British fortress and naval base. To close the strait reliably, Germany would have needed either Spain’s cooperation or an invasion of Spain, followed by the capture or neutralization of Gibraltar. This was the logic behind the German plan known as Operation Felix. But Franco’s Spain was exhausted after its civil war, dependent on imported food and fuel, and unwilling to enter the war unless Germany offered enormous guarantees. Hitler also had higher priorities, especially the coming invasion of the Soviet Union.

If Germany somehow had closed the strait in 1940 or 1941, the immediate effect would have been to cut the western entrance to the Mediterranean. British naval forces based at Gibraltar would be trapped, expelled, or destroyed, and Allied convoys from the Atlantic into the Mediterranean would become nearly impossible. Malta would be in much greater danger because many of its supplies and reinforcements came from the west. If Malta fell or was neutralized, Axis supply convoys from Italy to Libya would suffer fewer losses, giving Rommel’s Afrika Korps a better chance in North Africa.

That could have made the North African campaign more dangerous for Britain. Axis forces might have held Libya longer, perhaps advanced farther into Egypt, and possibly made a stronger attempt toward the Suez Canal. A closed Gibraltar would also have complicated or delayed Operation Torch, the Allied landings in North Africa in 1942, because Gibraltar was a crucial staging and command base for that operation.

But the blockade would not automatically have strangled Britain. By 1940, Britain had already largely stopped using the Mediterranean as its main imperial shipping route because Italy had entered the war. British shipping to India, the Middle East, and Australia was already being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope. That route was longer and more expensive, but it remained viable. Egypt could still be supplied from the east through the Red Sea and around Africa as long as the British held Suez.

Nor would closing Gibraltar solve Germany’s larger strategic problems. Germany would have had to occupy or heavily influence Spain, defend a long and vulnerable coastline, supply forces across poor Spanish infrastructure, and possibly deal with Allied attacks on the Canary Islands, Spanish Morocco, or Portugal’s Atlantic islands. It would also have risked pushing Britain and later the United States into wider operations against Iberia and northwest Africa. All of this would have consumed resources Germany badly needed against the Soviet Union.

So the most likely result is this: a successful German blockade of Gibraltar would have prolonged the Mediterranean and North African campaigns, made Malta and Egypt more vulnerable, and delayed Allied operations in North Africa and possibly Italy. It might have added months, perhaps even a year, to the Allied timetable in the Mediterranean. But unless it was combined with the capture of Malta, victory in Egypt, seizure of Suez, and a broader collapse of British power in the Middle East, it probably would not have changed the ultimate outcome of World War II. The United States, British Empire, and Soviet Union still possessed far greater long-term industrial and manpower resources than Germany and Italy.

items.question: What If You Opened a 10-Meter Drain to Space at the Bottom of Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up and suck it through. Cooool.
items.original_question: 如果在挑战者深渊底部创建一个半径 10 米通向太空的圆形入口，海洋的排空速度有多快？
items.model_answer:
If you opened a 10-meter-wide hole at the bottom of Challenger Deep that led to a maintained vacuum, seawater would blast through it violently, but it would not make the oceans disappear quickly.

At about 11 km depth, the pressure is roughly 110 MPa, about 1,100 atmospheres. That pressure head could accelerate water into the opening at an ideal speed of about

\[
v \approx \sqrt{2gh} \approx 460 \text{ m/s},
\]

roughly the speed of a rifle bullet but still well below the speed of sound in water. A 10 m diameter circular drain has an area of about 79 m², so the initial flow rate would be on the order of

\[
Q \sim 30{,}000\text{–}40{,}000 \text{ m}^3/\text{s},
\]

depending on losses. That is enormous locally: tens of millions of kilograms of water per second, with terawatts of power in the flow. Anything near the hole would be destroyed, and the surrounding seafloor would likely erode, collapse, and generate violent turbulence and sediment flows.

But globally, it is not an instant ocean drain. The oceans contain about \(1.3 \times 10^{18}\) m³ of water. At the initial rate, sea level would fall only a few millimeters per year. As sea level dropped, the pressure at the drain would decrease, so the flow would slow. Draining a major fraction of the oceans through a 10 m opening would take millions of years, not days or centuries.

The water would not “boil the ocean” at the hole. At the bottom, the pressure keeps it liquid. It would shoot through the drain as liquid water. On the space side, if it truly exited into vacuum, it would rapidly expand, flash partly into vapor, and freeze much of the rest into ice crystals. You would get a huge plume of vapor and ice. If the outlet were merely in near-Earth space, most of that water would not escape Earth permanently; its speed, a few hundred m/s, is far below Earth escape velocity, 11.2 km/s.
