It would form an icy cloud and much of it could eventually fall back unless the “drain” magically transported it far away.

So the direct answer is: you would create a catastrophic local underwater jet and a gigantic plume of freezing water in space, but a 10-meter drain would lower global sea level slowly, by millimeters per year at first. It would not immediately empty the ocean.

items.question: What If Earth Expanded by 1 Centimeter per Second?
human_answers: The Earth is not, currently expanding. Before the continental drift hypothesis was confirmed in the 1960s, people had noticed that the continents fit together.
items.original_question: 如果世界平均半径每秒扩大 1 厘米，人们需要多长时间才能注意到自己的体重增加？
items.model_answer:
Assuming Earth’s radius increased by 1 centimeter per second, the effect would be slow moment-to-moment but catastrophic on human and geological timescales.

A surface rise of 1 cm/s equals about 864 meters per day and about 315 kilometers per year. After one year Earth’s radius would be about 5% larger. Its surface area would grow by about 10%, its circumference by almost 2,000 km, and its volume by about 15%. After about 20 years, Earth’s radius would roughly double.

The crust could not tolerate this. Earth’s surface would have to stretch continuously; the circumference would need to grow by about 5.4 km every day. Rock fails at tiny strains, so within hours to days the crust would begin cracking globally. Within weeks there would be worldwide rifting, earthquakes, volcanic activity, and massive fault systems. Continents and ocean floors would be pulled apart unless new material somehow appeared to fill the gaps.

The oceans would also be severely disrupted. If the amount of water stayed the same while Earth’s surface area increased, the average ocean depth would fall over time, exposing some seafloor and radically changing coastlines. But in practice the constant earthquakes, rifting, seafloor deformation, and volcanism would produce enormous tsunamis and make coastal regions uninhabitable long before the simple sea-level effect mattered.

Gravity depends on what “expanded” means physically. If Earth’s mass stayed the same while its radius grew, surface gravity would decrease as \(1/R^2\). After one year, gravity would be about 9% lower; after 20 years, with twice the radius, gravity would be only one-quarter of today’s. The atmosphere would spread over a much larger area and be held less tightly, so surface pressure would drop significantly, eventually making breathing difficult and altering climate completely.

If instead Earth expanded by adding new material at roughly the same density, surface gravity would increase, because Earth’s mass would grow faster than its radius. At double radius, Earth would have eight times the mass and about twice the surface gravity. That would crush ecosystems, alter the Moon’s orbit, and create immense internal pressures and heat.

Earth’s rotation would change too. If mass stayed constant and angular momentum were conserved, the growing planet would spin more slowly, like a skater extending their arms. The day would lengthen; after one year it would be roughly 10% longer, and after a radius doubling it would be about four times longer.

The biggest issue is energy. Expanding Earth against its own gravity would require an enormous power input, on the order of \(10^{23}\) watts, millions of times more than the sunlight Earth receives. If that energy appeared as heat, Earth’s interior and surface would melt or vaporize. No known physical process could make a rocky planet expand this way without catastrophic consequences.

So the short answer is: Earth would not simply become a slightly larger planet. At 1 cm/s radial expansion, it would undergo continuous global fracturing, extreme earthquakes and volcanism, oceanic chaos, atmospheric and gravitational changes, and likely become uninhabitable very quickly—probably within months or less, depending on the mechanism.

items.question: What If the Romans Had Built a Working Steam Engine?
human_answers: This question explores technological determinism and the question of whether ancient civilizations could have industrialized earlier if exposed to key inventions. The Romans had many advanced technologies including concrete, aqueducts, road networks, and mi...
items.original_question: 如果罗马人发现一台可以工作的蒸汽机，他们是否能够复制和使用它？
items.model_answer:
If the Romans had built a genuinely working steam engine, the most likely result would not be an immediate ancient Industrial Revolution, but a limited and uneven technological acceleration—unless they also developed the surrounding machinery, materials, fuels, and economic habits needed to exploit it.

The Romans already had the conceptual seed of steam power in devices like Hero of Alexandria’s aeolipile, a spinning steam toy. The hard part was not realizing that steam could move things; it was turning steam into reliable, repeatable mechanical work. A practical engine would have required good boilers, tight pistons or turbines, valves, seals, metalworking precision, and a reason to invest in all of it.

If Rome somehow produced a low-pressure working steam engine, its first useful applications would probably have been in places where Rome already needed mechanical power: pumping water out of mines, lifting water for baths and cities, grinding grain, sawing stone or timber, and perhaps powering workshop machinery. Mining would be especially important. Steam pumps could have allowed deeper mines, increasing supplies of silver, copper, iron, lead, and coal. That could have strengthened Roman finances and metallurgy.

But steam power would still have faced serious limits. Roman metallurgy was impressive, but high-pressure boilers are dangerous even with much later technology. Without precision machine tools, standardized parts, and strong iron or steel production, engines would be inefficient, expensive, and prone to failure. Fuel would also matter. Wood was already heavily used, and large-scale steam power would have pushed Rome toward coal. The Romans knew of coal in some regions, especially Britain, but they did not build an energy economy around it.

Economically, steam power might have been adopted slowly. Roman society had abundant human and animal labor, including enslaved labor, and many elites preferred land, rents, status, and politics over industrial investment. That does not mean slavery would have prevented steam technology entirely, but it would have reduced the pressure to replace labor with machines. The state and army, however, might have funded engines if they were useful for mines, construction, siegecraft, or logistics.

Militarily, steam engines would probably not have produced steam-powered tanks or locomotives right away. Ancient engines would be heavy, weak, and fuel-hungry. They might help manufacture weapons, drain siege works, pump ships, or move heavy materials, but practical railways and steamships would require many additional innovations: better metallurgy, bearings, rails, condensers, and efficient boilers.

Politically, successful steam technology could have prolonged Roman power by improving mining, taxation, construction, and supply. A richer, more mechanized empire might have maintained larger armies and stronger infrastructure. But it could also have intensified existing problems: deforestation, pollution, dangerous mines, social inequality, and dependence on complex technical systems. Technology alone would not solve Rome’s succession crises, civil wars, monetary instability, plague, frontier pressures, or administrative burdens.

The biggest counterfactual change would come if the steam engine triggered a culture of sustained mechanical innovation. If Roman engineers, the army, and wealthy investors began systematically improving engines, building machine tools, exploiting coal, and applying power to production, then the Mediterranean world could have seen industrialization many centuries early. Cities would grow, manufacturing would expand, transport might eventually be transformed, and the balance between labor, capital, and state power would shift dramatically.

But if the Romans merely built one working steam engine without that broader ecosystem, it would likely have remained a remarkable specialized machine—useful in mines or imperial projects, admired by engineers, perhaps copied in a few places, but not transformative on its own. The steam engine mattered in modern history because it arrived together with coal mining, precision engineering, capitalist investment, scientific culture, and expanding markets. Rome had some pieces of that puzzle, but not all of them.

items.question: What If a Modern Programmer with a Laptop Entered World War II?
human_answers: This scenario explores the 'present-day expert sent back in time' trope with specific focus on computer technology. A modern programmer with a laptop would face significant challenges: 1.
items.original_question: 现代程序员和笔记本电脑被投入第二次世界大战，可能会破解恩尼格玛密码机，会产生什么影响？
items.model_answer:
A modern programmer with a laptop would not automatically “win World War II,” but in the right place, with the right access, they could become extremely valuable.

The laptop itself would be astonishing by 1940s standards: it could do in seconds calculations that wartime teams or early electromechanical machines might take hours, days, or weeks to perform. But its usefulness would be limited by practical problems. There would be no internet, no modern peripherals, no compatible networks, and possibly no easy way to recharge it until someone adapted the power supply. If the programmer only had a laptop with ordinary tools and no saved references, its value would mostly be as a fast calculator and programming environment. If it contained offline documentation, textbooks, maps, histories, engineering references, or Wikipedia-like data, it could be far more consequential.

The biggest impact would likely be in Allied codebreaking, logistics, ballistics, operations research, radar analysis, and early computing. At Bletchley Park, for example, a programmer who understood algorithms, statistics, automation, and modern cryptanalytic thinking could help automate parts of codebreaking work. A modern laptop could simulate machines, test hypotheses, search large keyspaces, and process intercepted messages much faster than 1940s equipment. That would not make cryptography trivial, because codebreaking still depended on captured materials, traffic analysis, cribs, language knowledge, and disciplined intelligence procedures. But it could accelerate work significantly.

In military logistics, the programmer might be even more useful. World War II was heavily shaped by shipping schedules, fuel distribution, convoy routing, aircraft maintenance, production planning, and troop movement. Modern optimization methods, databases, simulations, and statistical modeling could improve these systems. Even without internet access, a competent programmer could build tools to track inventories, forecast shortages, optimize routes, and analyze losses. These improvements would be less dramatic than “inventing a superweapon,” but they could save enormous resources and lives.

In weapons development, the laptop would help with calculations and modeling, but it would not magically create modern weapons. The 1940s lacked the manufacturing base for microchips, GPS, modern sensors, precision-guided munitions, and advanced materials. The programmer could explain principles of modern computing, software engineering, numerical simulation, error correction, networking, or digital control systems, but turning those ideas into reliable wartime hardware would take teams, factories, and time. They might accelerate projects like ENIAC, Colossus, radar signal processing, or fire-control computation, but not instantly produce 21st-century technology.

The person’s historical knowledge could be more powerful than their programming skill. If they knew major battles, invasion dates, code names, atomic bomb development, U-boat campaigns, and political decisions, that information could alter strategy. For example, warning the Allies about the timing of major offensives or explaining the importance of certain technologies could change priorities. But credibility would be a major obstacle. A stranger claiming to be from the future with an impossible machine would likely be detained, interrogated, or treated as a spy until they proved their value.

If they appeared in Germany, Japan, or the Soviet Union, the outcome would depend heavily on whether they were trusted or coerced. The Axis powers might gain technical or intelligence advantages, but their larger problems—fuel shortages, industrial limits, strategic overreach, bombing, blockade, and political dysfunction—would not disappear. A modern laptop would be nearly impossible for 1940s industry to reverse-engineer in full. They could learn concepts from it, but they could not simply copy its processor or memory.

The laptop would also be a security nightmare. If captured, it could reveal future history, modern science, or Allied plans depending on what it contained. Its battery would degrade, parts would eventually fail, and no one could manufacture replacements. Once the machine died, the lasting value would be whatever knowledge had been copied, taught, or converted into 1940s-compatible methods.

So the realistic answer is: a modern programmer with a laptop could be a major strategic asset, especially if placed with Allied scientific or intelligence organizations early in the war. They could accelerate computation, codebreaking, logistics, and engineering by months or even years. But they would not be a one-person war-ending miracle. Their impact would depend less on the laptop itself and more on access, trust, historical knowledge, institutional support, and the ability to translate modern ideas into technology the 1940s could actually build.

items.question: What If My Printer Could Really Print Money?
human_answers: In today’s article, I give shorter answers to several reader questions. (Previous installment here (http://what-if.xkcd.com/14/).) You can fit four bills on an 8.5”x11” sheet of paper: [Image: image] If your printer can manage one page (front and back) of f...
items.original_question: 如果我的打印机真的可以打印钞票，它会对世界产生那么大的影响吗？
items.model_answer:
If your printer could really print money that was physically indistinguishable from official currency, it would not make you “create wealth” in the broader economic sense. It would let you create claims on existing goods and services. In practice, that would be counterfeiting unless the money were legally issued by the government or central bank.

At first, if you printed a small amount and spent it, you would personally gain purchasing power. The loss would be spread across everyone else using that currency, because you would be adding money without adding any new goods, services, or productive capacity. Economically, it is like secretly taxing everyone by diluting the value of the money supply.

If many people had such printers, prices would rise rapidly. Money works partly because it is scarce, trusted, and difficult to forge. If anyone could print unlimited perfect cash, the supply of money would explode. Sellers would respond by raising prices, demanding alternative payment, or refusing the currency entirely. The currency could collapse into hyperinflation, where money loses value so fast that people rush to spend it immediately or switch to barter, foreign currency, commodities, or digital assets.

If only you had the printer and used it heavily, the effect would depend on scale. Printing a few thousand dollars might have no measurable macroeconomic effect but would still be illegal. Printing billions would noticeably increase the money supply, distort markets, trigger investigations, and likely destabilize parts of the economy. Banks, retailers, and governments track currency flows, serial numbers, deposits, and suspicious transactions, so spending large amounts of “new” cash would be hard to hide.

If the printer were legally authorized, then it would essentially be part of the central bank’s money-creation system. Modern governments already “print money,” mostly digitally rather than as paper cash. They can increase the money supply, but they must manage it carefully. Too little money can contribute to recession or deflation; too much can cause inflation.

So the short answer is: if your printer could print real money, you might become richer briefly, but you would not create real wealth. You would either be committing counterfeiting, or, if everyone could do it, the money would quickly stop being worth much. Real wealth comes from producing valuable goods, services, technology, infrastructure, knowledge, and resources—not from creating more pieces of currency.

items.question: What If You Tried to Launch a Real Rocket Using Only Model Rocket Engines?
human_answers: About 65,000, give or take a few. You’d have to arrange them like this: [Image: image] The rocket would weigh about as much as a tow truck.
items.original_question: 将真正的火箭发射到太空需要多少个模型火箭发动机？
items.model_answer:
If “launch” means “make a full-size rocket rise off the pad,” then yes, in principle: enough model rocket engines could produce enough thrust for a few seconds. If “launch” means “send a real rocket to space or orbit,” then no, not in any practical sense.

A typical Estes-style model rocket motor, say a D motor, produces on the order of 10–20 newtons of thrust for about 1–2 seconds, with a total impulse around 20 newton-seconds. A real orbital rocket needs millions of newtons of thrust and billions of newton-seconds of total impulse.

For example, a Falcon 9 produces roughly 7.6 million newtons of thrust at liftoff. Using 10-newton model motors, you would need roughly three-quarters of a million motors just to match liftoff thrust. They would burn out almost immediately, giving the vehicle only a tiny kick upward. It might hop, shake itself apart, or explode, but it would not meaningfully accelerate toward orbit.

The deeper problem is not just thrust; it is efficiency and mass ratio. Model rocket engines have low specific impulse compared with real launch-vehicle engines, and each tiny motor carries its own casing, nozzle, clay, and packaging. That means you are adding huge amounts of dead weight. The rocket equation punishes this severely. Even if you built many stages, each stage would spend most of its effort lifting thousands or millions of little spent motor casings and the next pile of motors.

There are also practical failures: igniting hundreds of thousands of motors simultaneously would be nearly impossible; some would fail, some would ignite late, and uneven thrust would tear the vehicle apart or send it tumbling. The exhaust plumes and heat would damage neighboring motors and structure. The wiring, mounting hardware, and control system would become absurdly heavy.

So the result would be: a spectacular, dangerous, very expensive firework. With enough model engines you could make a large object briefly leave the ground. But launching a real rocket to space, especially to orbit, using only ordinary model rocket engines is effectively impossible in practice.

items.question: What If Humanity Sped Up Earth's Rotation to Eliminate Leap Seconds?
human_answers: The Earth’s spin is slowing down. This is annoying.
items.original_question: 由于地球自转正在减慢，我们时不时地必须插入闰秒。我们能否加快地球自转，这样就不需要闰秒了？
items.model_answer:
If humanity tried to eliminate leap seconds by physically speeding up Earth, the required change in rotation rate would be tiny in everyday terms but enormous in engineering terms.

Leap seconds exist because atomic time counts exact SI seconds, while Earth’s rotation is slightly irregular and, on average, slowly slowing due mainly to lunar tides. Since 1972, UTC has needed 27 positive leap seconds, meaning Earth has lagged atomic time by roughly 27 seconds over about five decades. That corresponds to the mean solar day being about 1–2 milliseconds longer than 86,400 SI seconds.

To stop future leap seconds, humanity would need to shorten Earth’s day by about a millisecond or two. That means increasing Earth’s angular velocity by only about one part in 60–100 million. At the equator, the surface would move only a few micrometers per second faster. People would not feel lighter in any noticeable way, weather and tides would barely change, and the equatorial bulge or sea level redistribution would be tiny if the spin-up were done gently.

But the planetary-scale physics is brutal. Earth’s rotational angular momentum is about \(5.9 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}\). Changing the day length by about 1.4 ms would require adding roughly

\[
10^{26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}
\]

of angular momentum and about

\[
10^{22}\ \mathrm{J}
\]

of rotational energy.

That is on the order of ten years of total current human energy use, and the harder problem is not energy but angular momentum: you cannot just “add spin” to Earth without pushing against something else. You would need to exchange angular momentum with the Moon, asteroids, expelled mass, or some enormous space-based machinery. An impactor could do it in principle, but an impact large enough to matter would be globally catastrophic. A gentle gravitational or mass-driver scheme would be fantastically beyond present engineering.

Also, speeding Earth up once would not permanently solve the problem. Earth’s rotation varies because of tides, atmosphere, oceans, core motion, earthquakes, and long-term tidal braking. You would need continual active control of Earth’s rotation to keep atomic time and Earth-rotation time locked together.

If the goal were to “erase” the existing leap seconds, that is a different problem. You would need Earth to gain about 27 seconds of rotational phase relative to atomic time. A 1 ms/day speed-up would take about 74 years to catch up; a faster catch-up would require much larger torques and energies.

So the direct answer is: in principle, speeding up Earth could reduce or temporarily eliminate the need for leap seconds, and the direct physical effects of the slightly shorter day would be negligible. In practice, it would require absurd planetary-scale angular momentum transfer, would need constant maintenance, and would be vastly harder than simply changing the timekeeping rules. That is why the real-world solution is administrative: stop using leap seconds, or allow UTC to drift slowly from Earth rotation, rather than trying to spin up the planet.

items.question: What If One Extra Person Died Randomly Every Second?
human_answers: Every second, 1.8 humans die and 4.2 humans are born. Under Mr.
items.original_question: 如果在地球上的某个地方每秒随机选择一个额外的人死亡，这会对世界人口产生什么影响？
items.model_answer:
Assuming the rule is “once per second, one living human is chosen uniformly at random and dies,” the immediate effect would be enormous but not instantly civilization-ending.

One death per second is 86,400 extra deaths per day, or about 31.6 million extra deaths per year. The world currently has roughly 60–70 million deaths per year, so this would increase global mortality by about half. It would become the largest “cause of death” on Earth, exceeding heart disease and cancer individually.

For an individual person, the risk would be small in any given moment but significant over a lifetime. With about 8.1 billion people alive, your chance of being the randomly selected person in any one second would be about 1 in 8.1 billion. Over a year, that becomes roughly:

\[
\frac{31.6\text{ million}}{8.1\text{ billion}} \approx 0.39\%
\]

So each person would face about a 0.4% annual chance of dying from this random process. Over 80 years, assuming population size stayed similar, the cumulative chance would be around 27%. In other words, roughly one in four people would eventually be killed by the random-death mechanism before accounting for normal mortality.

The demographic effect would be severe but not immediately depopulating. Current global births are still far higher than deaths, by roughly 60–70 million per year. Adding 31.6 million deaths per year would reduce population growth sharply, but humanity would likely still grow at today’s birth rates, perhaps by around 30–40 million people per year instead of much more. However, as global fertility continues to fall, this extra mortality could push the world into population decline sooner.

The social effect would be much worse than the raw numbers suggest because the deaths would be random across age, health, location, and social role. Unlike ordinary mortality, which is concentrated among older people, this would kill infants, children, parents, doctors, pilots, teachers, heads of state, engineers, and caregivers in proportion to how many exist. The loss of life-years would be huge: each extra death would often remove decades of expected life. Globally, this could mean over a billion expected life-years lost every year.

There would also be secondary consequences. If deaths are sudden, some people would die while driving, flying, performing surgery, operating machinery, managing power systems, or caring for dependents. That would cause additional accidents and force society to redesign many systems around the assumption that anyone can vanish at any second. Critical roles would need redundancy everywhere.

Psychologically and politically, the world would change dramatically. Every day would bring 86,400 apparently arbitrary deaths. Families, workplaces, schools, militaries, governments, and hospitals would be in constant churn. Insurance, pensions, inheritance law, employment planning, and security systems would all have to adapt. The randomness would make it feel like a universal lottery of death.

So the short answer is: one extra random death per second would not immediately wipe out humanity, and at current birth rates it might not even make the global population decline right away. But it would be one of the greatest disasters in human history: 31.6 million additional deaths per year, a major reduction in life expectancy, vast psychological trauma, and serious disruption to every institution that depends on people reliably being alive tomorrow.

items.question: How Far Would You Have to Drop a Steak to Cook It?
human_answers: I hope you like your steaks Pittsburgh Rare. And you may need to defrost it after you pick it up.
items.original_question: 当牛排落地时，你需要从多高的地方扔下牛排才能将其煮熟？
items.model_answer:
In any realistic Earth-atmosphere scenario, you can’t cook a steak just by dropping it.

A simple energy estimate gives a tempting lower bound: meat has a specific heat of about \(3.5 \text{ kJ/kg·°C}\). To warm a steak from refrigerator temperature, say \(5^\circ\text{C}\), to a cooked internal temperature around \(60^\circ\text{C}\), you need roughly

\[
3.5\times 55 \approx 190 \text{ kJ/kg}.
\]

Gravitational potential energy is \(gh\), so if 100% of the fall energy went into heating the steak,

\[
h \approx \frac{190{,}000}{9.8} \approx 19{,}000 \text{ m},
\]

or about 20 km.

But that is an impossible best case. In reality, almost all the energy from falling through air goes into heating the surrounding air and stirring turbulence, not into the steak. The steak also reaches terminal velocity, probably on the order of tens of meters per second, so the final impact energy is tiny: enough to splatter it, not cook it. At terminal speed, the air friction would warm the air by only a few degrees at most, nowhere near enough to sear or cook meat.

If you dropped it from much higher, like from space, it would not become a nicely cooked steak either. It would freeze, tumble, dry out, char or ablate on the outside during reentry, and likely break apart or splatter on impact while remaining unevenly heated.

So the careful answer is: an idealized calculation says about 15–20 km if all the energy heated the steak, but in the real atmosphere there is no height from which you can drop a steak and have it cook properly.

items.question: What If You Went Swimming in a Spent Fuel Pool?
human_answers: Assuming you’re a reasonably good swimmer, you could probably survive treading water anywhere from 10 to 40 hours. At that point, you would black out from fatigue and drown.
items.original_question: 如果我在典型的乏核燃料池里游泳会怎么样？我是否需要潜水才能真正经历致命的辐射量？我能在水面安全停留多久？
items.model_answer:
If you went swimming at the surface of a properly maintained spent nuclear fuel pool, the radiation itself would probably not be what kills you.

Spent fuel pools are deep for a reason: several meters of water sit above the fuel assemblies, and water is an excellent radiation shield. The spent fuel at the bottom is intensely radioactive, but the radiation level near the surface of the pool is typically very low because the water absorbs most of the gamma rays and stops beta radiation entirely. In a normal pool, a brief swim near the surface could give you a radiation dose comparable to ordinary background levels, possibly less than many medical X-rays.

The danger changes dramatically if you dive down toward the fuel. Close to the spent fuel assemblies, radiation levels can become extremely high. Near freshly discharged fuel, a lethal dose could be received in a short time, potentially minutes or less depending on distance, fuel age, and shielding. Touching or approaching exposed spent fuel would be extremely dangerous.

Other practical hazards also matter: the water is chemically controlled, often borated, very pure, and not something you should drink; the pool is an industrial nuclear facility with strict security; and disturbing fuel racks or equipment would be a serious safety issue. You also would not “become radioactive” just from swimming in clean pool water, though contamination would be a concern if the pool were damaged or poorly maintained.

So the direct answer is: swimming on the surface of an intact spent fuel pool would likely be surprisingly safe from a radiation standpoint, but diving toward the fuel at the bottom could be fatal, and in real life you would never be allowed to do it.

items.question: What If You Flew an Ordinary Airplane over Other Worlds in the Solar System?
human_answers: Here’s our aircraft: [Image: image] The Cessna 172 Skyhawk, probably the most common plane in the world. Here’s our pilot: [Image: image] Here’s what happens when the aircraft is launched above the surface of the 32 largest Solar System bodies: [Image: imag...
items.original_question: 如果你尝试在不同的太阳系天体上空驾驶一架普通的地球飞机会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
An ordinary airplane would not work as an ordinary airplane anywhere else in the Solar System, mainly because its engine needs oxygen. No other planet or moon has an oxygen-rich atmosphere. But if you supplied power some other way, such as batteries, rockets, or onboard oxidizer, then the answer depends on air density and gravity.

On airless worlds such as the Moon, Mercury, most asteroids, and many moons, wings are useless. There is essentially no atmosphere, so the plane would not “fly”; it would follow a ballistic path and crash unless it had rockets.

On Mars, flight is barely possible but not for an ordinary airplane. Mars has only about 1% of Earth’s atmospheric pressure. Lower gravity helps, but not enough: a normal airplane would need to fly several times faster than on Earth to produce the same lift, often near or above the local speed of sound. Its propeller or jet engine also would not work normally because there is almost no oxygen and very little air to push against. Special aircraft can fly on Mars, but they need very light structures, large wings or rotors, and custom propulsion.

On Venus, aerodynamics would be easy but survival would not. Near the surface the atmosphere is extremely dense, so wings would generate enormous lift at low speed. But the surface is about 465°C, with around 90 times Earth’s pressure and corrosive chemistry, so an ordinary airplane would be crushed, cooked, and chemically attacked. Higher up in Venus’s atmosphere, around 50–60 km altitude, pressure and temperature are more Earthlike, and flight or floating would be quite feasible, but a normal engine still could not breathe the CO₂ atmosphere.

Titan, Saturn’s large moon, is probably the best place in the Solar System for airplane-like flight. It has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and very low gravity. A plane would need much less speed to stay aloft than on Earth; in principle, even human-powered flight would be much easier there. But Titan is extremely cold, about −180°C, and its atmosphere contains no oxygen, so a normal gasoline or jet engine would not run without onboard oxidizer or electric power.

The gas giants—Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune—have atmospheres, so winged flight is physically possible in some layers. But there is no solid surface or runway, no oxygen for normal engines, and conditions become rapidly more extreme with depth. Jupiter in particular has high gravity, intense radiation, strong winds, and turbulence. A specially designed powered glider or probe might fly temporarily, but an ordinary airplane would not survive or operate usefully.

Pluto, Triton, and similar icy bodies have atmospheres far too thin for normal flight. They are effectively vacuum from an airplane’s point of view.

So the short answer is: an unmodified ordinary airplane can only really fly on Earth. With a non-air-breathing power source and suitable materials, Titan would be the easiest place to fly, Venus’s upper atmosphere would also be promising, Mars would be difficult, and airless worlds would be impossible for winged flight.

items.question: What If Hubble Pointed at Earth Instead of Deep Space?
human_answers: This is a common question. The Hubble operators get it a lot, and their FAQ page answers it (http://hubblesite.org/reference_desk/faq/answer.php.id=78&cat=topten).
items.original_question: 如果哈勃望远镜瞄准地球，图像会有多详细？
items.model_answer:
If Hubble were simply pointed at Earth, it would not produce a spectacular “Hubble Deep Field of Earth.” In normal operation it probably would not be allowed: Hubble has pointing restrictions to avoid the bright Earth, Sun, and Moon, and its instruments are protected against excessive light and scattered glare.

If those protections were overridden, the main result would be a very bright, rapidly smeared image. Hubble orbits only about 540 km above Earth and moves about 7.6 km/s. A ground scene would race through its field of view; without special ground-tracking and very short exposures, features would blur across the detector. Daylit Earth is also enormously brighter than the faint galaxies Hubble usually observes, so ordinary exposures would saturate the cameras.

In principle, a Hubble-sized telescope looking down could be very sharp. Its diffraction-limited visible-light resolution is about 0.05 arcseconds, which from Hubble’s altitude corresponds to roughly 10–15 cm on the ground. That is in the range of seeing cars and large objects, not reading newspapers or seeing through roofs. Atmospheric turbulence, clouds, haze, focus differences, and motion would degrade that.

So the careful answer is: Hubble is not built or operated as an Earth-imaging spy satellite. If forced to point at Earth, it would likely get overexposed, motion-blurred, operationally unsafe images. If redesigned with proper tracking, filters, fast shutters, and Earth-observation software, a Hubble-class telescope in low Earth orbit could take very high-resolution pictures of small patches of the surface.

items.question: What If Every Ship Were Removed from Earth's Waters at Once?
human_answers: About six microns—slightly more than the diameter of a strand of spider silk. [Image: image] Archimedes’ principle tells us that the water displaced by a ship weighs as much as the ship itself.
items.original_question: 如果每艘船同时从地球水域移走，海平面会下降多少？
items.model_answer:
If every ship, boat, and vessel were removed from Earth’s waters at the same instant, the biggest immediate physical effect would be surprisingly small globally: sea level would fall by only a few micrometers to perhaps a few tens of micrometers.

That is because floating ships raise sea level only by the volume of water they displace. By Archimedes’ principle, a floating vessel displaces water equal to its own weight plus cargo, fuel, and contents. Even if the total floating mass of the world’s merchant, naval, fishing, and recreational fleets were several billion tonnes, that corresponds to only a few cubic kilometers of displaced seawater. Spread across the oceans’ roughly 361 million square kilometers of surface area, the average sea-level change is tiny: far less than a millimeter.

Locally, however, the effect could be dramatic for a moment. Each removed ship would leave behind a hull-shaped void in the water. Surrounding water would rush in to fill it, creating splashes, turbulence, and waves. In crowded harbors, canals, locks, naval bases, or marinas, the sudden disappearance of many vessels could produce noticeable surges and sloshing. A large ship displaces tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of cubic meters of water, so its instant removal could generate strong local waves, though not an ocean-wide tsunami.

There would be no major change to tides, ocean currents, Earth’s rotation, or climate from the physical removal itself. The mass of all ships is negligible compared with Earth and the oceans.

The real global consequences would be economic and logistical. International trade would be instantly crippled, because most bulk goods—oil, grain, coal, iron ore, manufactured goods, containers—move by sea. Fishing fleets would vanish from the water, naval power projection would stop, ferry routes would cease, and many island and coastal communities would be cut off. Fuel, food, medicine, and industrial supply chains would be heavily disrupted within days to weeks.

Environmentally, the oceans would quickly become quieter and safer for many marine animals. Ship strikes, underwater engine noise, anchor damage, bilge discharge, and shipping-related emissions would drop sharply. Industrial fishing pressure would also collapse if fishing vessels were included. But the human disruption would be enormous.

So the direct ocean-physics answer is: the seas would barely fall globally, but harbors would experience sudden local turbulence. The civilization-level answer is: global maritime trade and naval activity would stop almost instantly, causing severe worldwide disruption.

items.question: What If You Put a Running Hair Dryer in a Sealed 1x1x1 Meter Box?
human_answers: A typical hair dryer draws 1875 watts of power. All 1875 watts have to go somewhere.
items.original_question: 如果打开连续功率的吹风机并将其放入密闭的 1x1x1 米盒子中会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
A running hair dryer in a sealed 1 m × 1 m × 1 m box would turn essentially all of its electrical power into heat inside the box.

The fan would just circulate the same air around; it would not “cool” the box or remove heat, because no air or energy is leaving. A typical hair dryer uses about 1,000–1,800 W, and almost all of that becomes thermal energy. If the box were perfectly insulated and the dryer kept running, the temperature would keep rising until the dryer failed, shut itself off, melted, or possibly started a fire.

For scale: 1 cubic meter of air has a mass of about 1.2 kg. The heat capacity of that air is roughly 1.2 kJ per °C. So a 1,500 W hair dryer could, in an idealized case where only the air heats up, raise the air temperature by about

\[
\frac{1500\ \text{J/s}}{1200\ \text{J/°C}} \approx 1.25^\circ\text{C/s}
\]

That means the air alone could rise tens of degrees in under a minute. In reality, the box walls, the dryer body, and anything else inside would absorb heat too, so the temperature rise would be slower. If the box is not insulated, heat would leak through the walls, and the temperature would eventually settle at a value where heat loss through the box equals the dryer’s power input.

Because the box is sealed and rigid, the pressure would also rise as the air heats. For example, heating the air from 20°C to 100°C would raise the pressure by roughly

\[
\frac{373}{293} \approx 1.27
\]

so the pressure would increase to about 1.27 atmospheres, assuming the box does not expand or leak.

The most likely practical outcome is that the dryer overheats and its thermal cutoff shuts it down. If the safety cutoff fails, the plastic parts, wiring, or surrounding materials could melt, smoke, or catch fire. The sealed box would not explode just because of the fan, but heating the trapped air raises pressure, and fire or failure could create additional hazards.

So the direct answer is: the box gets hotter and more pressurized; the dryer recirculates hot air; eventually the dryer shuts off, fails, or becomes a fire hazard unless heat can escape through the box walls.

items.question: How Much Cornstarch Can You Pour down a Drain before Bad Things Happen?
human_answers: It depends what you consider unpleasant. If you watered down the cornstarch enough, you could likely pour it down the drain for years without any ill effects.
items.original_question: 在不愉快的事情开始发生之前，我可以将多少玉米淀粉冲入下水道？
items.model_answer:
Practically: don’t pour cornstarch down a drain at all, except for tiny residue amounts rinsed off dishes with plenty of cold water.

There is no safe universal threshold, because it depends on pipe size, trap shape, water flow, and whether the starch meets hot water or grease. But as a rough guide: a teaspoon or so accidentally rinsed away is unlikely to matter if flushed with lots of cold water. A few tablespoons can start accumulating in a P-trap. A cup or more is very likely to cause trouble, especially if it gets wet and settles. With hot water, cornstarch can gelatinize into a thick paste, making clogs worse.

Cornstarch does not dissolve like sugar or salt. It suspends in water, settles in low-flow areas, and can form a sticky, dense mass. In a drain trap it can combine with grease, food particles, soap scum, and hair, eventually making a blockage.

If you’ve already put some down the drain, flush immediately with a large amount of cold water. Avoid hot water. If a large amount went in, stop running water, scoop out what you can, and consider removing/cleaning the P-trap or calling a plumber.

Best disposal: put dry cornstarch in the trash or compost, or wipe wet cornstarch into the trash before washing the container.

items.question: What If a Stereo Flew Past at Twice the Speed of Sound?
human_answers: Yes. Technically, anyway.
items.original_question: 如果你设法让立体声以两倍音速传播，当它飞过时，对于一个只是随意坐在某处的人来说，它听起来会是倒退的吗？
items.model_answer:
Assuming an ideal stereo that survives and keeps playing, you would not hear it coming. At Mach 2 it is moving faster than the sound it emits, so its sound cannot spread out ahead of it. The sound is swept into a trailing Mach cone with half-angle

\[
\sin\theta=\frac{c}{v}=\frac{1}{2},
\]

so \(\theta=30^\circ\).

If it flew past you at some distance, you would first see it pass silently. A short time later, when the Mach cone reached you, you would hear a sharp sonic boom. For a closest-approach distance \(d\), that boom would arrive about

\[
\frac{\sqrt{3}\,d}{2c}
\]

after the stereo passed its closest point, where \(c\) is the speed of sound.

After the boom, you would hear the music in a very strange way. The sound emitted near the moment whose wavefront formed the Mach cone would arrive all bunched together, so it would be loud and highly compressed. Then later sounds would arrive normally but Doppler-shifted, while some earlier sounds from before the boom would arrive in reverse order. In other words, it would not sound like an ordinary stereo going by with a pitch shift; it would be mostly silence, then a sonic boom, then a distorted overlapping mixture of forward-playing and backward-arriving music.

In the real world, a stereo flying through air at Mach 2 would likely be torn apart or drowned out by aerodynamic shock noise, so the “music” would be much less noticeable than the sonic boom.

items.question: What If We Launched a One-Way Mission to Voyager 1 Today?
human_answers: Voyager I is farther from Earth than any other manmade object. After getting a pair of gravitational kicks from Jupiter and Saturn, it’s headed out of the Solar System at a pretty high speed, and nothing else we’ve built is on track to pass it.
items.original_question: 以今天的技术，是否有可能发起无人回收航行者一号任务？
items.model_answer:
If we launched a one-way spacecraft mission to Voyager 1 today, the main problem would not be “getting to space”; it would be catching something that already has a huge head start and is still moving away from the Sun at about 17 km/s.

Voyager 1 is now roughly 25 billion km from Earth, about 165–170 AU, with a one-way radio light time of about 23 hours. It is in interstellar space and moving outward by about 3.6 AU per year.

A chasing spacecraft would have to exceed Voyager 1’s outward speed. The catch-up time depends almost entirely on its final solar-system escape speed:

At 20 km/s outward, only slightly faster than Voyager, it would take roughly 250–300 years to catch up. At 30 km/s, it would take about 60 years. At 50 km/s, about 25 years. At 100 km/s, about 10 years. At 200 km/s, only a few years, but achieving that as an outbound interstellar trajectory is far beyond ordinary chemical launch capability.

With current or near-current technology, a realistic uncrewed fast probe using a heavy rocket plus gravity assists, perhaps a solar Oberth maneuver, might reach Voyager 1’s distance in several decades, but not soon. It would probably intercept Voyager somewhere around 250–400 AU from the Sun, depending on speed.

There is also a major distinction between a flyby and a rendezvous. A flyby is much easier: the probe just crosses Voyager’s path and photographs or scans it at high relative speed. A rendezvous is far harder because the probe would need to slow down and match Voyager 1’s velocity after catching it. That could require tens of km/s of braking delta-v, which is extremely difficult without a large propulsion system and fuel supply.

By the time such a mission arrived, Voyager 1 itself would almost certainly be dead. Its plutonium power source is declining, and NASA expects its instruments and transmitter to become unusable around the late 2020s or 2030s. Decades later, a chasing probe would likely find a silent, frozen spacecraft coasting through interstellar space.

So the direct answer is: yes, an uncrewed one-way mission to Voyager 1 is physically possible, but with present technology it would probably be a decades-long high-speed flyby, not a rendezvous. A human one-way mission is not realistically feasible. The most practical version would be a specialized interstellar precursor probe launched on a very high-energy trajectory to overtake Voyager 1 far beyond the heliosphere.

items.question: What If Everyone in America Drove West?
human_answers: [Image: image] Thanks to plate tectonics, the United States is drifting west at about (http://hypertextbook.com/facts/ZhenHuang.shtml) a centimeter per year. (The people who live there, on the other hand, are on average drifting west at about a centimeter p...
items.original_question: 如果美国每个人都向西行驶，我们可以暂时停止大陆漂移吗？
items.model_answer:
If everyone in the United States tried to drive west at the same time, the main result would be a nationwide traffic disaster, not a dramatic physical effect on Earth.

Roads would jam almost immediately, especially around cities, bridges, tunnels, mountain passes, and the limited east–west highways. Gas stations would be overwhelmed, emergency services would be blocked, and many people would never get far. People already near the West Coast would quickly run out of land unless they turned, stopped, or drove into the Pacific.

If the question is about whether this would affect Earth’s rotation, the answer is: technically yes, but by an absurdly tiny amount. Suppose about 330 million people each drove west in a car at highway speed. The cars would gain westward angular momentum, so Earth would gain a tiny compensating eastward angular momentum and spin very slightly faster. The length of the day would shrink by roughly a nanosecond, about one-billionth of a second, and when the cars stopped, that effect would mostly disappear.

If everyone permanently relocated westward, even that would barely matter geophysically. The shift in Earth’s center of mass would be microscopic, far too small to affect tides, earthquakes, climate, or the planet’s orbit.

So the realistic answer is: America would experience catastrophic gridlock and fuel shortages; Earth itself would barely notice.

items.question: What If a High-Speed Train Had to Go through a Vertical Loop?
human_answers: No. Since this is kind of a disappointing answer, I tried relaxing the requirements a little.
items.original_question: 高速列车能否像过山车一样在垂直环路中运行，同时让乘客感到舒适？
items.model_answer:
A conventional high-speed train could not safely do it. A purpose-built vehicle could, but it would have to be more like a giant roller coaster or maglev system than a normal train.

At high speed, the limiting issue is centripetal acceleration. For a train moving through a vertical loop of radius \(R\) at speed \(v\), the required inward acceleration is

\[
a = \frac{v^2}{R}.
\]

At the bottom of the loop, passengers feel heavier:

\[
\text{load} = 1 + \frac{v^2}{Rg}.
\]

At the top, gravity helps provide the inward acceleration. To avoid falling away from the track without restraints, the train needs roughly

\[
\frac{v^2}{R} \ge g.
\]

Take a typical high-speed train speed of about 300 km/h, or 83 m/s. If it went through a circular loop at that speed, then to keep the bottom force to about 2 g, the loop radius would need to be around

\[
R \approx \frac{v^2}{g} \approx 700 \text{ m}.
\]

That means a loop diameter of roughly 1.4 km. A “comfortable” high-speed train loop would be enormous, taller than many mountains or skyscrapers.

If the loop were smaller, the g-forces would become severe. For example, if the train entered a simple unpowered circular loop just fast enough to stay on the track at the top, the bottom of the loop would impose about 6 g. That is dangerous for passengers and likely beyond what a normal train structure, bogies, couplers, and track could tolerate.

There is also an energy problem. A train entering at 300 km/h has enough kinetic energy to climb only about 350 m vertically if unpowered, ignoring losses. A gentle loop suitable for that speed might need to be far taller than that, so the train would need powerful propulsion throughout the climb.

The track would also need to be completely different. Ordinary steel rails rely on gravity keeping the wheels on the track. In a vertical loop, the train would need captive wheels, clamps, guide rails, or magnetic guidance to prevent derailment, especially near the top. Passengers would need restraints, luggage would have to be secured, fluids and equipment would need special design, and the train cars would need to handle huge bending and coupling forces.

So the short answer is: a high-speed train could go through a vertical loop only if the loop were gigantic and the train were specially built for it. A normal high-speed train on normal rails would derail, overstress its structure, and subject passengers to dangerous forces.

items.question: What If a Bowling Ball Were Enlarged to the Size of Earth?
human_answers: A good, professional-quality bowling ball is smoother than the Earth. Phil Plait, of Bad Astronomy, took a look at the claim that the Earth was smoother than a billiard ball.
items.original_question: 有人告诉我，如果地球缩小到保龄球大小，它会比保龄球更光滑。我的问题是，如果保龄球被吹到地球那么大，会是什么样子？
items.model_answer:
If a normal bowling ball were scaled up so its diameter matched Earth’s, it would not remain a recognizable giant bowling ball for long.

Assuming it keeps roughly the same material density, about 1.3–1.5 g/cm³, an Earth-sized bowling ball would have about one quarter of Earth’s mass. Its surface gravity would be only about 2.5 m/s², roughly one quarter of Earth gravity, and its escape velocity would be around 5–6 km/s.

The finger holes would become enormous: a 2.5 cm finger hole would scale to roughly 1,500 km wide, and a several-centimeter-deep hole could become thousands of kilometers deep. But those holes could not survive. At Earth size, the ball’s own gravity would create internal pressures of several to around ten gigapascals, far beyond what bowling-ball resin or filler materials can support. The holes and any large surface features would collapse, flow, fracture, and slump inward. The object would settle into a roughly spherical low-density planet or dwarf-planet-like body.

It would also likely heat dramatically. If the enlargement involved assembling that much material under gravity, the released gravitational energy would be enough to melt or severely alter much of the material. Instead of a polished plastic bowling ball, you would get a hot, crushed, chemically altered planet made of bowling-ball-like material.

If, on the other hand, you somehow enlarged the ball’s size without adding mass, then it would have an absurdly tiny density, far below even a good laboratory vacuum, and it could not behave like a solid object at all.

So the short answer is: an Earth-sized bowling ball with scaled-up mass would be a low-gravity planet at first, but gravity would crush the holes and destroy its bowling-ball shape.

items.question: What Would an Alien Civilization on the Nearest Habitable Exoplanet See When Looking at Us?
human_answers: Answer: [Image: image] Let’s try a more complete answer. We’ll start with ...
items.original_question: 让我们假设最近的宜居系外行星上有生命，并且他们拥有与我们相当的技术。如果他们现在看着我们的星星，他们会看到什么？
items.model_answer:
Assuming the nearest habitable exoplanet means Proxima Centauri b, about 4.24 light-years away, an alien civilization there would see Earth as it was 4.24 years ago, not as it is now. In May 2026, they would be receiving light and radio signals that left Earth around early 2022.

To their unaided eyes, they would not see Earth at all. They would see the Sun as a bright, ordinary-looking star in their sky, roughly magnitude 0.4, comparable to some of the brighter stars seen from Earth. Earth would be far too small and faint, and it would appear extremely close to the Sun from their point of view.

With advanced telescopes, they could in principle detect Earth as a very faint “pale blue dot” near the Sun. Its maximum apparent separation from the Sun would be only about 0.8 arcseconds, and it would be around ten billion times fainter than the Sun in visible light. They would need powerful optics or interferometry to separate Earth’s light from the Sun’s glare.

If they could analyze Earth’s light, they might infer a lot. They could detect that Earth has an atmosphere, oceans, clouds, and possibly continents. Spectroscopy could reveal water vapor, oxygen, ozone, carbon dioxide, and methane—strong hints of biology. With sufficiently precise observations, they might notice a 24-hour rotation, seasonal changes, weather patterns, and possibly even a vegetation “red edge.”

They probably would not see Earth transit the Sun, because Proxima Centauri is not aligned with Earth’s orbital plane in the right way. So Earth would not conveniently pass across the face of the Sun from their viewpoint.

If they had very sensitive radio instruments, they could also detect some human-made radio emissions that left Earth about 4.24 years earlier. Ordinary TV and radio leakage would be weak and hard to distinguish at that distance, but powerful radar transmissions or directed signals would be easier to notice.

So the direct answer is: from the nearest potentially habitable exoplanet, aliens would see the Sun as a bright star and, with sufficiently advanced technology, Earth as a tiny, faint, blue-white planet showing signs of oceans, atmosphere, and life—specifically Earth as it was a little over four years in the past.

items.question: What If the Sun Suddenly Went Out?
human_answers: This is probably the single most popular question submitted to What If. Part of why I haven’t answered it is that it's been answered already.
items.original_question: 如果太阳突然熄灭，地球会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If the Sun suddenly “went out” meaning it stopped producing light and heat but still kept its mass, Earth would not notice instantly. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth, so for that long everything would look normal. Then the sky would go dark in daytime, the Moon would go dark, and most planets would become very hard or impossible to see except by their own faint heat or reflected artificial light.

Earth would keep orbiting normally, because the Sun’s gravity would still be there. There would be no immediate change in tides or orbit if only the Sun’s radiation stopped.

The biggest effect would be loss of heat. Temperatures would not instantly plunge, because the oceans, land, and atmosphere store a lot of warmth, but the cooling would be severe. Within days to weeks, average surface temperatures would fall below freezing. After a few months, much of the surface would be far below zero. After about a year, average temperatures could be around −70°C or lower. The oceans would begin freezing from the top down; however, thick ice would insulate the deeper water, so parts of the deep ocean could remain liquid for a very long time, helped by geothermal heat from Earth’s interior.

Photosynthesis would stop almost immediately. Plants would begin dying, then herbivores, then predators. Most surface ecosystems would collapse. Some life could survive around deep-sea hydrothermal vents or underground, where energy comes from Earth’s internal heat and chemistry rather than sunlight.

Human survival would become extremely difficult but not instantly impossible. People could survive in sealed, insulated habitats using stored food, nuclear power, geothermal energy, or other artificial energy sources. Long-term survival would require living underground or under ice, with artificial lighting and controlled agriculture.

Over much longer timescales, the atmosphere itself would begin to freeze out. Water vapor and carbon dioxide would condense first; eventually, if Earth cooled enough, even oxygen and nitrogen could liquefy or freeze. Earth would become a dark, frozen world drifting around a dark Sun.

If instead the Sun literally vanished, not just went dark, then after about 8 minutes Earth would also stop feeling its gravity and would fly off in a straight line tangent to its former orbit. But if the Sun merely “went out,” Earth stays in orbit and slowly freezes.

items.question: What Would It Be Like to Row across Lakes of Mercury, Bromine, Gallium, Tungsten, Liquid Nitrogen, or Liquid Helium?
human_answers: Let's take these one at a time. Bromine and mercury are the only known pure elements that are liquid at room temperature.
items.original_question: 驾驶划艇穿过水银湖会是什么感觉？溴呢？液态镓？液态钨？液氮？液氦？
items.model_answer:
Assuming each “lake” is a stable open body of the liquid and you somehow have a compatible boat and protective gear, the experience would range from mechanically rowable to instantly fatal.

Mercury would be one of the most rowable mechanically, but very dangerous chemically. Mercury is about 13.5 times denser than water and only modestly more viscous, so a boat would float extremely high, almost as if sitting on a hard metallic surface. Oar blades would get a strong bite because the fluid is so dense, but they would also feel heavy and resist sudden motion. The lake would look like a bright silver mirror with sluggish, heavy-looking ripples. The main problem is toxicity: mercury vapor is hazardous, and splashing or contamination would be a serious long-term poison risk.

Bromine would be rowable in principle but nightmarish in practice. Liquid bromine is dense, red-brown, volatile, corrosive, and gives off choking toxic fumes. A boat would float well because bromine is about three times denser than water, and the liquid is not so viscous that rowing would be impossible. But the air above the lake would be full of bromine vapor; exposed skin, lungs, eyes, metals, and many plastics would be attacked. It would look like rowing across a dark red, fuming chemical spill. Without full chemical protection, you would not survive long.

Gallium would be surprisingly plausible if it were kept just above its melting point, about 30 °C. It is dense, silvery, and fairly low-viscosity, so a boat would float high and rowing would feel somewhat like rowing on a dense metallic liquid. It is much less volatile and less acutely poisonous than mercury or bromine. The big practical issue is materials: gallium attacks and embrittles aluminum and can wet or infiltrate some metals. A normal aluminum boat could be ruined. Also, if the lake cooled slightly, it would begin freezing into soft metal.

Tungsten would be impossible in any ordinary sense. Tungsten melts only around 3422 °C. A lake of liquid tungsten would be an incandescent white-hot metal lake. The radiant heat alone would ignite, melt, or vaporize ordinary boats, oars, clothing, and people from a distance. Even refractory materials would be under extreme stress. Mechanically, a boat could float very high because liquid tungsten is extremely dense, but you would never get the chance to row it. It would be more like approaching lava far hotter than most natural lava, except metallic and vastly denser.

Liquid nitrogen would be mechanically difficult and physically deadly. It is less dense than water, about 0.8 times water’s density, so a boat would float lower than on water and carry less load. It is also very cold, −196 °C, and would boil violently around anything warm. The lake surface would be covered in fog and bubbling nitrogen gas. Oars and hull materials would become brittle; water vapor and oxygen from the air could condense or freeze nearby; exposed flesh would freeze rapidly. Rowing might be possible briefly with a specially designed cryogenic craft, but the boiling around the boat would make the interaction with the liquid erratic, and the nitrogen gas could displace oxygen and suffocate you.

Liquid helium would be the least rowable of the cryogenic lakes. It is extremely cold, around 4 K at atmospheric pressure, and very low density, only about one-eighth that of water. A normal boat would have very little buoyant support unless it were extremely light and broad. Liquid helium has extraordinarily low viscosity and low surface tension, so oars would get little “grip” compared with water. Any heat leaking from the boat, oars, or environment would boil it rapidly, surrounding you with helium gas and intense cold. If the helium were below the lambda point and became superfluid helium, ordinary rowing would become even stranger: a frictionless component would not respond to oars in the usual way. In practice, you would freeze equipment, boil away the lake locally, and asphyxiate long before having a normal rowing experience.

So the rough ranking is: gallium and mercury are mechanically the most rowable, though mercury is highly toxic; bromine is rowable but chemically horrific; liquid nitrogen is barely conceivable only with specialized cryogenic engineering; liquid helium is almost unrowable and extremely dangerous; and liquid tungsten is effectively impossible because of its extreme temperature.

items.question: What If You Dropped 3,000 Super Balls onto a Pedestrian from a Seven-Story Parking Garage?
human_answers: After falling from seven stories, the mass of bouncy balls would be moving at about 20 meters per second. 20 meters per second is about how fast an average person with a good arm could throw a bouncy ball.
items.original_question: 如果将 3,000 个弹力球从七层停车场扔到下面人行道上行走的人身上会怎样？如果这个人活下来，需要多少个弹力球才能杀死他？会发生什么伤害以及相关的犯罪是什么？
items.model_answer:
From a seven-story parking garage, the Super Balls would hit at roughly 20 m/s, about 45 mph, assuming a height around 20–25 meters. A typical small Super Ball has only a few joules of kinetic energy at that speed, so one ball would be painful but usually not catastrophic, more like being hit by a very hard-thrown rubber ball or large hailstone.

But 3,000 of them changes the situation. Depending on size, that could be something like 30–60 kg or more of rubber falling from the garage, with total energy on the order of 10,000 joules. If they were loose and spread out, the pedestrian would likely be battered, bruised, possibly knocked down, and at serious risk of eye, face, scalp, or fall injuries. It would be very dangerous, but not automatically fatal because the energy is divided among many small impacts and many balls would bounce or miss.

If, however, the balls arrived in a dense cluster or inside a bag/container so that the mass hit as one compact falling object, it could easily cause severe trauma or death. The biggest realistic dangers from loose balls would be head and eye injury, being knocked off balance, and then slipping or falling on the bouncing balls afterward.

So: loose 3,000 Super Balls would be a serious, potentially injurious assault; compacted or contained, it could be lethal.

items.question: What If You Drained the Oceans through a 10-Meter Hole at Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker...
items.original_question: 如果在海洋最深点“挑战者深渊”的底部建造一个半径 10 米通向太空的圆形入口，海洋的排水速度有多快？当水被排干时，地球会发生什么变化？
items.model_answer:
Assuming the “10-meter hole” is a circular 10 m diameter drain at Challenger Deep that leads to a magical empty reservoir and never clogs, the oceans would not vanish quickly. They would drain on a million-year timescale.

At Challenger Deep the water pressure is about 110 MPa, roughly 1,100 atmospheres. That pressure could drive water through the hole at an ideal speed of about

\[
v \approx \sqrt{2gh} \approx \sqrt{2(9.8)(10900)} \approx 460\ \text{m/s}.
\]

A 10 m diameter hole has an area of about 78.5 m², so the initial ideal flow rate would be about

\[
Q \approx 3.6\times10^4\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}.
\]

With real losses, turbulence, and contraction at the opening, something like 20,000–30,000 m³/s is more plausible. That is a huge flow, but still only around a tenth of the Amazon River’s discharge.

Spread over the whole ocean surface, the initial sea-level fall would be only a few millimeters per year, roughly comparable to modern sea-level rise but in the opposite direction. Since the oceans contain about \(1.3\times10^{18}\) m³ of water, the absolute lower-bound drain time is about 1 million years. Because the pressure head decreases as sea level falls, the actual idealized time would be more like a few million years.

The effects would be dramatic but slow. Continental shelves would gradually become land. Shallow seas would disappear. Land bridges would form. Climate and ocean circulation would change profoundly. But there would be no sudden global whirlpool or bathtub-style vortex. Far from the hole, ocean currents caused by the drain would be tiny.

In the real world, it would not work as a clean drain. A 10 m hole into Earth’s crust would likely collapse, clog with debris, or become a violent hydrothermal/volcanic system. Water entering hot rock would flash into steam or supercritical fluid, fracture rock, deposit minerals, and probably seal the passage. Also, once sea level fell far enough, many ocean basins would become isolated by ridges and sills, so a single hole at Challenger Deep would not literally empty every basin unless channels were somehow maintained.

So the direct answer is: with a magical uncloggable drain, the oceans would lower by millimeters per year and take on the order of millions of years to drain; with real geology, the hole would almost certainly fail or seal long before the oceans disappeared.

items.question: What If You Dumped Earth's Oceans onto Mars?
human_answers: In the previous What If (http://what-if.xkcd.com/53/), we opened a portal at the bottom of the Mariana Trench and let the oceans drain out. We didn't worry too much about where the oceans were draining to.
items.original_question: 假设你做了“排干海洋”，并将水倒在好奇号火星车顶部，随着水的积累，火星会发生什么变化？
items.model_answer:
Assuming you magically placed Earth’s oceans on present-day Mars rather than letting them hit at interplanetary speed, Mars would briefly become a flooded planet, then mostly an ice-covered one—not a second Earth.

Earth’s oceans contain about \(1.3 \times 10^9\) cubic kilometers of water. Mars has a surface area of about \(1.45 \times 10^8\) square kilometers, so if that water were spread evenly it would make a global layer about 9 kilometers deep. Because Mars has huge elevation differences, the water would first fill the northern lowlands and giant basins, producing deep oceans, while the highest southern highlands and volcanic regions—especially Olympus Mons and parts of Tharsis—would remain as islands or continents.

At first the result would be violent: global floods, enormous erosion, landslides, steam, fog, snow, and intense weather. Some water would boil because Mars’ current atmospheric pressure is near the triple point of water, but the boiling would not remove the ocean. Evaporation would cool the water and create a water-vapor atmosphere, much of which would then condense or freeze.

The key point is that Mars is cold and lacks a thick greenhouse atmosphere. Mars receives only about 43% as much sunlight as Earth, and its thin CO₂ atmosphere cannot keep a planet-wide ocean warm. The surface would freeze over. You would likely end up with a thick global ice shell, perhaps kilometers thick, with liquid water surviving underneath in many places because ice is an insulator and Mars has some geothermal heat.

The added water would not make Mars breathable. Water vapor is not oxygen, and although sunlight can split some water into hydrogen and oxygen, the hydrogen would escape to space and the oxygen would react with the Martian surface or be lost over time. Mars’ weak gravity and lack of a global magnetic field would make long-term atmospheric retention difficult compared with Earth.

So the final state would be something like a frozen ocean world: Mars covered by immense seas that quickly become ice-covered, with possible subsurface oceans beneath. It would be wetter, heavier, and geologically transformed, but it would not become Earthlike without also adding a thick, stable atmosphere and a strong long-term warming mechanism.

items.question: What If You Tried to Hold an Airplane to the Ground with a Rope?
human_answers: Ah, the Just Cause 2 scenario (http://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=just+cause+2+plane+grapple). At takeoff, a 747's four engines can each generate 281.57 kN of thrust.
items.original_question: 如果你想将一架飞机固定在地面上，使其无法起飞，那么绳子必须用什么材料制成？
items.model_answer:
If you tied an airplane to a solid anchor with a rope and then advanced the throttles, the airplane would not take off in calm air as long as the rope, anchor, and attachment point could withstand the force.

The key point is that an airplane needs airspeed over its wings to make enough lift. Engines provide thrust, which normally accelerates the airplane down the runway; the wing lift comes from that motion through the air. If a rope prevents the airplane from moving, the wings do not get takeoff airspeed, so they do not produce enough lift to fly.

What happens instead is simple but violent: the engines pull against the rope. The rope tension rises roughly to the airplane’s available thrust, minus small effects like wheel friction and aerodynamic drag. For a small propeller plane, this might be a few thousand newtons, so a strong rope and good anchor could hold it. For a jet airliner, the thrust can be hundreds of thousands of newtons. A normal rope, vehicle, tree, or weak ground anchor would likely fail catastrophically. The rope could snap, the anchor could rip out, or the part of the airplane you tied to could be damaged.

If everything were absurdly strong, the airplane would just sit there with its engines blasting. The brakes and tiedowns on aircraft already do a version of this during engine run-ups, though within safe limits.

There are exceptions. If there were a strong headwind equal to or greater than takeoff speed, the airplane could generate lift while stationary relative to the ground. Then it might rise like a tethered kite, limited by the rope, or it might overload the rope or airframe. But in normal calm runway conditions, tying an airplane to the ground does not make it “fight upward”; it mostly makes it pull horizontally until something gives.

items.question: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?
human_answers: The one-inch gap would take about 70 milliseconds to close. Don't stick your hand in.
items.original_question: 如果一座巨大的山峰（比如麦金利山）的底部一英寸消失了怎么办？山体下降1英寸的影响会发生什么？ 1英尺呢？如果山脚升高到山顶现在的高度，然后让整个山落到地上怎么办？
items.model_answer:
A real mountain does not have a clean “bottom inch” like a block sitting on a table; it is continuous with the crust beneath it. But if, by magic, a one-inch-thick horizontal layer under the whole mountain suddenly vanished, the overlying rock would lose support and begin to collapse into the gap.

It would not fall far: only about 2.5 cm. In free fall over that distance, the rock would hit the lower surface at only about 0.7 m/s, roughly walking speed. But because the mass involved is enormous, the energy release would be huge. For a large mountain with a mass around \(10^{15}\) kg, dropping one inch releases roughly

\[
E \approx Mgh \approx 10^{15} \times 9.8 \times 0.025 \approx 2.5 \times 10^{14}\text{ J},
\]

which is comparable to tens of kilotons of TNT. For an even larger massif, it could be hundreds of kilotons equivalent.

The result would be a violent local geologic event: intense cracking, crushing of the bottom rock, seismic waves, rockfalls, landslides, and possibly a quake-like shock felt far away. The mountain would not leap into the air or disappear; it would mostly settle downward by about an inch, but unevenly and destructively. The impact and stress redistribution would pulverize rock in places and could destabilize slopes over a wide region.

It would not destroy the planet or launch the mountain upward. It would be more like a sudden, shallow, mountain-sized collapse producing a significant earthquake and catastrophic landslides near the mountain.

items.question: What If a Spacecraft Used Rockets to Slow to a Few Miles per Hour during Reentry?
human_answers: The answers to these questions all hinge on the same idea. It's an idea I've touched on in other articles, but today I want to focus on it specifically: The reason it's hard to get to orbit isn't that space is high up.
items.original_question: 如果航天器使用火星天空起重机等火箭助推器在重返大气层时减速至每小时几英里会怎么样？它会消除对隔热罩的需要吗？
items.model_answer:
Yes, in principle a spacecraft could use rockets to slow to only a few miles per hour during reentry, but for an orbital spacecraft it would be extremely inefficient and would require a huge amount of propellant.

A spacecraft in low Earth orbit is moving about 17,500 mph, or 7.8 km/s. To slow almost to a stop using rockets, it would need to cancel nearly all of that orbital velocity. That is roughly comparable to the velocity change needed to reach orbit in the first place. Because rockets must carry their own propellant, the mass penalty is enormous: the spacecraft would need to launch with many times its dry mass in fuel just to brake itself back down.

Also, slowing to a few miles per hour high in the atmosphere would not solve the whole problem. If the spacecraft is still tens of kilometers above the ground and moving only a few mph, it will simply begin falling again under gravity. It would then need to keep firing rockets all the way down, essentially hovering or performing a powered descent, which costs still more propellant.

If the spacecraft waits until lower altitude to use rockets, it still has to survive the earlier high-speed atmospheric entry. Aerodynamic drag would produce intense heating unless the vehicle had already slowed significantly before encountering dense air. That is why most returning spacecraft use the atmosphere itself as a “free brake”: the heat shield absorbs and dissipates the orbital kinetic energy, then parachutes, wings, or small landing rockets handle the final descent.

So the answer is: it is physically possible, and vehicles can use rockets for part of reentry or landing, but using rockets to slow an orbital spacecraft to a few miles per hour during reentry would be impractical for most missions because the propellant requirement would be enormous. It is far more efficient to use atmospheric drag for most of the braking and reserve rockets, parachutes, or wings for the final landing phase.

items.question: What If You Tried to Print the Entire English Wikipedia in Real Time?
human_answers: This many: [Image: image] That's surprisingly few printers! But before you try to create a live-updating paper Wikipedia, let's look at what those printers would be doing ...
items.original_question: 如果您有整个（例如英文）维基百科的印刷版本，您需要多少台打印机才能跟上对实时版本所做的更改？
items.model_answer:
If you mean “print a current snapshot of the English Wikipedia, and keep the paper copy current as edits happen,” the result is a huge but not physically impossible printing job; the absurd part is maintaining it.

The English Wikipedia is on the order of several billion words. Printed as ordinary text, with references and formatting, it would be roughly 10–20 million printed pages. On double-sided paper, that is millions of sheets: tens of tonnes of paper and a stack well over a kilometer high if piled up. A normal office laser printer printing 30–60 pages per minute would take months to print one full copy.

But Wikipedia would not sit still while you printed it. The English Wikipedia receives roughly one to two edits per second, or around 100,000+ edits per day. If every edit forced you to print a replacement page, you would need several office printers running continuously just to keep up with the changes, plus an enormous system for collating, replacing, recycling, and rebinding pages. If you reprinted entire edited articles rather than just changed pages, the demand would grow to many more printers.

If you interpreted the task even more literally—reprint the entire encyclopedia every time it changes—it becomes hopeless. With edits arriving every second or so and each full copy requiring millions of pages, you would need millions of pages per second of printing capacity.

So the direct answer is: printing a static English Wikipedia is merely gigantic; printing it “in real time” as a perfectly current physical encyclopedia is effectively impractical. You could keep up with the raw edit stream using a modest bank of printers, but producing a usable, always-current printed Wikipedia would be a logistical nightmare of paper, ink, sorting, and constant obsolescence.

items.question: What If You Jumped from a Plane with Helium Tanks and a Giant Balloon?
human_answers: As ridiculous as it sounds, this is—sort of—possible. Falling from great heights is dangerous.[citation needed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Republic_Presidential_Unit_Citation)] A balloon could actually help save you, although a regular helium...
items.original_question: 如果我带着几罐氦气和一个巨大的未充气的气球从飞机上跳下来怎么办？然后，在下降时，我释放氦气并填充气球。我需要下落多长时间才能让气球减慢我的速度以便我能够安全着陆？
