items.model_answer:
If you jumped from a plane carrying helium tanks and a giant balloon, it would almost certainly not save you. You would likely fall, fail to inflate the balloon safely, and hit the ground at a lethal speed.

A helium balloon can lift you only by displacing air. At sea level, supporting a person plus gear of about 100 kg would require roughly 100 cubic meters of helium, corresponding to a spherical balloon about 6 meters across. At typical aircraft altitude, where the air is thinner, you would need an even larger balloon—perhaps 8–10 meters across or more—to get the same lift.

The helium tanks are a major problem. To lift 100 kg, you need on the order of 15–20 kg of helium, plus the weight of the balloon, harness, valves, and tanks. High-pressure helium cylinders capable of carrying that much gas would be very heavy, possibly heavier than the lift they help create. So carrying enough helium in tanks while jumping is not practical.

Inflating the balloon during the fall would also be extremely difficult. You would be falling at perhaps 50–60 m/s before slowing, with violent airflow whipping the balloon around. A giant lightweight balloon would tangle, tear, or fail to deploy cleanly. If it inflated suddenly, the deceleration could injure or kill you, much like opening an enormous parachute incorrectly.

Even if the balloon did inflate, it would not behave like a parachute. A parachute is designed to open in high-speed airflow and create stable drag. A helium balloon is designed for buoyancy, not violent deployment. It could rupture, spin, collapse, or drag you unpredictably.

If, by magic, you already had a large enough fully inflated helium balloon attached before leaving the plane, then you might descend slowly or even float upward depending on the lift. But that would be more like stepping out with a small airship or balloon system, not jumping with tanks and inflating it midair.

So the direct answer is: with real equipment, you would probably die. The tanks are too heavy, the balloon would be too large, and deployment during free fall would be uncontrollable. A parachute is vastly simpler, lighter, and safer because it is designed for exactly this job.

items.question: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?
human_answers: [Image: image] Google almost certainly has more data storage capacity than any other organization on Earth. Google is very secretive about its operations, so it's hard to say for sure.
items.original_question: 如果所有数字数据都存储在打孔卡上，谷歌的数据仓库有多大？
items.model_answer:
If all digital data were stored on punch cards, modern computing would become physically and logistically impossible.

Take a standard IBM-style punch card: about 80 characters of data, roughly 80 bytes in ordinary use. A single 1 MB file would need about 12,500 cards. A 1 GB movie would need about 12.5 million cards. A 1 TB drive would require about 12.5 billion cards.

For the world’s digital data, the numbers become absurd. Humanity has on the order of 100–200 zettabytes of digital data, depending on what is counted. Using 150 zettabytes as a rough estimate:

150 ZB = 150,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 bytes.

At 80 bytes per card, that would require about 1.9 sextillion punch cards:

1,900,000,000,000,000,000,000 cards.

Physically, that is catastrophic. A punch card is thin, but not that thin. Stacked together, those cards would form a pile tens of light-years long. As a dense block, ignoring shelving and access space, they would occupy a cube roughly 170 kilometers on each side. Their mass would be on the order of several quintillion kilograms of cardstock, far beyond any realistic paper industry and vastly beyond Earth’s available forests if made from wood pulp.

Access speed would be even worse. A fast punch-card reader might read around 1,000–2,000 cards per minute, which is only a few kilobytes per second. Reading a modern hard drive’s worth of data would take years. Searching, copying, backing up, or streaming data would require immense mechanical warehouses full of readers, sorters, conveyors, and workers or robots. A single video stream, database query, or software update could involve moving mountains of cards.

Reliability would also be poor. Punch cards can last a long time in controlled archival conditions, but they are vulnerable to fire, water, mold, tearing, misordering, and physical wear. Digital error correction and redundancy would require even more cards, multiplying the already impossible storage burden.

So the practical result would be that most modern digital life would disappear. No large-scale internet, no cloud computing, no streaming media, no real-time search engines, no modern AI training, no global software distribution, and no dense personal storage. Society would have to store only tiny amounts of essential data, and computing would resemble mid-20th-century batch processing: slow, expensive, physical, and heavily rationed.

In short: storing all digital data on punch cards is not merely inefficient; it would turn the information age into a planet-scale paper-handling problem, and the system would collapse under its own size.

items.question: What If You Began Rising Upward at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: Did you bring a coat? A foot per second isn't that fast—it's substantially slower than a typical elevator.[1]Otis: About Elevators (http://www.otisworldwide.com/pdf/AboutElevators.pdf) It would take you 5-7 seconds to rise out of arms' reach, depending how...
items.original_question: 如果你突然开始以每秒一英尺的速度稳定上升，你到底会怎么死？你会先被冻住还是窒息？或者其他什么？
items.model_answer:
If you only had an initial upward speed of one foot per second, normal gravity would stop you almost immediately: you would rise only about half a centimeter before falling back down. So the interesting version is: some mysterious force keeps you rising at a constant 1 ft/s, about 0.3 m/s.

At that speed you would climb about 3,600 feet per hour, or 26 km per day. For the first few minutes it would just be dangerous and awkward: after 30 seconds you are 30 feet up, already high enough that falling could injure or kill you. After an hour you are around 1.1 km up; after 5 hours, around 5.5 km, where the air is thin enough that an unacclimatized person would be badly impaired. You would also be getting very cold.

Without rescue, oxygen, and warm gear, you would probably become confused and incapacitated after several hours. By about 8–10 hours, you would be near Everest/commercial-airliner altitudes, where the air pressure is far too low for normal survival and temperatures may be around −40 to −60 °C. You would likely be unconscious and soon dead from hypoxia and exposure.

If you had supplemental oxygen and heavy insulation, you could last longer, but pressure would become the next problem. Around 18–19 km up, reached after roughly 17 hours, you approach the Armstrong limit, where body fluids can boil at body temperature unless you are in a pressure suit. Above that, an oxygen mask is not enough; you need a pressurized suit or cabin.

With a full pressure suit and life support, you would reach the edge of space, about 100 km up, after about 91 hours, or just under 4 days. But you would not be “in orbit”; one foot per second is far, far too slow for that. If the upward force stopped, you would fall back to Earth. If it kept going, you would simply drift slowly outward, taking about 15 days to reach the altitude of the ISS and about 40 years to reach the Moon’s distance.

So, in ordinary clothes, the answer is: you could be saved early, but if not, you would die within the first day, probably within the first 8–12 hours, from cold and lack of oxygen.

items.question: What If the Wind Reached 500 Miles per Hour?
human_answers: Absolutely! [Image: image] Some things don't work like they do in the movies.
items.original_question: 如果风速达到 500 英里/小时，它会卷起人吗？
items.model_answer:
A 500-mile-per-hour wind at ground level would be catastrophically destructive. It would be stronger than the winds in the most violent tornadoes and far beyond any normal hurricane.

At 500 mph, the air is moving about 223 meters per second, roughly two-thirds the speed of sound. The wind pressure would be enormous: about 30,000 pascals, or around 0.3 atmospheres of dynamic pressure. That is enough to tear apart houses, rip steel roofing and siding from buildings, snap or uproot trees, overturn vehicles, destroy power lines, and turn debris into high-speed projectiles. A person exposed in the open would not be able to stand or breathe normally and would likely be lifted, tumbled, or struck by debris almost immediately.

Most ordinary buildings would fail. Wood-frame houses would be shredded. Windows would explode inward or outward depending on pressure differences. Roofs would be peeled off, walls could collapse, and even many reinforced structures would suffer severe damage if they were not specifically designed for extreme wind loads. Skyscrapers might not simply “blow over,” because they are engineered for wind, but windows, cladding, antennas, and exterior equipment would be heavily damaged or stripped away.

If this wind occurred over the ocean, it would generate extreme waves, dense sea spray, and potentially devastating storm surge near coasts. Ships would be in grave danger. If it swept over land for an extended time, it would scour soil, flatten forests, destroy crops, and fill the air with dust, sand, vegetation, glass, metal, and wreckage.

It would not be like a nuclear blast, and it would not by itself strip away Earth’s atmosphere or level mountains. But at the surface, a sustained 500 mph wind would make most exposed areas unsurvivable and would leave damage comparable to or worse than the core of the most violent tornadoes, especially because the destruction would be spread over whatever area the wind covered.

items.question: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?
human_answers: Last week, we looked at at life on a giant world (http://what-if.xkcd.com/67/). This week, let's look at a small one.
items.original_question: 如果一颗小行星很小但质量却很大，你真的能像小王子一样住在上面吗？
items.model_answer:
If you lived on a tiny but ultra-massive asteroid, the main problem would be gravity. A small radius plus a huge mass gives enormous surface gravity:

\(g = GM/R^2\)

So if the asteroid were only a few hundred meters wide but had the mass of a planet, you would not “walk around” on it. You would be crushed almost instantly, and the difference in gravity between your feet and your head could be large enough to stretch or tear you apart. That tidal force scales roughly as \(2gh/R\), so on a very small massive body it becomes severe.

It also would not behave like a normal asteroid. Ordinary rock could not remain a lumpy asteroid under that much self-gravity. It would collapse into a sphere and, if dense enough, into exotic matter. If its mass were packed inside its Schwarzschild radius,

\(R_s = 2GM/c^2\),

it would be a black hole, meaning there would be no solid surface to live on at all.

If the mass were carefully chosen so that surface gravity was about Earth-like, the world would still be bizarre. For example, a 100-meter-radius object with 1 g gravity would have a circumference of only about 628 meters. The horizon would be very close, gravity would noticeably weaken as you climbed even a few dozen meters, and orbital speed near the surface would be only tens of meters per second. But such a tiny world could not naturally hold a breathable atmosphere for long unless it were sealed or artificially maintained.

So the direct answer is: if it were merely “tiny but dense” and tuned to Earth-like gravity, you could survive only in an engineered habitat and the environment would feel very strange. If it were truly ultra-massive, you could not live there—the gravity, tides, pressure, and possible collapse into a black hole would make it instantly fatal.

items.question: Could You Boil Water by Stirring It?
human_answers: No. The basic idea makes sense.
items.original_question: 我心不在焉地搅拌着一杯热茶，心里想：我这不是给杯子里加了动能吗？我知道搅拌确实有助于冷却茶，但如果我搅拌得更快怎么办？我可以通过搅拌来煮一杯水吗？
items.model_answer:
Yes, in principle you can boil water by stirring it, because stirring does mechanical work on the water, and that work is eventually dissipated as heat through viscosity and turbulence.

For example, to heat 1 liter of water from 20°C to 100°C requires about

\[
Q = mc\Delta T \approx (1\,\text{kg})(4180\,\text{J/kg·°C})(80°C) \approx 334{,}000\,\text{J}.
\]

So if you could put 100 watts of mechanical power directly into the water as stirring and keep it well insulated, it would take roughly

\[
334{,}000/100 \approx 3300\,\text{s} \approx 55\,\text{minutes}
\]

just to reach the boiling point. To actually boil away a significant amount of water requires much more energy, because vaporization takes about 2.26 million joules per kilogram.

In practice, boiling water by hand-stirring is essentially impossible: a person cannot sustain enough power into the water, and heat losses to the container and air would usually exceed the heating from stirring. But with a powerful mechanical stirrer, blender, or paddle in a well-insulated vessel, yes, the water could eventually be heated to boiling purely by stirring.

So the careful answer is: yes physically, but not realistically by ordinary hand stirring.

items.question: What If a Nearby Supernova Hit Earth with Lethal Neutrino Radiation?
human_answers: The phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" is a weird one. I had to turn it over in my head a few times after I heard it.
items.original_question: 距离超新星有多近才能获得致命剂量的中微子辐射？
items.model_answer:
A supernova can only give Earth a lethal neutrino dose if it is absurdly close: roughly within a few astronomical units of the collapsing core, comparable to the scale of the inner Solar System, not “nearby” in the usual astronomical sense of tens or hundreds of light-years.

In that scenario, the neutrino burst would arrive first. A core-collapse supernova releases about \(10^{58}\) neutrinos in roughly 10 seconds. Almost all of them would pass straight through Earth, but at a distance of only a few AU the flux would be so enormous that enough would interact inside living tissue to deliver a fatal whole-body radiation dose. Shielding would not help: the neutrinos would pass through the atmosphere, oceans, mountains, bunkers, and the entire planet. People on the night side of Earth would be irradiated almost as much as people facing the supernova.

The immediate biological effect would be acute radiation exposure throughout the body. At a merely “lethal” dose, humans and many animals would not necessarily die instantly, but would suffer severe radiation sickness and die over hours to weeks. At closer distances, the dose could be high enough to cause rapid neurological failure and near-immediate death. Microbes and some radiation-resistant life might survive the neutrino burst itself, depending on the dose.

But the neutrinos would not be the main long-term problem. If a supernova were close enough for its neutrinos to be lethal, the rest of the explosion would be catastrophically worse. The optical, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma-ray output would bake and ionize the atmosphere and surface. Later, the expanding supernova ejecta would arrive and could strip atmosphere, vaporize oceans, and sterilize or physically devastate the planet. At a few AU, Earth would be inside the supernova’s immediate blast environment.

So the direct answer is: Earth would receive a planet-wide, unshieldable burst of radiation lasting seconds, likely killing most complex life everywhere at once or soon after. But a supernova close enough to do that with neutrinos would also destroy Earth’s habitability by ordinary radiation and blast effects shortly afterward. For any realistic supernova at stellar-neighborhood distances, such as tens or hundreds of light-years away, neutrino radiation would be harmless; the danger would come from photons, cosmic rays, and atmospheric damage, not neutrinos.

items.question: What If Humans Kept Growing at the Rate of a One-Month-Old Baby?
human_answers: Tall. According to the National Center for Health Statistics, the average newborn's height (length) is approximately 0.5 meters,[1]or 0.56 meters in heels.
items.original_question: 如果我们在整个发育期（即直到十几岁/二十岁出头）都以与第一个月相同的速度生长，人类会达到什么高度？
items.model_answer:
If humans kept growing at the absolute growth rate of a typical one-month-old baby, they would become giants but not survive in anything like a normal human form.

A one-month-old baby gains roughly 0.7–1 kg per month and grows about 3–4 cm in length per month. If that continued linearly until age 18, a person could be around 7–9 meters tall and weigh perhaps 170–220 kg based only on the baby’s monthly weight gain.

But that body would not work. A human scaled up to 7–9 meters tall with normal proportions would weigh several tons, not a couple hundred kilograms, because volume and mass scale roughly with the cube of height. The skeleton, heart, lungs, joints, and blood vessels would fail under square-cube-law effects: bones and muscles would not become strong enough fast enough to support the mass, circulation would be extremely difficult, and heat regulation would be a major problem.

If “rate” meant percentage growth rather than absolute growth, the result would be far more absurd. Babies grow by a large fraction of their body size each month; maintaining that exponential rate for years would produce bodies of impossible size, eventually asteroid-scale in mass.

So the careful answer is: if growth continued at a one-month-old’s absolute rate, adults would be several meters tall and biologically nonviable; if it continued at the same percentage rate, the growth would become catastrophically exponential and physically impossible very quickly.

items.question: What If a Tyrannosaurus Rex Were Released in New York City?
human_answers: About half of an adult, or one ten-year old child: [Image: image] Tyrannosaurus rex weighed about as much as an elephant.[1]This always seemed a little off to me; my mental image of elephants is that they're in the same size range as cars or trucks, whereas...
items.original_question: 如果霸王龙被释放到纽约市，它每天需要消耗多少人才能获得所需的卡路里摄入量？
items.model_answer:
If a Tyrannosaurus rex were suddenly released in New York City, the result would be dangerous and chaotic at first, but it would probably not become a long-term city-destroying catastrophe.

A T. rex was an enormous predatory animal, roughly 12–13 meters long and weighing several tons. In a dense urban area, it could kill people, crush cars, break storefronts, and cause mass panic. Its bite would be devastating, and ordinary barriers like glass doors, light fencing, or parked vehicles would not reliably stop it. The greatest immediate danger might come from crowds fleeing, traffic accidents, subway and street evacuations, and confusion rather than from the animal killing large numbers of people directly.

However, a T. rex would also face serious limits in New York City. It was not a movie monster with unlimited stamina or intelligence. It would be confused by noise, lights, vehicles, buildings, slick pavement, and dense obstacles. Manhattan streets are narrow relative to its body size, full of hard surfaces, and surrounded by barriers, tunnels, bridges, and water. It would have difficulty maneuvering in many areas, could injure itself on pavement or debris, and would likely avoid some loud or unfamiliar stimuli.

Police and emergency services would likely establish a perimeter, evacuate nearby streets and buildings, shut down traffic and transit in the area, and track it with helicopters, drones, and cameras. The goal would probably be containment first, then tranquilization or, if necessary, lethal force. Sedating an animal that large would be difficult: the dose would need to be accurate, and tranquilizers do not work instantly. A wounded or partially sedated T. rex could remain dangerous for several minutes. If it posed an immediate threat to many people, authorities might use heavy firearms or military support.

Could it survive? Not for long on its own. It would need enormous amounts of food, water, and space. New York has plenty of potential prey in the form of humans, dogs, horses, zoo animals, and refuse, but the city is not an appropriate habitat for a giant theropod. It would be isolated, highly visible, and quickly surrounded. Disease exposure, stress, injury, and lack of suitable territory would all work against it.

So the likely outcome is: several hours of extreme disruption, possible deaths and injuries, major property damage, a massive emergency response, and then capture or killing of the animal. It would be terrifying, but modern surveillance, vehicles, barriers, weapons, and coordinated emergency services would make it very unlikely that a single T. rex could roam New York City for more than a short time.

items.question: What If You Dumped All the World's Tea into the Great Lakes?
human_answers: Weak, bordering on homeopathic. The standard cup of tea, as described by the International Organization for Standardization in ISO 3103 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=8250), contains two grams of tea per 100 mL of water.[1]Further ISO...
items.original_question: 如果我们把世界上所有的茶叶都倒进五大湖怎么办？与普通的茶相比，湖茶的浓度如何？
items.model_answer:
Assuming “all the world’s tea” means about one year of global dry tea production, roughly 6–7 million metric tons, the Great Lakes would not become a giant drinkable pot of tea.

The Great Lakes contain about 22,700 cubic kilometers of water, or about 2.27 × 10¹⁶ liters. Spreading 7 million tons of dry tea through that volume gives only about 0.3 milligrams of tea leaves per liter of lake water. A normal cup of tea is brewed with something like 8 grams of leaves per liter, so the Great Lakes mixture would be around 25,000–30,000 times weaker than ordinary tea, even before accounting for the fact that cold lake water would extract tea compounds poorly.

If all that tea were brewed first and then poured in, it would still be tiny compared with the lakes. One year’s tea would make under 1 cubic kilometer of beverage, diluted into 22,700 cubic kilometers of lake water. If it were boiling hot, it would warm the Great Lakes by only a few thousandths of a degree Celsius. The lake level would rise by only a few millimeters.

Chemically, the caffeine would be measurable but not stimulating. If the tea were about 3% caffeine by dry mass and all of it dissolved, the lakes would end up around 5–10 micrograms of caffeine per liter. You would need thousands of liters of lake water to get the caffeine in a single cup of tea.

The main effects would be local pollution, not lake-wide tea. If dumped in one place, the tea leaves would form huge floating and sinking mats, clog shorelines and water intakes, stain the water brown nearby, and decompose. That decomposition could consume oxygen and cause localized fish stress, bad smells, bacterial growth, and nutrient pulses, especially in shallower areas like Lake Erie. Cleanup would be annoying and expensive.

But on the scale of the whole Great Lakes system, all the world’s annual tea production is surprisingly small. It would make a mess where you dumped it, but it would not turn the Great Lakes into tea, noticeably heat them, or make them caffeinated in any meaningful human sense.

items.question: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?
human_answers: It would be a huge pile, but human viruses would make up only a tiny fraction of it. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, has killed tens of millions of people worldwide, and over 30 million people are currently living with HIV.
items.original_question: 如果世界上的所有病毒都集中到一个区域会怎样？它们会占据多少体积以及它们会是什么样子？
items.model_answer:
If all the world’s viruses were magically gathered into one place, the result would not be a planet-sized blob or an instant “super-plague.” It would be a large but finite mass of microscopic particles, mostly harmless to humans, but ecologically disastrous.

Earth is estimated to contain roughly \(10^{31}\) virus particles. Most are bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria and archaea, especially in oceans, soils, and sediments. If packed tightly, all those virions might occupy on the order of a few cubic kilometers, perhaps a cube roughly 1–2 km on a side, depending on average virus size and packing. Their total mass could be billions of tonnes, comparable to a large mountain or a small lake’s worth of material, but not enough to noticeably affect Earth’s gravity.

The pile itself would not crawl, spread, or reproduce. Viruses cannot multiply without host cells. A sealed container full of every virus on Earth would mostly be an enormous biochemical archive: protein shells, genetic material, and lipid envelopes. Many viruses would degrade over time from heat, drying, UV light, chemical decay, and lack of suitable hosts.

It would still be extremely dangerous if uncontained. The human-infecting fraction would be tiny compared with the total, but it would include every known and unknown human pathogen, including respiratory, blood-borne, gastrointestinal, and neurological viruses. Anyone exposed through inhalation, wounds, mucous membranes, contaminated water, or animal vectors could face multiple infections. However, even then, most viruses in the pile would be unable to infect human cells because viruses are usually highly host-specific.

The larger catastrophe would come from removing viruses from everywhere else. Viruses are central to ecosystems. In the oceans, bacteriophages kill vast numbers of microbes every day, recycling nutrients and controlling bacterial populations. In soil, they shape microbial communities. In animals, plants, fungi, and bacteria, they influence evolution, immunity, population balance, and gene transfer. Suddenly removing all viruses would disrupt microbial food webs, nutrient cycles, carbon cycling, algal blooms, bacterial populations, and probably global ecosystems. Some diseases would vanish temporarily, but the biosphere would be thrown badly out of balance.

So the short answer is: gathered together, all the world’s viruses would form a surprisingly small “mountain” of microscopic particles, mostly incapable of infecting humans, but potentially the worst biohazard ever created. The place they were gathered would be dangerous; the rest of the world, suddenly virus-free, might suffer even more because viruses are deeply woven into Earth’s ecology.

items.question: What If You Tried to Catch a Bullet after It Slowed Down?
human_answers: Yes. The "bullet catch" is a common magic trick in which a magician appears to catch a fired bullet in mid-flight—often between their teeth.
items.original_question: 有没有什么方法可以让枪射击后子弹飞到空中，然后可以安全地用手接住？例如射手位于海平面，捕手位于山上，位于枪的最远射程处。
items.model_answer:
If a bullet has truly slowed to a harmless speed, then yes: it’s just a small piece of metal, and you could catch or pick it up.

But if you mean a real bullet in flight that has “slowed down” from air resistance, trying to catch it barehanded would still be a bad idea. Bullets are small, dense, and often still moving very fast. Even after losing much of their muzzle speed, they can carry enough energy to break skin, damage fingers, or penetrate flesh because the force is concentrated on a tiny area.

For example, a 9 mm bullet is only about 7–8 grams. At muzzle speed it has hundreds of joules of energy. Even slowed to 50 m/s, it still has around 10 joules, delivered through a small hard object; that can hurt badly and may injure you. A falling bullet that was fired upward may reach terminal velocity on the way down, often around tens to over 100 m/s depending on shape and tumbling, so it can still be dangerous.

The only moment when a bullet fired straight up is momentarily “stopped” is at the top of its trajectory, but that point is high in the air and lasts an instant. You could not practically stand there and pluck it out of the air, and once it starts falling again it quickly becomes hazardous.

So the short answer is: in principle, yes, if it has been slowed to roughly hand-safe speeds. In any realistic “bullet still flying” situation, no—you should not try to catch it.

items.question: What If Astronauts Tried to Reach the Moon by Hitting Golf Balls in Orbit?
human_answers: It depends how good your swing is. That sounds glib, but it's sort of true.
items.original_question: 假设你有一艘绕地球轨道运行的宇宙飞船，你能通过向另一个方向击打高尔夫球来推动你的飞船达到超过逃逸速度的速度吗？如果是这样，需要多少个高尔夫球才能到达月球？
items.model_answer:
They wouldn’t reach the Moon, and neither would the golf balls—assuming they start from a normal low Earth orbit like the ISS.

A golf ball hit by even an excellent golfer leaves the club at roughly 70–90 m/s, maybe less in a spacesuit. But from low Earth orbit, a ball needs about 3,100–3,200 m/s of extra speed to enter a lunar-transfer orbit. That’s over thirty times faster than a golf shot.

If an astronaut hit the ball forward along the direction of orbit, it would just enter a slightly higher elliptical Earth orbit. From ISS altitude, a 90 m/s hit would raise the ball’s farthest point by only a few hundred kilometers, nowhere near the Moon’s ~384,000 km distance. If hit backward, it could lower its orbit enough to reenter the atmosphere and burn up.

Using golf balls as propulsion for the astronaut would also be hopeless. A golf ball has a mass of only about 46 grams, so each hit gives a tiny recoil. And because the “exhaust velocity” of golf balls is only tens of meters per second, the rocket-equation mass requirement to reach lunar-transfer speed would be absurdly large.

So the result would be space debris, not a lunar mission. To reach the Moon from Earth orbit, you need a rocket burn, not a golf swing.

items.question: How Powerful Would Radar Have to Be to Stop a Speeding Car?
human_answers: Radio waves exert force on things. Not a lot of force.
items.original_question: 我偶尔会在限速标志上看到“雷达强制执行”，我不禁要问：无线电波必须有多强才能阻止汽车超速，如果尝试这样做会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
To stop a car with radar, the radar would have to push on it using radiation pressure. That requires enormous power.

For electromagnetic radiation,

\[
F \approx \frac{P}{c}
\]

if the beam is absorbed, or

\[
F \approx \frac{2P}{c}
\]

if it reflects perfectly, where \(P\) is the power hitting the car and \(c\) is the speed of light.

Take a typical car:

\[
m \approx 1500\ \text{kg}
\]

moving at highway speed:

\[
v \approx 30\ \text{m/s}
\]

Its momentum is

\[
mv \approx 45{,}000\ \text{kg m/s}
\]

To remove that momentum using radiation, the beam must deliver energy roughly

\[
E \approx mvc \approx 1.3 \times 10^{13}\ \text{J}
\]

if absorbed, or about half that if perfectly reflected.

So if you wanted to stop the car in 1 second, the radar power hitting the car would need to be about

\[
P \approx 10^{13}\ \text{W}
\]

or around 10 terawatts. If you allow a few seconds, it is still several terawatts.

That is comparable to a large fraction of total human electrical power production. A normal police radar gun emits something like milliwatts to watts, so this would require roughly 10 trillion to 100 trillion times more power.

In practice, such a “radar” would not gently stop the car. It would dump kiloton-scale explosive energy into or around it, ionize the air, create plasma, and likely destroy the car and everything nearby. So the answer is: radar could stop a speeding car in principle via radiation pressure, but it would need terawatt-scale power, making it catastrophically destructive rather than a practical braking tool.

items.question: What If All the CO2 in Bottled Soda Were Released into the Atmosphere?
human_answers: For most of the history of civilization, there were about 270 parts per million of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. In the last hundred years, industrial activity has pushed that number up (http://www.skepticalscience.com/print.php?r=45) to 400 parts per m...
items.original_question: 全球瓶装碳酸饮料库存中含有多少 CO 2？需要多少苏打水才能使大气中的CO 2 恢复到工业化前的水平？
items.model_answer:
If all the CO₂ dissolved in bottled soda were suddenly released into the atmosphere, the climate effect would be essentially negligible.

A typical liter of soda contains about 5–8 grams of dissolved CO₂, depending on carbonation level. Global carbonated soft drink production is on the order of hundreds of billions of liters per year. Even if we generously counted an entire year’s worth of soda and released all its CO₂, that would be roughly 1–2 million metric tons of CO₂.

For comparison:

Human activity emits about 37 billion metric tons of CO₂ per year.

One atmospheric ppm of CO₂ is about 7.8 billion metric tons of CO₂.

So soda CO₂ from a full year of production would raise atmospheric CO₂ by only about 0.0001–0.0003 ppm, far below measurable significance globally.

If you mean only the soda currently sitting in bottles and cans at one time, the amount would be even smaller, likely a tiny fraction of that.

Locally, opening huge quantities of soda at once could produce foam, pressure release, and in enclosed spaces a possible CO₂ buildup hazard. But for the atmosphere as a whole, releasing all the CO₂ in bottled soda would make no meaningful difference to climate or global CO₂ concentration.

items.question: What If I Threw a Tungsten Countertop into the Sun?
human_answers: Not very far. With its high melting point, tungsten is a good[1]Except that the word "good" implies that you have some kind of goal you're working toward, which—given how strange the thing you're doing is—I'm not sure about.
items.original_question: 如果我把钨制台面扔进太阳里，它会下降多远？
items.model_answer:
If you somehow put a tungsten countertop on a collision course with the Sun, it would not survive as a countertop. It would melt, vaporize, and become a tiny amount of tungsten plasma mixed into the Sun’s outer layers.

Tungsten is extremely heat-resistant: it melts at about 3422°C and boils around 5555°C. The Sun’s visible “surface,” the photosphere, is about 5500°C, and the material below it gets rapidly hotter and denser. So tungsten might remain solid longer than most metals during the approach, but near the Sun it would melt, then boil away and ionize. The Sun has no solid surface for it to hit; it would plunge into hot gas.

A typical tungsten countertop would be very heavy. For example, a slab a few meters long and a few centimeters thick could easily weigh around a tonne, because tungsten is about 19 times denser than water. Falling into the Sun, it would hit the solar atmosphere at hundreds of kilometers per second. Its kinetic energy might be comparable to tens of tons of TNT, but that is absurdly tiny compared with the Sun’s energy output. The Sun emits about 3.8 × 10²⁶ joules every second, so the countertop’s impact would be completely negligible.

Locally, it might make a brief tiny flash or disturbance as it ablated and vaporized, but it would be far too small to matter astronomically. The tungsten atoms would become ionized, mix with the solar plasma, and eventually be just an immeasurably small addition to the Sun’s “metal” content.

So the direct answer is: it would melt and vaporize before or as it entered the Sun, add a minuscule amount of tungsten to the solar plasma, and have no meaningful effect on the Sun.

items.question: What If Earth Spun Fast Enough for a Day to Last One Second?
human_answers: If this is going to happen, I hope it doesn't happen late in the afternoon next Friday. The Earth rotates,[citation needed (https://web.archive.org/web/20151210155028/http://www.timecube.com/)] which means its midsection is being flung outward by centrifuga...
items.original_question: 如果地球自转加速到一天只持续一秒钟会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If Earth completed one rotation every one second, it would not remain a planet. It would tear itself apart almost immediately.

A one-second day means an angular speed of about \(2\pi\) radians per second. At the equator, Earth’s surface would move at roughly:

\[
v = \frac{40{,}000\ \text{km}}{1\ \text{s}} \approx 40{,}000\ \text{km/s}
\]

That is about 13% the speed of light. For comparison, Earth’s current equatorial speed is only about 0.46 km/s.

The required centripetal acceleration at the equator would be:

\[
a = \omega^2 R \approx 2.5 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s}^2
\]

That is about 25 million times Earth’s gravity. Gravity is nowhere near strong enough to hold the planet together under those conditions.

In fact, Earth would start shedding material long before reaching a one-second rotation period. The rough “breakup” rotation period, where centrifugal effects at the equator match gravity, is around 80–90 minutes, not one second. Faster than that, material at the equator would become effectively weightless and then be flung outward. At a one-second day, the surface, oceans, atmosphere, crust, and mantle would be violently ejected into space.

The rotational energy would also be enormous, vastly exceeding Earth’s gravitational binding energy. That means the planet would not merely deform into an oblate spheroid; it would be catastrophically disrupted. Much of Earth would become an expanding cloud, ring, or disk of superheated debris and vaporized rock. The atmosphere and oceans would be lost immediately. No structure, life, or recognizable surface could survive.

So the direct answer is: if Earth spun fast enough for a day to last one second, Earth would disintegrate. It would not have “extreme weather” or “short days”; it would cease to be a coherent planet.

items.question: What If Rain Broke a Windshield before Speed Did?
human_answers: Fast. [Image: image] Raindrops are tiny.
items.original_question: 如果下雨的话，挡风玻璃会被雨打碎，你需要以多快的速度行驶？
items.model_answer:
If rain broke a windshield before “speed” did, the failure would be from localized high-speed raindrop impacts, not from the average force of the rain.

At ordinary car speeds, rain is nowhere close to breaking glass. Even in a violent storm, the total mass of water in the air is tiny compared with the mass of air hitting the car, so rain adds very little overall pressure. The windshield survives because each drop spreads, splashes, and transfers only a small impulse.

But as speed rises into the hundreds of meters per second, raindrops stop behaving like harmless drops. They become tiny high-speed water projectiles. Water is about 800 times denser than air, so a droplet impact can create very large local pressures even when the overall aerodynamic pressure is still modest. Around transonic aircraft-like speeds, roughly a few hundred m/s, heavy rain can pit, craze, erode, or crack exposed materials. This is why high-speed aircraft and missiles care about rain erosion.

A normal car windshield in such a scenario would probably not “pop” cleanly from rain like in a movie. It would first become damaged and opaque: pitted, abraded, and spiderweb-cracked by repeated impacts. Since automotive windshield glass is laminated, it would tend to crack and hold together for a while rather than explode inward immediately. Eventually, enough cracks or delamination would let air and water tear it apart.

So the careful answer is: in normal conditions, rain will not break a windshield before speed-related forces do. But at very high speeds, especially several hundred m/s in heavy rain, raindrop impacts can plausibly damage or break glass before the steady air pressure alone would crush it. At that point, however, the vehicle itself would already be in aircraft/missile territory, and many other parts would be failing too.

items.question: What If You Drank the Blood of a Drunk Person?
human_answers: You would have to drink a lot of blood. A person contains about 5 liters of blood, or 14 glasses.
items.original_question: 喝醉人的血会醉吗？
items.model_answer:
If you drank the blood of a drunk person, you would almost certainly not get drunk from it.

Alcohol in blood is much more dilute than in alcoholic drinks. For example, a legally drunk person at 0.08% BAC has about 0.8 grams of alcohol per liter of blood. Even someone very intoxicated at 0.30% BAC has about 3 grams per liter. A standard drink contains about 14 grams of alcohol, so you would need to drink several liters of that person’s blood to get the alcohol equivalent of one drink, which is unrealistic and dangerous.

The bigger concern is not alcohol; it is disease and toxicity risk. Drinking blood can expose you to blood-borne infections such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and other pathogens, especially if you have cuts in your mouth, gum disease, ulcers, or other mucosal injury. Blood can also irritate the stomach and cause nausea or vomiting, and ingesting larger amounts can cause gastrointestinal problems.

So the direct answer is: you probably would not become drunk, but you could get sick or expose yourself to serious infections. If this happened in real life, especially with someone whose infection status is unknown, it would be wise to contact a medical professional or poison control for guidance.

items.question: How Many Birds Would It Take to Collapse into a Giant Bird Ball?
human_answers: The video shows starlings, birds which ... • gather in giant flocks of sometimes more than a million animals • can talk (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VZYG00_qvE) • sound like R2-D2, though not as much as bobolinks (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ABjBl...
items.original_question: 我在观看这段视频时想知道：需要多少只鸟才能让重力接管并迫使它们变成一个巨大的鸟球？
items.model_answer:
There is no single exact threshold, but with reasonable assumptions the answer is about \(10^{17}\) pigeon-sized birds.

Treat the birds as water-density material, \(\rho \sim 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3\), and ask when the self-gravity of the pile creates pressures comparable to atmospheric pressure, enough to crush/pack the birds into a self-gravitating “bird ball.” For a uniform sphere,

\[
P_c \approx \frac{2\pi}{3}G\rho^2R^2 .
\]

Setting \(P_c \sim 10^5\ \text{Pa}\) gives

\[
R \sim 3\times 10^4\ \text{m},
\]

so the bird ball would be tens of kilometers across. Its mass would be

\[
M \sim \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3\rho \sim 10^{17}\ \text{kg}.
\]

For a \(0.3\ \text{kg}\) pigeon,

\[
N \sim \frac{10^{17}}{0.3} \sim 3\times 10^{17}
\]

birds.

So, order of magnitude: a few hundred quadrillion birds. If you used chickens, it would be more like \(10^{16}\)–\(10^{17}\); if sparrows, closer to \(10^{18}\). If you meant collapse into a black hole, the number would be vastly larger, around \(10^{39}\) birds.

items.question: What If All the Water on Earth Vanished?
human_answers: As is often the case with these questions, everyone would die. The first people to notice would be swimmers and boaters, for obvious reasons.
items.original_question: 如果地球上所有的水体都神奇地消失了，会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If all the water on Earth vanished instantly, Earth would become a dead, dry rocky planet almost immediately.

The oceans, lakes, rivers, glaciers, groundwater, clouds, and atmospheric water vapor would disappear. About 71% of Earth’s surface would suddenly be exposed as ocean basin, including vast muddy or salty seafloors that would quickly dry out. Sea level would drop to essentially nothing, revealing deep trenches, mid-ocean ridges, and continental shelves.

If the water inside living organisms also vanished, nearly all life would die at once. Humans and animals are mostly water, so they would not merely become thirsty; their cells, blood, and organs would collapse chemically and physically. Plants, microbes, fungi, and marine life would also die. If only environmental water vanished but body water remained, life would still die very quickly from dehydration, heat stress, ecosystem collapse, and lack of food.

The atmosphere would remain mostly in place because it is mainly nitrogen and oxygen, not water vapor. But there would be no clouds, no rain, no snow, no oceans to moderate temperature, and no water cycle. Weather would not stop entirely—winds and dust storms would still happen because the Sun would heat the surface unevenly—but Earth would become far drier and more temperature-extreme. Days could become very hot in many regions, while nights would become much colder, especially without humid air and clouds to trap heat.

The climate system would collapse into something more like a harsher version of Mars, though Earth would still have a thicker atmosphere and stronger gravity. Without oceans, Earth would lose its main heat reservoir and its main carbon dioxide buffer. The ocean currently absorbs enormous amounts of heat and CO₂; without it, atmospheric chemistry and surface temperatures would change dramatically.

Geologically, the disappearance of ocean water would reduce Earth’s mass slightly, but not enough to drastically change its orbit or gravity. However, removing the weight of the oceans would let oceanic crust rebound upward, causing major earthquakes and crustal adjustments. Over longer timescales, plate tectonics could weaken or change because water helps rocks melt, deform, and subduct. A completely dry Earth would likely become more geologically stagnant over time.

Photosynthesis would cease because plants and algae need water. Oxygen would not disappear immediately, but with life gone and no photosynthesis replacing it, atmospheric oxygen would slowly be consumed by oxidation and chemical reactions over long timescales.

In short: Earth would not explode, fly out of orbit, or instantly lose its atmosphere. But it would become uninhabitable almost immediately. The biosphere would collapse, the oceans would be replaced by dry basins, weather would become dusty and waterless, and over geological time Earth would become a dry, lifeless rocky world.

items.question: How Long Could Humanity Survive on Cannibalism Alone?
human_answers: There are about 500 trillion calories of human in the world. If it could be frozen or otherwise preserved, that would be enough—at least in terms of raw calories—to keep a tiny breeding population (http://www.newscientist.com/article/dn1936-magic-number-for...
items.original_question: 人类仅靠同类相食还能生存多久？
items.model_answer:
Humanity could not survive indefinitely on cannibalism alone. Humans do not create food energy; they only store a limited amount of it in body tissue. Once other food sources disappear, cannibalism is just spending down the existing human biomass.

A rough calculation gives the scale. An average human body contains about 100,000–150,000 usable food calories, while a living person needs roughly 2,000 calories per day. So one dead person would feed one living person for only about 50–75 days.

With about 8 billion people alive, feeding everyone by cannibalism would initially require on the order of 100–150 million bodies per day. As the population shrank, fewer people would need feeding, so the decline would be exponential rather than simply linear. In an idealized model with perfect use of every corpse, no spoilage, no disease, no conflict, and enough water, the time until only one person remained would be roughly:

\[
\frac{100{,}000\text{–}150{,}000}{2{,}000} \times \ln(8\times10^9)
\]

That works out to about 3–5 years.

In reality it would be much shorter, because bodies spoil, not all tissue is usable, distribution would be impossible, disease and violence would explode, and social organization would collapse. If a small group killed and preserved billions of bodies as a stockpile, a tiny remnant could theoretically last much longer, but that requires unrealistic preservation and logistics.

So the direct answer is: as a species-wide food system, cannibalism alone would sustain humanity for only a few years at most under ideal assumptions, and probably far less in reality.

items.question: What If I Fired an Infinitely Powerful Laser into the Sky?
human_answers: A lot of the time, if a question includes the word "infinity," the answer is "an infinite amount"—when there's an answer at all. An infinitely strong laser pointer would deliver an infinite amount of energy to the air in its path, which would in turn radiat...
items.original_question: 如果我向天空中的任意一点发射无限强的激光束，会造成多少伤害？
items.model_answer:
You couldn’t get a clean “infinite laser beam” shooting into space. Long before that, the air above the laser would stop behaving like ordinary transparent air.

A sufficiently powerful laser aimed upward would ionize the atmosphere in its path, turning it into plasma. That plasma would absorb, scatter, and reflect more of the beam, rapidly heating and expanding. The result would be less like a flashlight beam into the sky and more like a vertical nuclear-scale explosion: a blinding plasma column, intense X-rays/gamma rays, a shock wave, and catastrophic heating of the nearby ground and air.

As the power rises, the damage scales upward: the atmosphere becomes an exploding fireball, the ground around the laser is vaporized, and eventually large parts of the planet could be stripped, melted, or blown off. At extreme intensities, even “empty” space is no longer empty in the usual sense; quantum effects can create particle-antiparticle pairs, and general relativity becomes important.

If you literally mean “infinitely powerful,” the question stops having a normal physical answer. Infinite power means infinite energy delivered in any finite time, which implies infinite mass-energy. In general relativity, concentrating enough energy in a region forms a black hole; with truly infinite energy, the situation is not a bigger laser beam but a breakdown of the premise. The Earth, the atmosphere, the laser, and the surrounding region would not survive as recognizable things.

So the direct answer is: a very powerful laser would explode the atmosphere and devastate the launch area; an “infinitely” powerful laser is physically impossible, and if treated literally would destroy the setup rather than send a neat beam into the sky.

items.question: What If One Person Owned All the Money in the World?
human_answers: So you've somehow found a way to gather all the world's money. We won't worry about how you did it—let's just assume you invented some kind of money-summoning magic spell.
items.original_question: 人们有时会说“如果我拥有世界上所有的钱……”来讨论如果他们没有财务限制他们会做什么。但我很好奇，如果一个人拥有世界上所有的钱，会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If one person somehow owned all the money in the world, the result would not be “one person can buy everything and everyone else is permanently poor.” More likely, the monetary system would break or be replaced.

Money is not the same as wealth. Wealth includes land, buildings, factories, machines, food, energy, intellectual property, skills, and labor. If one person owned every dollar, euro, yen, bank deposit, and coin, other people would still own homes, farms, companies, tools, and their own labor. The rich person would own all the liquid purchasing power, but not all real assets.

The immediate effect would be a liquidity crisis. Nobody else could buy goods, pay wages, repay loans, or settle taxes using money. Shops could not function normally because customers would have no cash or bank balances. Employers could not pay workers unless the one money-owner spent or lent money back into circulation. Debts would default en masse because debtors would have no money with which to pay. Banks and financial markets would likely seize up.

But the situation would be unstable. For the money to remain valuable, other people must accept it in exchange for real goods and services. If the single owner hoarded all money and refused to spend it, the economy would quickly switch to alternatives: barter, private credit, IOUs, commodity money, cryptocurrencies, local currencies, or newly issued government money. Governments and central banks could also create new currency, redenominate accounts, impose emergency taxes, freeze assets, or simply declare a new monetary system.

If the person tried to spend the money, ownership of money would immediately spread back out. Every purchase transfers money to someone else. If they bought food, land, companies, or labor, sellers would receive money. The monopoly on money would disappear unless the person somehow forced every unit of money to return to them.

If they tried to buy “everything,” prices would not stay fixed. Sellers would raise prices massively, refuse to sell, demand political protection, or ask for non-money compensation. Since real wealth is finite and socially protected, the person’s nominal money holdings would not automatically grant control over all resources.

So the most realistic answer is: the world economy would suffer a severe monetary shock, but not permanent absolute domination by one person. Either the person would have to spend or lend the money, redistributing it, or society would abandon that money and create substitutes. Money has power only while everyone else agrees to use it.

items.question: What If Everything except Earth Were Made of Antimatter?
human_answers: This one doesn't end well for us. But—unlike most scenarios involving the word "antimatter"—the end is surprisingly slow and drawn-out.
items.original_question: 如果除了地球之外一切都是反物质怎么办？
items.model_answer:
If everything except Earth were made of antimatter, Earth would not instantly blow up just because the rest of the universe is antimatter. Antimatter only annihilates with matter when they physically meet. Since space is mostly vacuum, distant anti-stars, anti-planets, and anti-galaxies would look and gravitate almost exactly like ordinary ones.

The anti-Sun would shine almost normally. Photons are their own antiparticles, so sunlight from an antimatter Sun would still be ordinary light. Earth’s orbit would be unchanged, and chemistry and gravity elsewhere would behave the same. The main difference would be in particles: the solar wind would be made of antiprotons and positrons, anti-meteorites would fall on Earth, and escaped ordinary atoms from Earth would annihilate when they met the surrounding antimatter environment.

The dangerous part is contact at Earth’s outer boundary. Antimatter solar wind, anti-dust, anti-micrometeorites, and anti-gas would annihilate in the upper atmosphere or near the magnetosphere. Each kilogram of antimatter that meets a kilogram of ordinary matter releases about

\[
2mc^2 \approx 1.8\times 10^{17}\text{ joules},
\]

roughly 43 megatons of TNT per kilogram of antimatter.

Even tiny anti-meteorites would be devastating. A gram of antimatter dust annihilating in the atmosphere would release energy comparable to a tens-of-kilotons nuclear weapon. A kilogram-scale anti-meteor would be a major thermonuclear-scale airburst. Ordinary Earth currently sweeps up cosmic dust continuously; if that dust were antimatter, the upper atmosphere would be bombarded by constant annihilation radiation.

The anti-solar wind alone could be serious. If a significant fraction reached the atmosphere, its annihilation power could be comparable to a large fraction of the sunlight Earth receives, but delivered as gamma rays, particle showers, and atmospheric ionization rather than gentle visible light. Earth’s magnetic field would deflect much of the charged anti-solar wind, but not neutral anti-dust and not all plasma leakage.

So the answer is: Earth would not vanish instantly, and the sky could initially look mostly normal, but Earth would be surrounded by a hostile antimatter environment. Continuous annihilation in the upper atmosphere from anti-solar wind, anti-dust, and anti-meteoroids would produce intense radiation, destroy atmospheric chemistry, likely strip or heat the upper atmosphere over time, and make the planet rapidly uninhabitable. Large antimatter impacts would be catastrophically explosive. The planet itself might remain gravitationally intact for a long time, but life on it would probably not survive.

items.question: What If You Teleported to the Surface of the Sun for One Nanosecond?
human_answers: Believe it or not, this wouldn't even warm you. The temperature of the surface of the Sun is about 5,800 K,[1]Or °C.
items.original_question: 当我大约 8 岁的时候，在科罗拉多州寒冷的天气里铲雪时，我希望自己能立即被传送到太阳表面，只持续一纳秒，然后立即被传送回来。我想这足以让我暖和起来，但又不足以伤害我。实际上会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If you teleported to the Sun’s “surface” — the photosphere — for exactly one nanosecond and then returned, you would almost certainly survive essentially unharmed.

The Sun has no solid surface; the photosphere is a hot, glowing gas layer at about 5,800 K. That sounds instantly fatal, but one nanosecond is so short that very little energy can actually transfer into your body.

The solar radiative flux at the photosphere is about 6 × 10⁷ W/m². Over 1 nanosecond, that is only:

6 × 10⁷ W/m² × 10⁻⁹ s ≈ 0.06 J/m²

That is tiny. Even if your whole body absorbed more than this from multiple directions, the total deposited heat would be far too small to burn you or noticeably raise your temperature. The hot gas around you also would not have time to conduct much heat into your skin; particles only travel microscopic distances in a nanosecond.

Other effects are also negligible over that time. Solar gravity is strong, about 28 times Earth gravity, but in 1 ns it would change your position by an absurdly tiny distance. Radiation pressure would not matter. You would not be vaporized, explode, or be torn apart.

The main caveats are that the photosphere is not a solid place to stand, and the details depend on what “teleporting” means — for example, whether solar gas is displaced or appears inside your body. But physically, if you simply appear at the photosphere for 1 ns and then reappear back on Earth, you would likely experience at most an incredibly brief flash of light and no significant injury.

If the duration were microseconds, milliseconds, or longer, the situation would become much more dangerous very quickly. But for one nanosecond: probably survivable.

items.question: What If Auto Racing Had Only One Rule: The Driver Must Survive?
human_answers: The best you'll be able to do is about 90 minutes. There are lots of ways you could build your vehicle—an electric car,[1]With wheels designed to dig into the pavement on turns.
items.original_question: 如果你抛开赛车比赛的所有规则，举办一场比赛，只是让一个人以尽可能快的速度绕赛道 200 倍，那么什么策略会获胜呢？假设赛车手必须生存。
items.model_answer:
If auto racing had only one rule—“the driver must survive”—it would stop looking like Formula 1 or NASCAR and become an engineering arms race somewhere between land-speed record attempts, military aerospace, and demolition derby.

The cars would quickly become less like cars and more like guided missiles with a human survival capsule inside. Designers would remove every restriction that normally keeps racing recognizable: no engine limits, no fuel limits, no aerodynamic limits, no tire rules, no crash-structure standards except whatever helps the driver live. You would see jet engines, rocket assist, active aerodynamics, fan suction, computer-controlled stability systems, exotic materials, and perhaps enclosed armored cockpits with ejection or impact capsules.

The main limit would not be horsepower. It would be human tolerance.

A human can only survive so much acceleration, braking, cornering force, vibration, and crash deceleration. In ordinary racing, rules keep speeds and cornering loads within a manageable range. With no rules, engineers would push until the driver’s body became the weak component. The driver would likely lie reclined in a pressure-suit-like capsule, with the head and spine immobilized, oxygen supplied, cooling systems installed, and the cockpit designed more like a spacecraft reentry pod than a racing seat.

On straight tracks, speeds could become enormous. Existing land-speed vehicles have already exceeded the speed of sound on land, and those are built under real-world engineering and safety constraints. With racing money and only driver survival as the rule, straight-line “cars” could plausibly reach hundreds of miles per hour routinely, and perhaps over 1,000 mph on specially prepared courses.

On circuits, the problem is harder. Corners dominate lap time, and cornering creates lateral g-forces. Even if the machine can generate absurd downforce or use fan suction to stick to the ground, the driver still has to survive the load. Sustained 5–6 g is already brutal; much beyond that becomes impractical without fighter-pilot-style support systems, and even then only for limited periods. So the track would matter enormously: a huge, gently curved course would allow far higher speeds than a tight road circuit.

The race would also become far more dangerous for everyone except, perhaps, the driver. If the only rule protects the driver, there is no rule protecting pit crews, spectators, marshals, other drivers, the environment, or the track. So unless “driver must survive” is accompanied by ordinary legal constraints, the sport becomes socially impossible. A vehicle that keeps its driver alive while disintegrating at 700 mph could still send debris for kilometers.

There is also a loophole: if “auto racing” does not require the vehicle to stay on the ground, the optimal design may become an aircraft. A winged, powered vehicle could complete many courses faster and more safely than a ground vehicle. If it must remain a ground car, then tires, surface strength, downforce, and crash survival dominate the design. If rails are allowed, it might become a train-like rocket sled. If remote control is allowed, the “driver” could sit safely somewhere else, making survival trivial—so the rule would need to specify that the driver is physically onboard.

So the direct answer is: racing would become dramatically faster, wildly more expensive, and almost unrecognizable. The winning machines would be armored human-carrying rockets optimized around g-force tolerance and crash survivability. The limiting factor would no longer be the car’s engine or the rulebook; it would be the biological fragility of the person inside.

items.question: What If Your Income Materialized around You in Cash?
human_answers: First, let's think about coins. The US federal minimum wage in the US is \$7.25/hour, which is about \$15,000/year for a full-time job.
items.original_question: 如果人们的收入以现金的形式实时出现在他们身边会怎样？你需要赚多少钱才会陷入真正的麻烦？
items.model_answer:
If your income literally materialized around you as physical cash, the main surprise is that normal income in high-denomination bills would not take up much space. The inconvenience would be security, accounting, banking, and taxes—not being buried in money.

For U.S. paper money, every bill weighs about 1 gram and has a volume of about 1.1 cubic centimeters, regardless of denomination. So if you earned $100,000 per year and it appeared as $100 bills, that would be only 1,000 bills: about 1 kilogram of paper, roughly 1.1 liters in volume, a stack about 11 cm tall. If it appeared monthly, each paycheck would be a small handful of bills.

If the same $100,000 appeared as $1 bills, it would be much more dramatic: 100,000 bills, about 100 kilograms, around 112 liters of volume, enough to fill several large trash bags and heavy enough to be dangerous if it appeared above you or in a confined space. In coins it could become genuinely hazardous; $100,000 in pennies would weigh about 25 metric tons.

At ordinary income levels, cash materializing continuously would also be underwhelming. A $100,000 annual salary is about $0.003 per second, so in $100 bills you would get one bill roughly every 8.8 hours. A median-income person would get about one $100 bill every day or two.

For very high incomes, it becomes dangerous even in $100 bills. A $10 million annual income would be 100,000 bills, weighing 100 kg and occupying about 112 liters. A $1 billion annual income in $100 bills would weigh 10 metric tons and occupy about 11 cubic meters—enough to crush you or fill a small room if it appeared all at once.

Legally and economically, it would still count as income. You would owe taxes, need to secure it, deposit it, document its origin, and avoid theft. If the cash were newly created rather than replacing bank deposits, it would also expand the money supply and, at large scale, cause inflation. If it simply replaced normal electronic payment, the macroeconomic effect would be smaller, but banks, employers, and governments would face huge cash-handling problems.

Physically, if money truly “materialized” from nothing, that violates conservation of mass-energy unless some enormous energy source is involved. But assuming magic handles that safely, the practical answer is: for most people, high-denomination cash would be manageable but annoying; low-denomination cash or extremely high income could quickly become a heavy, dangerous pile of paper or metal.

items.question: What If You Used Lasers to Evaporate the Rain before It Hit the Ground?
human_answers: Stopping rain with a laser is one of those ideas that sounds totally reasonable, but if you— [Image: image] While the idea of a laser umbrella might be appealing, it— [Image: image] Ok. The idea of stopping rain with a laser is a thing we're currently talki...
items.original_question: 用雨伞或帐篷阻止雨水落在某物上是很无聊的。如果你试图用激光来阻止雨，在每个进入的水滴到达地面十英尺之前瞄准并蒸发它，会怎么样？
items.model_answer:
In principle, yes: if you put enough laser energy into each raindrop, you can heat it to boiling and vaporize it before it reaches the ground. In practice, it would be an absurdly powerful, dangerous, and mostly self-defeating way to stay dry.

The energy requirement is huge. To turn liquid rainwater at about room temperature into water vapor takes roughly

\[
2.5 \times 10^6 \text{ joules per kilogram}
\]

including heating it up and providing the latent heat of vaporization.

A moderate rain rate of about 1 cm/hour delivers 10 kg of water per hour onto each square meter of ground. Vaporizing that requires about

\[
\frac{10 \times 2.5\times10^6}{3600} \approx 7{,}000 \text{ watts}
\]

per square meter.

So to protect an umbrella-sized area, you would need several kilowatts of perfectly absorbed laser power. For heavy rain, it could be tens of kilowatts per square meter. Protecting a house, street, or city would require power-plant-scale to civilization-scale energy.

And that assumes ideal efficiency. Real lasers would waste energy in the air, scatter off droplets, miss many drops, and create glare, heat, and hazards. A laser powerful enough to evaporate rain would also be powerful enough to blind people, burn surfaces, ignite materials, and heat the air violently.

There is another problem: evaporating the rain does not remove the water. It turns the falling drops into water vapor. In rainy weather the air is often already near saturation, so the vapor may quickly condense again into mist, fog, or new droplets. You might replace rain with hot humid air, steam, and re-forming drizzle.

So the short answer is: you could evaporate rain with lasers if you supplied enormous power, but it would be dangerous, inefficient, and likely just produce a hot cloud of humid air rather than a clean dry zone. An umbrella is vastly better.

items.question: What If Every River in America Froze in Midsummer?
human_answers: This is another question that turns out even worse than I expected. [Image: image] For starters, pretty much every animal in the water would die.
items.original_question: 如果美国所有的河流在仲夏时节立即结冰，会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If every river in America froze in midsummer, it would be a national-scale disaster, not a scenic oddity.

Assuming this means the rivers suddenly developed winter-level ice cover, transportation on major waterways such as the Mississippi, Ohio, Missouri, Columbia, and Hudson would stop immediately. Barges carrying grain, fuel, fertilizer, coal, chemicals, and construction materials would be stranded. Ports and river terminals would jam up, and supply chains would shift abruptly to rail and trucking, which could not fully replace the lost capacity.

Water supply would be one of the biggest problems. Many cities, farms, power plants, and industries draw water directly from rivers. Ice would clog intakes, damage pumps, block irrigation canals, and reduce available cooling water for power plants. Hydroelectric dams could lose flow or suffer mechanical stress from ice. Thermal and nuclear power stations near rivers might have to reduce output or shut down if cooling-water systems were compromised.

Agriculture would be hit hard because midsummer is peak growing season. Irrigated crops in the West and Midwest could lose water just when demand is highest. If the freezing were caused by an actual atmospheric cold event, crops would also suffer frost damage, potentially ruining large portions of the corn, soybean, fruit, vegetable, and hay harvests.

Ecologically, the shock would be severe. Warm-water fish, amphibians, aquatic insects, mussels, and plants would experience sudden thermal stress. Ice cover would reduce oxygen exchange, and shallow streams could become lethal quickly. Spawning cycles, migration, feeding, and riverbank ecosystems would be disrupted. If the rivers froze solid rather than merely icing over, the mortality would be catastrophic.

The thaw could be even more dangerous than the freeze. As ice broke up, it would form ice jams at bends, bridges, dams, and narrow channels. Those jams could cause sudden upstream flooding and then destructive downstream surges when they failed. Bridges, levees, docks, riverfront roads, and water-treatment infrastructure could be damaged by moving ice.

Physically, this scenario would require an enormous removal of heat from flowing water in the hottest part of the year. If only the river surfaces froze while summer air remained warm, the ice would melt quickly but still cause chaos. If the entire water columns froze, it would imply a planet-scale climate or energy anomaly far beyond ordinary weather, and the broader consequences—crop failure, infrastructure collapse, mass ecological die-off, and widespread economic disruption—would be much worse than the frozen rivers themselves.

items.question: What If You Made a Lava Lamp with Real Lava?
human_answers: This is a surprisingly reasonable idea, by What If standards. I mean, it's not that reasonable.
items.original_question: 如果我用真正的熔岩制作一盏熔岩灯会怎么样？我可以使用什么作为透明介质？我能站在多近的距离观看它？
items.model_answer:
A lava lamp made with real lava would not behave like a normal lava lamp; it would be a small furnace and an extreme explosion/fire hazard.

A normal lava lamp works because two carefully chosen liquids have similar densities and do not mix. Heat makes the wax slightly less dense, so it rises; cooling makes it sink. Real lava is molten rock at roughly 700–1,200°C, far hotter, denser, more corrosive, and much more dangerous than lamp wax.

If you put real lava into a regular lava lamp, several things would happen almost immediately: the glass would crack or soften from thermal shock, the liquid inside would violently boil, and any oil or wax would ignite or decompose. If water were present, it could flash into steam so fast that the lamp could burst or explode. The expanding gases in a sealed container would make it even more dangerous.

Even if you built a special high-temperature transparent container, it still would not look like a classic lava lamp. The lava would be much denser than most liquids, so it would sink rather than form floating blobs. Most surrounding liquids would either boil, burn, or chemically break down. The lava would also begin to cool and solidify unless continuously heated by a powerful furnace.

So the practical answer is: a “real lava lamp” would be less like a decorative lamp and more like a hazardous molten-rock experiment. It would glow, radiate intense heat, probably destroy its container if not specially engineered, and could explode if any volatile liquid or trapped gas were involved.

items.question: What If Every Child's First Laugh Created an Immortal Fairy?
human_answers: "There are always a lot of young ones," explained Wendy, who was now quite an authority, "because you see when a new baby laughs for the first time a new fairy is born, and as there are always new babies there are always new fairies. They live in nests on t...
items.original_question: 如果每个仙女都是从孩子的第一声笑声中诞生并且仙女是不朽的，那么会有多少仙女飞来飞去？
items.model_answer:
If every child’s first laugh created an immortal fairy, the biggest consequence would be that humanity would generate a permanently accumulating second population.

A child’s first real laugh usually happens around 3–4 months of age. With roughly 130–140 million births per year today, the world would create about 130–140 million new fairies every year. If this had been true for all of human history, there would likely be on the order of 100 billion fairies already, roughly comparable to the total number of humans who have ever lived.

The physical impact depends on what “fairy” means. If fairies are nonmaterial magical beings that do not eat, breathe, occupy space, or consume energy, then the main effects would be cultural, religious, legal, and psychological. Every baby’s first laugh would become an event of enormous importance. Families might celebrate it like a birth, governments might register fairies, and societies would form entire institutions around fairy rights, fairy duties, and fairy-human relationships.

If fairies are physical beings, the consequences become much more serious. Immortality means their population never decreases, so even a small annual addition eventually becomes enormous. If each fairy had mass, needed food, used energy, or occupied living space, Earth would face a steadily worsening resource burden. A population of 100 billion tiny beings might be manageable if they were insect-sized and low-energy, but disastrous if they were human-sized or metabolically active. Even at modest energy use, billions of immortal beings could consume a significant fraction of global resources.

Scientifically, the creation event would violate ordinary conservation laws unless the fairy’s matter and energy came from somewhere. If each laugh literally produced mass from nothing, physics would need a new mechanism allowing sound, emotion, or neurological development to trigger matter creation. If the fairy’s body were assembled from surrounding air, dust, or some hidden energy field, then researchers would intensely study first laughter as a reproducible matter-generation event.

Socially, birth rates would take on a new meaning. Having children would not only create humans but also immortal fairies, so population ethics would change. Pronatalist societies might value fairy creation; others might worry about immortal overpopulation. There could be debates over whether delaying or suppressing a baby’s first laugh was ethical. Children who never laughed because of illness, neglect, or developmental differences might be treated with tragic or mystical significance, which could create harmful stigma unless societies were careful.

Over long timescales, immortality is the central problem. Human populations rise and fall, but fairy populations would only rise. After thousands or millions of years, unless fairies could leave Earth, enter dormancy, shrink their footprint, or exist outside normal ecology, their accumulation would dominate the biosphere. The world would eventually become less a human planet than a fairy-human civilization shaped by every baby’s first joy.

So the direct answer is: every child’s first laugh creating an immortal fairy would turn laughter into a biological-cosmic reproduction mechanism. In the short term it would make infancy sacred and socially transformative; in the long term it would create an ever-growing immortal population whose impact would range from harmlessly mystical to ecologically catastrophic depending on whether fairies need matter, space, and energy.

items.question: What If There Were a Lake on the Moon?
human_answers: This would be so cool. In fact, I honestly think it's cool enough that it gives us a pretty good reason to go to the Moon in the first place.
items.original_question: 如果月球上有一个湖会怎样？在里面游泳会是什么感觉？假设它被隐藏在一个规则的大气层中，比如某个巨大的圆顶或其他什么地方。
items.model_answer:
An exposed liquid lake on the Moon would not remain a lake for long.

Because the Moon has essentially no atmosphere, the pressure at the surface is near vacuum. Liquid water is not stable under those conditions. If you somehow placed a lake of liquid water on the lunar surface, the top layer would begin to boil rapidly, even if the water were cold, because there is almost no air pressure holding it in liquid form. That boiling would carry away heat, so the remaining water would quickly cool and start to freeze. The result would be a violent mix of boiling, vapor, frost, and ice.

After the initial chaos, the lake would mostly become ice. Any exposed ice would slowly sublimate: it would turn directly from solid into vapor, especially in sunlight. Some of that water vapor would escape into space, while some molecules might hop across the lunar surface and eventually collect in very cold, permanently shadowed craters near the poles. In direct sunlight, the ice would disappear much faster; in a permanently shadowed crater, it could survive for a very long time as ice, but not as an open liquid lake.

If the lake were inside a sealed dome with Earth-like air pressure and temperature, then it could exist as a normal liquid lake. It would still feel “lunar” in some ways: gravity is only about one-sixth of Earth’s, so waves would move more slowly, splashes would rise higher, and objects would feel lighter. Boats would float similarly in terms of how much of them sits above water, because both weight and buoyancy scale with gravity, but motions on and in the water would be slower and more exaggerated.

So the direct answer is: an open lake on the Moon would boil, freeze, and gradually vanish into space or migrate as ice to cold traps. A lasting liquid lake would require an artificial atmosphere or enclosure.

items.question: What If You Dropped a 7-Kilogram Bowling Ball into the Mariana Trench?
human_answers: It is a good thing you mentioned the weight, because of a very surprising fact: Most bowling balls float. It's true.
items.original_question: 您正坐在马里亚纳海沟上方的船上。如果将一个 7 公斤重的保龄球从侧面掉下来，需要多长时间才能落到底部？
items.model_answer:
A 7‑kilogram bowling ball would sink to the bottom of the Mariana Trench, but not dramatically fast.

A regulation bowling ball is about 22 cm in diameter. At 7 kg, its average density is greater than seawater, so buoyancy would not hold it up. After hitting the water, drag would quickly slow it to a terminal sinking speed of roughly 1–2 m/s, depending on the exact ball, finger holes, surface roughness, and water density. Since the Challenger Deep is about 11 km deep, the trip to the bottom would take on the order of 2–3 hours.

The pressure at the bottom is enormous: about 110 megapascals, or roughly 1,100 atmospheres. But pressure acts from all directions, so the ball would not be “squashed flat” like in a cartoon. A typical solid bowling ball would compress slightly, perhaps by millimeters to a few percent in volume depending on its material. If it had trapped air pockets or sealed cavities, those could collapse or crack the ball. Open finger holes would simply fill with water.

When it reached the seafloor, it would not hit like a meteor. At terminal speed its kinetic energy would be only a few to perhaps tens of joules, so it would make a small puff in the sediment and settle there.

So the short answer is: it would sink slowly for a few hours, compress slightly under the immense pressure, maybe crack if it contained trapped air, and then come to rest on the trench floor.

items.question: What If There Were Both a Space Elevator and a Stairway to Space?
human_answers: A week or two, if you're a champion stair-climber. Or 12 hours if you're on a motorcycle.
